News.title: Kenyan authorities scramble to find passengers on Ebola flight
News.content:
Authorities are racing to track down passengers who boarded a flight from Uganda to Kenya on Saturday alongside a man infected with Ebola.

The man travelled by bus from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the epicentre of an Ebola outbreak that has killed 4,000 people, to Kampala, Uganda. He then boarded a flight to Nairobi on Saturday, October 3, which was operated by the African airline Jambojet.

The patient went to a hospital in Nairobi and died just 48 hours later, meaning the journey took place in the final days of infection, the stage at which patients who die of the disease are most contagious. By October 6 authorities had tracked down 28 contacts, including family members of the deceased, but said they urgently needed to track down 23 passengers and crew who had travelled on the same flight.

The man is Kenya’s first ever case of the disease. Ebola does not typically spread through the air like Covid-19 or measles, requiring close contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person to spread. However, an aeroplane cabin significantly intensifies these risks because passengers share cramped spaces for prolonged periods and touch the same surfaces, such as a cabin toilet.

“We are working closely with the Ministry of Health, Port Health Services and other relevant authorities to support the ongoing public health response, including the identification and management of the other guests and crew who may have been in contact with the individual,” a spokesperson for Jambojet said on Tuesday.

After landing in Kenya, airport staff screened the patient, standard protocol for people travelling from at-risk countries during the current Ebola outbreak, but allowed him to continue his journey into Nairobi.

Kenya’s health ministry director-general, Patrick Amoth, said the patient may have passed through airport screening because medication had masked his symptoms.

News.title: Africa embraces ‘Go to Work on an Egg’ to boost maternal health and nutrition
News.content:
The sun is barely up when villagers start queuing for eggs at the metal gate of Shamim Haried’s home.

By noon, all that day’s supply is usually sold out, but people keep coming and asking if there are any left.

Demand is so high that arguments can break out in the queue, says the mother-of-two who lives outside Malawi’s capital, Lilongwe.

Her eggs are cheaper and fresher than those sold in the market.

“The people almost fight for eggs: it’s hard to watch,” she explains.

“Eggs are the cheapest healthy protein that they can get and it’s better for them to buy here than anywhere else.”

Her flock of 1,400 chickens lay around 1,000 eggs each day, but she reckons she could sell three times that.

News.title: What is pneumonic plague? Symptoms and how it spreads
News.content:
The death of a researcher at a plague laboratory in Siberia has prompted the World Health Organization to press Moscow for answers.

Russian officials have yet to share details of what caused the worker’s illness, and this information vacuum has fuelled speculation.

But what is the disease, and how much of a threat does it pose?

What is pneumonic plague?

Plague is a rare and serious infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals such as rodents and their fleas. Pneumonic plague is the most virulent of plague’s three forms, and is a severe infection of the lungs.

The other types are bubonic plague – the Black Death that laid waste to much of Europe during the Middle Ages – which attacks the lymph nodes, and septicaemic plague, which attacks the blood. Either can develop into the pneumonic form if the infection spreads.

Pneumonic plague is rarer than the bubonic form, but more dangerous.

Each year, the world records an estimated 1,000 to 3,000 plague cases of all types, though the number fluctuates.

Most cases are bubonic, and spread by the bite of an infected flea, and most occur in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of Congo. But infections are also found in countries including Russia, India, China and the United States.

News.title: Weight loss jabs are safe for obese teenagers, WHO announces
News.content:
Obese teenagers can safely be given weight-loss drugs and undergo bariatric surgery, the World Health Organization (WHO) has said.

The recommendations form part of the first set of global guidelines released by the WHO for the treatment of obese children and adolescents.

Previously, the WHO only recommended weight-loss drugs like Mounjaro and Wegovy and bariatric surgery, which alters the stomach and reduces appetite, for the treatment of obese adults – defined as someone with a body mass index of 30 or above.

However, the new guidelines say children over the age of 10 can safely be given the drugs, as well as undergo weight-loss surgery, if all other options, like managed exercise and diet programmes, have been exhausted. Children under that age should not be given drugs or surgery.

Obese children in the UK are currently not eligible for weight-loss drugs or surgery on the NHS, although specialised clinics may offer them to children over 12 under very strict conditions.

The WHO recommends first and foremost that obese children and teenagers undertake a structured diet programme and physical activity, which for children over five should include an average of at least 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous activity across the week.

According to Unicef an estimated 188 million children and adolescents are obese, and last year, the number of overweight children exceeded the number of underweight children for the first time in history.

While obesity rates are beginning to plateau in many rich countries, childhood obesity is rising rapidly in the developing world, including in sub-Saharan Africa, which is home to nearly a quarter of the world’s overweight children.

The drivers of obesity are complex, but experts believe a switch from traditional, fibre-rich diets to cheap, high-fat, high-sugar food has played a significant role in growing global obesity rates.

Obesity at any age carries significant health risks – but the consequences are thought to be more acute if obesity begins in childhood, accelerating the development of severe and life-threatening conditions, including type-2 diabetes, cardiovascular dysfunction, and liver disease.

The WHO guidelines also emphasise the importance of addressing mental health issues that are often associated with obesity and contribute to unhealthy eating patterns – including anxiety and depression, low self-esteem, and bullying.

“Our priority must be to ensure that every child and adolescent can access quality care and supportive environments from an early age, helping them achieve and maintain a healthy weight and laying the foundation for lifelong health and well-being,” Dr Luz María De Regil, Director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, WHO.

News.title: Russia’s plague shouldn’t scare us – its secretive bioweapons should
News.content:
The facts about the laboratory accident in Russia are scant.

A lab technician at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Siberia is dead, 200 people have been quarantined, and the state security services are saying “nothing to see here, folks”.

Denials from the country that has run a covert biological weapons programme since the Cold War have done nothing to quieten speculation about what is really going on in the vast Siberian tundra.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, demanded on Tuesday that Russia be “transparent” about the situation, which he said Washington was monitoring “very closely”.

“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Mr Rubio said during a trip to Iceland.

A death from plague is a tragedy, but should not be something we need to worry about. We have moved on from the Middle Ages, when the Black Death laid waste to much of Europe.

It’s treatable with antibiotics and does not spread as fast as diseases like Covid. Its replication or R number does not get above 1.5 – measles, for example, has an R number of 12 to 18.

News.title: Kane’s record-equalling cap was no different to his first
News.content:
One expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

“Availability,” he said, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

No team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. Another great performance from Jude Bellingham and also from Morgan Rogers, in place of Bukayo Saka. Another dominant Elliot Anderson performance in midfield. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

England kept the ball with such authority, and none more so than Bellingham. Trent Alexander-Arnold came back at right-back. Myles Lewis-Skelly returned for another bite at a Wembley midfield job. As in Prague last week, there was a self-inflicted Czech calamity in the first half. The captain Vladimir Coufal appeared to lose his cool at the threat of the England attack all over the Czechs’ half. No other reason for this Premier League experienced full-back to fling himself at Kane’s cross and drill the ball past Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek on 27 minutes.

Tielemans was one of several players who was in the hot seat for the question, alongside Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Andrey Santos, Carlos Baleba, Ayden Heaven and Matheus Cunha.

What many people don’t remember, however, is that the 59-year-old was once on the path hoping to land medals for Great Britain.

Sports.title: Sir Alex Ferguson reveals emotional moment he broke down in tears after telling Man Utd stars he was retiring
Sports.content:
Next

SIR ALEX Ferguson cried after he told his Manchester United players he would be stepping down as manager in May 2013.

News of Ferguson’s impending exit leaked on the Tuesday night before he gathered the United squad and his backroom staff at their Carrington training complex on the Wednesday morning.



Ferguson writes in Games of My Life.: “It wasn’t until I got back to the office and shut the door that everything caught up with me; I just sat at my desk and cried.

“After I wiped my eyes, I thought I had better clear out quickly before the news was made public. The last thing I wanted was to have to deal with the press.”



Before his final match in charge at West Brom – a 5-5 draw – United players presented Ferguson with a scrapbook charting his career and a Rolex watch with “Thanks for everything” inscribed on it.

Having penned two autobiographies, two seasonal diaries in the Nineties, a book on his first six years in charge of United and a study in leadership, Ferguson has released a seventh book at the age of 84.



His latest memoir sees him pick the 21 matches that have meant the most to him, dating back to his schoolboy days in Glasgow.

Ferguson also wonders what might have materialised had his New York dinner with future Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola in September 2012 taken place two months earlier.

Guardiola had started a year-long sabbatical after his departure as Barcelona coach and Ferguson claims the Catalan had already agreed to take over at Bayern Munich in the summer of 2013.

Fergie wrote: “If I could rewind time, we would have dined some months earlier, I would have poured plenty of Tignanello and I would have tried my hardest to convince him that his future lay in Manchester.



“Unfortunately for us, it did. Enough said.”

In his previous book, Leading, Ferguson suggested that Guardiola had not “signed on the dotted line” with Bayern, writing: “I asked Pep to phone me before he accepted an offer from another club, but he didn’t and wound up joining Bayern Munich in July 2013.”

The death of Ferguson’s sister-in-law, Bridget, in October 2012 convinced him to retire at the end of that season and he informed his late wife, Lady Cathy, around Christmas time.



The book is dedicated to Lady Cathy, who passed away in October 2023.

Ferguson mentions United’s owners, the Glazers, only once in the 336 pages but there is no mention of co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who stripped Ferguson of his £2million-a-year ambassadorial role.

However, Fergie does muse on the current United structure of a chief executive and director of football above the head coach.

He writes: “I suppose the owners like the idea of a ‘coach’ because he, in their minds, is just one part of a bigger machine.

“If he goes, the machine is intact – or, at least, that’s the theory.



“Even though at the big clubs, the authority has moved away from the touchline to the sporting director or football CEO, in the eyes of the press and the fans, it remains the head coach who shoulders the responsibility if things go wrong.”

Ferguson pointedly stresses: “Formidable, sustainable financial strength is closely correlated with success on the pitch.”

United’s debt now stands at £1.15BILLION.



The Scot also offers an olive branch to Roy Keane, his captain at United for more than eight years.

Ferguson and Keane have never repaired their relationship since the former midfielder was unceremoniously sacked by United in November 2005, and they have barely spoken since Keane’s stint as Sunderland manager ended in 2008.

United’s 3-2 comeback triumph at Juventus in the 1999 Champions League semi-final, one of Ferguson’s defining games, is best remembered for Keane’s Herculean performance, which the Scot dwells on again.

Ferguson says: “I know Roy isn’t an attention-seeker and shrugs off the praise that others heap on him.

“He poured every ounce of his being into that game. It was his greatest night in red.



“For as long as tales are told about the exploits of United, Roy’s performance amid the smoke flares and drumming of the Stadio Delle Alpi is one that will stay with me for ever and deserves to be passed down through the generations.”

“Fergie time” is referred to nine times by Ferguson: “The words ‘The fourth official has indicated there will be a minimum of . . .’ are among my favourite in the English language.”

He fondly recalls Michael Owen’s 96th-minute winner against Manchester City in September 2009 and quips that the “the wonderful fourth official probably should, at the very least, have been awarded an MBE”.

The fourth official was Alan Wiley.

Less than a month later, Ferguson complained that Wiley “wasn’t fit enough” during United’s 2-2 home draw with Sunderland.



Ferguson received a two-match touchline ban.

Fergie also randomly reflects on his chalk-and-cheese dynamic with Nottingham Forest legend Brian Clough.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Clough arrived for a game at Old Trafford and asked the United apprentice Deiniol Graham to shine his shoes.



Ferguson says he was “furious and handed [Clough] his shoes, which I had instructed Deiniol and our kit-man not to touch, and told him never to pull that stunt again.”

Sports.title: Arsenal ace Max Dowman presented with three Guinness World Records certificates after record-breaking rise
Sports.content:

MAX DOWMAN has been presented with three Guinness World Record certificates.

The 16-year-old Arsenal star has officially been honoured as the youngest player to both score a goal in and win the Premier League, and as the youngest player in Champions League history.



Dowman made his Premier League debut from the bench against Leeds, aged just 15 years and 235 days in August 2025, becoming an instant fan-favourite at the Emirates.

He went on to overtake Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko to become the youngest-ever Champions League player at 15 years and 208 days.



By scoring his first league goal against Everton aged 16 years and 73 days he also picked up the record for youngest scorer in the Premier League.

This was followed by being crowned as the youngest-ever Premier League winner at 16 years and 144 days after the club ended a 22-year wait for the title.



Dowman has been snapped with his certificates outside the Gunners’ training base to kick off Guinness World Records‘ Class of ’27.

Senior Editor of Guinness World Records Football Edition 2027, Tom Beckerlegge, has praised Dowman’s remarkable rise through professional football.

Beckerlegge said: “The youngest player on our list, Max sums up what the Class of ’27 is all about. To have already achieved three Guinness World Records titles before turning 17 is extraordinary, and his story captures exactly why this generation of players is so exciting.

“Football never stands still. Records are broken, new stars emerge and every season brings fresh moments of genius that light up the game. The Guinness World Records Football Edition 2027 celebrates all of that – from the biggest stars in world football to the young players whose stories are only just beginning.”

Dowman’s on-field success is especially impressive as he is yet to sign a full professional contract with Arsenal, instead being tied to a scholarship deal with the club.

But the young Gunner is set to earn a fortune after his parents incorporated his own image rights company, with a £35,000-per-week contract lined up for when he turns 17 in December.

Dowman has already made an impact this season, scoring two goals in the Carabao Cup and earning an England U19 call-up.

Sports.title: Sir Alex Ferguson reveals hopes to attend new Manchester United stadium opening in ‘person or spirit’

SIR ALEX Ferguson hopes to live long enough to attend the opening of Manchester United’s new stadium.

United co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe outlined his preference to build a new 100,000-seater stadium in February 2024, dubbing the proposal a “no-brainer”.



Architects Foster+Partners unveiled designs in March 2025 and United bought land near their 116-year-old stadium for £63.5million in the summer.

The club initially eyed a move-in date of 2030 but that has been scrapped, with no specific date now targeted.



United do hope to host games during the 2035 Women’s World Cup, though.

Ferguson, 84, has been a regular at Old Trafford since he retired from management in 2013 and has a seat reserved in the directors’ box.

In his latest book, Games of My Life, Ferguson admits that the prospect of United moving into a new-build left him in a reflective mood.

He writes: “I found myself wondering whether I would be around to celebrate its opening.

“I hope they get to break ground quickly, because if it takes five years to complete, I’ll be pushing ninety.

“However, I know I’ll be at the ceremony one way or another – in person or in spirit.”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

The 13-time Premier League winner first visited Old Trafford in 1984 to watch Celtic face Rapid Vienna in a European Cup Winners’ Cup replay, relocated to Manchester after crowd trouble at Celtic Park.

Ferguson was appointed United manager in 1986 and took charge of 724 games at Old Trafford, although he missed the December 1998 defeat to Middlesbrough to attend a funeral in Scotland.

The United great suffered a brain haemorrhage in May 2018 and left Old Trafford in an ambulance shortly after arriving for the fixture against Liverpool in May this year due to a heart issue.

Ferguson also arrived for United’s first home game of the season against Ipswich Town in August with his left foot encased in a protective boot, having injured his Achilles.

Old Trafford’s North Stand was renamed the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand in November 2011 to commemorate Ferguson’s 25th anniversary at the club.



United then installed a statue of Ferguson outside the stand bearing his name in November 2012.

A nearby road was also renamed Sir Alex Ferguson Way in 2013.

Sports.title: Sir Alex Ferguson brands Arsenal fans who abused Arsene Wenger ‘a stain on the club’ despite epic Man Utd rivalry
Sports.content:

SIR ALEX Ferguson has dubbed Arsenal fans’ treatment of Arsene Wenger during his latter years as manager as a “stain on the club’s reputation”.

Wenger left the Gunners in May 2018 after almost 22 years in charge, having won three Premier League titles and seven FA Cups.



Arsenal did the double in two of their title triumphs and went the whole season unbeaten with their third in 2003-04.

However, they failed to add to their title tally during Wenger’s final 14 years in the dugout and there were repeated calls for him to walk.



During an FA Cup tie at Brighton in 2013, Gooners unfurled a banner that read, “Arsene thanks for the memories but it’s time to say goodbye”.

Arsenal endured a nine-year trophy drought between 2005 and 2014 until they won the FA Cup.

They retained the trophy in 2015, yet those domestic successes failed to quieten a vocal contingent of the support.

The rise of fan TV in the mid-2010s saw Wenger repeatedly targeted by Arsenal’s performative fans on YouTube and social media.

In his latest book, Games of My Life, Ferguson declares him and Wenger as the “last two monuments in Premier League management”.

The Manchester United legend sympathises with his rival’s struggles, which he pins on Arsenal’s move from Highbury to the 60,000-capacity Emirates Stadium in 2006.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Wenger had the opportunity to manage Real Madrid before Arsenal upped sticks for Ashburton Grove but remained in north London. Ferguson feels Wenger’s “loyalty” contributed to Arsenal’s “faltered form”.

Arsenal lost several key players shortly after the relocation. Manchester City signed Kolo Toure, Emmanuel Adebayor, Gael Clichy and Samir Nasri within a third-year period after their 2008 takeover by the Abu Dhabi United Group.

Cesc Fabregas left for Barcelona the same summer that Nasri headed to Manchester in 2011 and Thierry Henry and Alexander Hleb moved to Catalonia in successive summers.

Ferguson even prised Robin van Persie from Arsenal in 2012 after the Dutchman entered the final year of his contract, a move that inspired United’s last title victory in 2013.

And Fergie has now written of Wenger’s struggles: “I’m glad I never felt such pressure at Old Trafford.



“The banks even made a contract extension for Arsene a condition of their financing. He was trapped.

“The way he was treated by some Arsenal fans at the end of his managerial career was a stain on the club’s reputation.”

Despite a bitter rivalry during Wenger’s first 12 years at Arsenal, Ferguson and Wenger had a warmer rapport from around 2008.

JUST when Manchester City fans thought things could not get any worse, Mikel Arteta has signed a new contract at Arsenal.

The Spanish boss extending his seven-year stay at the Emirates until 2030 was the least surprising event of an extraordinary international break which saw City found GUILTY of breaching Premier League finance rules.



Arteta’s new deal underlines that while things are uncertain at the Etihad, the Gunners are rock solid and seem certain to dominate English football for years to come.

In September 2019, Pep Guardiola claimed he was “pretty sure” Arteta, his City assistant at the time, would succeed him.



But two months later, the Basque returned to former club Arsenal to become manager.

There were theories that Arteta could still return to City to take over from Guardiola.



But after securing the Prem title in North London five months ago — the first time Arsenal had been crowned champions since 2004 — that was never going to happen.

Arteta has faced some tough questions as his spell in Manchester overlapped with the period of City’s alleged rule-breaking.

And he has always offered a firm “no” when asked if he had witnessed any wrongdoing at the Etihad.

He will be quizzed on the crisis at his old club again tomorrow when he addresses the media ahead of Saturday’s lunchtime clash with Leeds.

Yet there appears to be no stopping Arteta and Arsenal.

Arteta, who was already on £10million a year, will see his salary rocket to £20m including bonuses.

It feels a world away from the Covid era when he was still finding his feet as manager.

When the pandemic struck, Arteta and his players accepted a pay cut.

His job title changed from head coach to first-team manager back in September 2020 and, since then, he has been all-powerful.

Arteta was under huge pressure as Arsenal kept coming close but failed to win anything before it all fell into place in May.

Sports.content:

CRISTIANO RONALDO has sent a classy message offering his “respect” to rival Lionel Messi after his Argentina farewell.

Messi, 39, closed the chapter on his 21-year spell with the national team this week after playing his final game against Benin.



The former Barcelona superstar bid an emotional goodbye as he started the 3-0 victory and finished on 208 caps.

It was the perfect ending for Messi as he chipped in with two assists and scored from the penalty spot.



Messi – who helped Argentina win the 2022 World Cup – struggled to hold back tears after the game while giving his send-off speech.

He also released a lengthy statement on Instagram later on.

And his biggest footballing nemesis Ronaldo put aside their long-running rivalry to pay tribute to the veteran star in the comments.

He said: “Leo, so many years defending your country and a story that will live on forever.

“You have all my respect for everything you’ve achieved with Argentina. A hug.”

Messi and Ronaldo duelled each other for the Ballon d’Or on a number of occasions, with the Argentine winning eight and the Portugal captain claiming five.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Ronaldo himself is an icon for Portugal after appearing 234 times for his country – but this week he ruled out his own retirement despite his fallout with boss Jorge Jesus.

Messi released a full statement after his Argentina farewell hailing his “incredible journey”.

He wrote: “Yesterday was my last match, and I already miss wearing the sky blue and white. I know I’m making the right decision.

“It was an incredible journey, full of joy and some sadness, but I know for sure that every step I took was worth it.



“This journey would have been impossible without my family, who were always by my side and supported me, especially during the difficult times when I needed it most.

“My friends, all the teammates and coaches I had, along with their staff, were also essential.

“Thank you to the clubs I played for, for always respecting my feelings and allowing me to dedicate myself to my country when it was time to wear the national team jersey.

“And of course, thank God: without His guidance and His will, we wouldn’t even be dreaming of having gotten this far.



“I am so grateful. I love you all so much, I’m going to miss you, and I will always thank you for being by our side, by my side.”

Messi walked out for the game with his three sons – Thiago, 13, Mateo, 10, and Ciro, eight.

He was given in incredible send-off by an 85,000 sell-out crowd in Buenos Aires as he gave a speech lasting around ten minutes.

His team-mates were left in tears as he claimed he wished he could play for Argentina forever.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Messi added: I’m going to miss playing here so much. I love you all, and I’m proud to be Argentine.



“I leave grateful, proud and at peace. Thank you for everything.”

Sports.title: Donnarumma agent reveals Man City chiefs have told stars club will win appeal as ‘sporting justice’ is on their side
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER City bosses have told stars they should not be worried about the club’s Prem guilty verdict – because they have “sporting justice” on their side.

Top flight rivals want an unprecedented penalty against the Etihad-based club after they were found to have committed more than 100 breaches of League financial rules.



City have vowed to fight the “opinion” of the commission all the way, accusing it of swallowing “Premier League conspiracy theories” and launching an appeal.

And the agent of keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma said his player and others had been given reassurances that “sporting justice” would prevail.



Enzo Railo told Italian radio: “Will the Manchester City chaos change anything?

“No, nothing will change for us or for Gigio.

“News comes out periodically. The club has spoken with Gigio and everyone is calm.

“Now there are important games against Liverpool and PSG, then sporting justice will take its course.

“But Gigio has had reassurances from Manchester City.”

City remain vehement their “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence” will see the verdict overturned.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

What are Man City charged with? THE Premier League claim Man City hid £900m in 'sham' deals across a nine-year period. They were found guilty on 114 of the initial 115 charges – with the number now up to 130 charges – which fit into six categories… Failing to give accurate financial information over sponsorship revenue, related parties and operating costs between 2009-10 and 2017/18. Total charges: 50

Failing to provide full details of managerial remuneration between 2009/10 and 2012/13. Total charges 8

Failing to provide full details of player remuneration between 2010/11 and 2015/16. Total charges 12

Failing to comply with Uefa Licencing and Financial Fair Play regulations between 2013/14 and 2017/18. Total charges 5

Breaching Premier League Profitability and Sustainability rules between 2015/16 and 2017/18. Total charges 25

Failing to co-operate with the Premier League investigation between 2018/19 and 2022/23. Total charges 30

Total charges: 130

In an official statement confirming their appeal, the club said: “Manchester City Football Club can confirm that at 7pm on Thursday, October 1, 2026, the club lodged its comprehensive Appeal against the opinion of the Premier League Commission, in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter.

“The club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

“The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

“We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete.”

Donnarumma and the rest of the City squad who were away on international duty will return to training on Thurs ahead of Sunday’s Prem clash at Liverpool.



That will give boss Enzo Maresca his first chance to address the entire squad in person.

Sports.title: Why Sprint in Singapore adds new twist to F1's toughest race
Sports.content:
Formula 1 stages its sixth and final Sprint event of the year this weekend to conclude the first flyaway triple header of the sport's busy 2026 season run in.

And, for the first time, the Sprint format is being used at the Singapore Grand Prix and its Marina Bay street track, home of the sport's original night race.

But on a track not known for its overtaking, what kind of weekend can we expect with two qualifying sessions and two races?

How the Singapore GP weekend will be different to normal

When the Sprint format was first introduced at three races for the 2021 season, the tracks selected - Silverstone, Monza and Interlagos - were ones deemed to be particularly good for racing so to justify the addition of a 100km race on the Saturday as an appetiser to the main Sunday Grand Prix.

That has generally continued to be the case in the selection of Sprint venues up to this year, with perhaps the inclusion of Imola in 2022 the surprise exception.

Street tracks, which by their nature traditionally aren't as overtaking-friendly as conventional permanent tracks, have generally not featured on that yearly list.

Azerbaijan did host a Sprint in 2023, but Baku's wall-lined street track features the longest straight on the calendar and so allows passing.

Singapore certainly falls more into the category of conventional street track - there are no long straights of note and overtaking opportunities are severely limited around the confined, twisty layout.

Image: The Singapore GP takes place this weekend, live on Sky Sports F1 (HOCH ZWEI/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images)

The floodlit race is instead most known for its physicality owing to the hot and humid conditions of the Asian country and the fact the 62-lap race pushes towards the two-hour limit around a 19-corner lap that features plenty of 90-degree turns.

So, holding a second race this weekend appears counterintuitive in one sense to the original purpose of the Sprint format. However, there are flip sides to the decision.

The first relates to qualifying. Given the lack of passing opportunities in the race, qualifying is always considered absolutely essential at Marina Bay and, like all street tracks where the walls are so close, the Saturday spectacle is often spectacular.

The circuit was the scene of one of the most famous qualifying laps in the sport's recent history when Lewis Hamilton surged to pole position for Mercedes in 2018, while numerous drivers have come a cropper against the barriers over the years when pushing for a decisive, grid-defining lap.

This year there will be two such sessions - Sprint Qualifying on Friday followed by Grand Prix Qualifying on Saturday - which means double the qualifying challenge and, therefore, double the jeopardy for drivers.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from qualifying at the 2025 Singapore Grand Prix.

The Sprint format also means drivers and teams will have two-thirds less time to hone their cars' set-ups and settings for the competitive sessions given there is only a single one-hour session of practice running instead of the usual three.

Building up rhythm and confidence is crucial on a street track so drivers know they will have to shortcut that process this time in Singapore. However, that is clearly easier said than done, increasing the likelihood of mistakes in sessions that count and teams going down set-up cul-de-sacs.

A further potential twist comes in the scheduling of the sessions.

That sole practice takes place in the hours before sunset at 4.30pm local time (9.30am BST) whereas Sprint Qualifying is at 8.30pm (1.30pm BST) when the floodlights will be in full effect and temperatures will be a little cooler, creating a set-up conundrum for teams as cars, engines and tyres won't necessarily behave the same in different conditions.

Parc-ferme conditions mean teams can't then touch the cars again for Saturday's Sprint, which takes place during the late afternoon like practice.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the 2025 Singapore Grand Prix from the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

A precursor to Monaco 2027

Next season the Sprint format is being expanded to 10 events and, when the full 2027 calendar was published last month, the surprise news came from the fact that Monaco had been selected to host one of them.

The Principality's street circuit is even narrower and harder to pass on than Singapore's, which has increasingly made qualifying the standout aspect of that particular race weekend as cars have become wider and more reliable.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player F1 drivers share their opinions following the announcement that the Monaco Grand Prix will get a Sprint race next year.

Staging two races there next year therefore appears to be as counter-intuitive as it does in Singapore, yet the opposite thinking in terms of doubling up on qualifying and building in the potential for more unpredictability now appears to be a balancing factor.

It will be interesting to hear what drivers, who have mostly been supportive about bringing the Sprint to Monaco next year, make of the Singapore Sprint experience as it unfolds.

A four-team fight for Singapore victory?

Irrespective of how much unpredictability there is this weekend on Singapore's Sprint debut, the weekend promises to be competitive in the battle for victory at the front.

Max Verstappen's impressive win for Red Bull last week in Malaysia means F1's 'Big Four' teams have now all won at least one race in the first year of the sport's new regulations, with Mercedes' early-season dominance a thing of the past despite the Silver Arrows' continued command of both world championship races.

Marina Bay was actually one of only two races that Mercedes won last year although George Russell, who dominated that weekend, already knows his hopes of going back-to-back are effectively over thanks to a grid penalty for excess engine usage that will send him to the back of Sunday's grid.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater explains why George Russell's Singapore GP grid penalty could end his chances of a world title this season.

Russell will still hope to be a factor at the front in Saturday's Sprint, though, where the grid penalty does not apply.

But it is clearly championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who dominated Monaco but crashed in Baku qualifying, who will be carrying Mercedes' front-running hopes into Sunday on a weekend the team bid to get a handle on why their big aerodynamic upgrade brought to Malaysia did not deliver the expected step forward.

Who has won on 2026's Sprint weekends so far? Race weekend Sprint winner Grand Prix winner China George Russell Kimi Antonelli Miami Lando Norris Kimi Antonelli Canada George Russell Kimi Antonelli Britain Kimi Antonelli Charles Leclerc Netherlands George Russell Lando Norris

The in-form Verstappen will also likely be a factor at the front for resurgent Red Bull as he finally looks to win the Singapore Grand Prix - at the 10th attempt.

Marina Bay is the one long-standing track on the current calendar (Madrid, where Verstappen finished second last month, only joined the schedule this year) that the Dutchman has yet to win at.

Verstappen has qualified and finished second in each of the last two years, so has certainly been knocking on the door to do so. Red Bull will hope their recent performance gains elsewhere transfer to the unique demands of Singapore.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player On the F1 Show podcast, David Croft looks at Red Bull's strengths following Max Verstappen's dominant win at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

Then there is McLaren, who claimed dominant victories with Lando Norris on F1's last visits to high-downforce tracks in Hungary and Zandvoort but have hitherto not enjoyed great success across the first two legs of the Azerbaijan-Malaysia-Singapore triple header.

The absence of long straights is good news for Ferrari, who will hope the race pace that allowed Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to recover strongly from the team's disastrous slick-tyre strategy at the start of last Sunday's delayed Sepang race will transfer to the slower-speed streets of Singapore.

Sports.title: What's next for Littler? Can he still qualify for Players Championship Finals?
Sports.content:
Two-time world champion Luke Littler can still qualify for the Players Championship Finals in Minehead – but what else can he win?

His unprecedented 12-month clean sweep may be over following a crushing 10-4 defeat by Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam and a shock first-round exit at the World Grand Prix, but he can still qualify for next month's Players Championship Finals.

The world No 1 had won the first six premier events of the season following his World Championship triumph at Alexandra Palace in January with the World Masters, UK Open, Premier League, World Cup of Darts and World Matchplay.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dan Dawson discusses Luke Littler's early World Grand Prix exit

Darts in 2026 Event Winner Dates World Championship Luke Littler Dec 11-Jan 3 World Masters Luke Littler Jan 29-Feb 1 UK Open Luke Littler March 6-8 Premier League* Luke Littler Feb to May World Cup* Luke Littler and Luke Humphries June 11-14 World Matchplay Luke Littler July 18-16 World Series of Darts Finals* Ross Smith September 17-20 World Grand Prix Luke Humphries Sept 28-Oct 4 European Championship October 22-25 Grand Slam of Darts November 14-22 Players Championship Finals November 27-29 *Non-ranking event

He had been hoping to add the World Series of Darts Finals, World Grand Prix, European Championship, Grand Slam of Darts and Players Championship Finals trophies to complete a historic clean sweep of the year. But his bid was derailed by Clayton, who reeled off seven of the final eight legs to defeat the teenager before overcoming Luke Woodhouse in Leicester, where he suffered a 2-1 defeat in the double-in, double-out tournament.

At the weekend, 19-year-old Littler was beaten by Cam Crabtree in the semi-finals of the World Youth Championship.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Love The Darts, Paul Nicholson has backed Littler's reduced schedule for the rest of the season

Had he gone on to win the title, Littler would have become the first player to hold both the World Championship and World Youth titles.

The final will take place on Sunday, November 29, in Minehead as part of the Players Championship Finals, a tournament Littler won last year but has yet to qualify for this time around.

What could the rest of Littler's year look like? Players Championship 33 (Leicester) November 4 Players Championship 34 (Leicester) November 5 Grand Slam of Darts* (Wolverhampton) November 14-22 Players Championship Finals* (Minehead) November 27-29 World Championship* (Alexandra Palace) December 11-January 3 *denotes major

With just two floor events remaining before the Players Championship Finals, Littler can still earn enough prize money to qualify for the tournament - but will he make the trip to Leicester on November 4 and 5?

The top 64 players on the ProTour Order of Merit qualify for the Minehead showpiece, with the projected cut-off expected to exceed £30,000 after all 34 events. Littler currently sits in 126th place with £10,500, while Mike De Decker occupies the final qualifying spot in 64th with £29,250.

That leaves 'The Nuke' with a slim route into Minehead, but he would likely need to reach the final of at least one - and potentially both - of the final two ProTour events to force his way into the field.

Littler won the 2025 title, defeating Nathan Aspinall 11-8 in the final.

This was a world championship, and I don't ever want to exist in a world of sport where someone is excluded from a world championship for being too good.

And then to Alexandra Palace where the teenager will bid to become a triple world champion.

He is aiming to become the first player to win three world titles in a row since Phil Taylor did it in 2006, although 'The Power' did win eight in a row from 1995 to 2002.

Sports.title: Rahm to quit LIV Golf over 'unacceptable' terms
Sports.content:
Jon Rahm is set to quit LIV Golf after deeming the terms proposed to him for the relaunch of the series “unacceptable”; Rahm is reportedly owed up to $150m (£113m) from the contract he signed three years ago, with both sides now working towards a separation agreement

Jon Rahm withdrew from this week's Open de Espana as he expects the birth of his fourth child

Jon Rahm is to quit LIV Golf after deeming the terms offered for the proposed relaunch of the breakaway series “unacceptable”.

LIV Golf is currently going through Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in the US after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its support at the end of the season, having invested $5bn (£3.7bn) over four years.

While players including Sergio Garcia successfully petitioned the court to lift the automatic stay on their contracts, effectively freeing them to explore other opportunities for next year, Rahm was not granted the same route out.

The Spaniard is one of LIV Golf's two biggest names, alongside Bryson DeChambeau, and is reportedly owed up to $150m (£113m) for the remainder of the contract he signed almost three years ago.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jon Rahm says he's willing to honour his contract with LIV Golf but his future beyond that remains a doubt.

"Mr Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0 and has determined that those terms are unacceptable to him, and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0," attorney John Beck told a bankruptcy hearing.

The Athletic has also reported that Rahm and LIV are working towards a separation agreement, with a deal expected to be finalised by October 15.

Rahm withdrew from this week's Open de Espana in Madrid to remain at home with wife Kelley, who is expecting their fourth child.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Geraint Hughes explains what is next for LIV Golf and what will happen to their players after they filed for bankruptcy.

The 31-year-old has already taken steps towards a potential return to the traditional tours. In May, he ended his dispute with the DP World Tour and paid around £2.21m in fines for playing in conflicting events, securing conditional releases for 2026 and making him eligible for the Ryder Cup.

Rahm previously declined the PGA Tour's offer of reinstatement through a specially created Returning Member Program, which was made available to him, Cameron Smith, Bryson DeChambeau and Brooks Koepka. Koepka was the only player to accept.

As a result, Rahm would face a mandatory one-year suspension before being eligible to return to the PGA Tour, meaning he could not play on the circuit until late August next year.

Sports.title: Garcia targets Ryder Cup return
Sports.content:
Sergio Garcia is desperate to be involved in next year's Ryder Cup, either as a player or vice-captain, with his time on LIV Golf appearing to be coming to an end.

The Saudi-backed breakaway league filed for bankruptcy last month, with its restructuring plan likely to release players from their existing contracts ahead of a potential LIV 2.0 relaunch.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Garcia is Europe's all-time leading points scorer at the Ryder Cup

This week, Garcia successfully secured a court ruling to lift an automatic stay on his contract, allowing him to seriously consider his options for 2027.

Europe's all-time leading Ryder Cup points scorer now has his sights firmly set on Adare Manor next September.

"I think everything is an option," he told a press conference at the Open de Espana in Madrid.

"That doesn't mean I won't go or that I'll definitely stay with LIV, but settling the LIV 1.0 matter now avoids potential repercussions related to that contract.

"I don't really know how things will end up with the DP World Tour regarding LIV 2.0, we'll have to see, [but] I want to try and give myself the best chance of making that team.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Garcia was successful in getting a court to lift an automatic stay on his contract and can now assess his options in 2027

"Everyone knows how much I love the Ryder Cup and the possibility of playing in another one, or if not, finding some way to help in another way, as vice-captain or something like that could be something very interesting."

Garcia, who has spoken to European captain Luke Donald, added: "I told him that I'm going to do everything possible to see if I can get into that team and I also told him that if I don't get into that team, I'll help in any way I can."

The 2017 Masters champion would first need to regain his DP World Tour membership.

Garcia resigned his membership in 2023 after being sanctioned for playing in conflicting LIV events. He later paid around £750,000 in fines in an unsuccessful bid to qualify for the Ryder Cup at Bethpage last year, but ultimately lost his card after failing to meet the minimum number of events.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jon Rahm has previously said Sergio Garcia should be allowed to play at the Ryder Cup

Garcia has also not ruled out a return to the PGA Tour, although under its rules he would have to serve a suspension until August.

"It's definitely a possibility. I turn 47 in January, and the Champions Tour is a possibility," he said.

"Besides, I'd like the chance to play some of those tournaments, especially the big ones on the Champions Tour. These are things that I'm starting to consider at my age."

Sports.title: Eckert’s Spygate ban may be lenient, but no sane manager will try the same trick again
Sports.content:
“Hi Tonda, are you a cheat?” That simple, succinct, question cut to the heart of a matter that has vexed the Football Association all summer. It was posed by the Northern Echo’s Dominic Shaw after Southampton overcame Middlesbrough in the second leg of May’s Championship playoff semi‑final and proved the cue for Tonda Eckert to walk out of his press conference at St Mary’s.

Although Southampton’s manager subsequently admitted to authorising spying on opponents, England’s football authorities struggled to decide what punishment best fitted an act some regard as heinous but which others fail to take seriously. Now, in autumn, we finally have an FA verdict, with Eckert given a six-week ban suspended until the end of the 2027-28 season, a £28,000 fine and a reprimand.

Despite the apparent leniency of the sanction, one thing is clear: Eckert’s summer in purgatory surely dictates no sane England-based coach would contemplate engaging in espionage now.

Eckert may wish he could turn back time to early May and rewrite history. On the eve of the playoff semi-final first leg on Teesside, William Salt, then an intern Southampton first-team analyst, was caught lurking awkwardly beside a tree while filming a Middlesbrough training session on his iPhone. Spygate was born and an independent disciplinary commission convened by the Football League (EFL) expelled Southampton from the playoff final against Hull after their win against Boro across two legs. The governing body also decreed the Saints would begin the current Championship season on minus four points.

View image in fullscreen Tonda Eckert on the touchline at Middlesbrough’s Riverside Stadium during the first leg of Southampton’s playoff semi-final. Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/Reuters

By then Southampton had also admitted to spying on Oxford and Ipswich training. There is a certain irony that Eckert’s team won none of the three games – albeit Middlesbrough were ultimately beaten on aggregate – involving covert surveillance. Yet the EFL independent disciplinary commission panel made plain its discomfort regarding the “particularly deplorable” pressure placed on a young worker hired on a temporary contract. Salt has since been given a staff job as an analyst in Southampton’s academy and is reportedly progressing well.

With the EFL empowered to sanction clubs but not individuals in such cases, it was down to the FA to punish Eckert. The 33-year-old German issued a public apology in June but was not charged with misconduct by the FA until late July. A further hiatus ensued before a hearing at Wembley on 24 September.

This extraordinary delay afforded Eckert ample time to regret dispatching Salt to Middlesbrough’s training ground adjacent to the luxury Rockliffe Hall Hotel and golf course just south of Darlington. Salt’s primary mission was to discover whether Hayden Hackney, Middlesbrough’s star midfielder and the Championship player of the season, was fit after injury. Unfortunately, clandestine manoeuvres were evidently not his strong suit. Salt soon found himself being chased into hotel toilets, and realised that using his bank card to buy a coffee at Rockliffe had not been the smartest move. That payment facilitated a search for his name on Southampton’s website. It was swiftly identified, enabling Steve Gibson, Middlesbrough’s owner, to make a formal complaint to the EFL regarding a breach of its anti-spying regulations.

It is understood that, until this point, Southampton’s manager remained unaware of the Bev Priestman precedent. The former head coach of Canada Women was banned from all football activity for a year by Fifa after being found guilty of initiating spying. During the 2024 Paris Olympics her staff secretly filmed a New Zealand training session using a drone and the former England women’s assistant manager paid a high price.

It is unclear whether Eckert has since been in touch with the 40-year-old, now in charge of Wellington Phoenix. Priestman met such extreme hostility in previously welcoming Canada that she relocated her family to New Zealand. During ‘Spygate’, Eckert’s wife was heavily pregnant and based in Berlin, preparing for the birth of their first child. Back in Hampshire, her husband received death threats via LinkedIn. Southampton supplied the manager with protection while police advised him that driving his own car was unsafe and that he should restrict his movements.

Plenty of people were extremely angry, with St Mary’s regulars polarised between those who believed the manager had shamed their club and should be sacked, and others who reflected that what is euphemistically called “training observation” of opponents is commonplace and largely unpunished across tracts of Europe. The second camp remembered that, seven years ago, Leeds were fined £200,000 after the club’s then manager, Marcelo Bielsa, sent an analyst to monitor a Derby training session. Frank Lampard, then in charge of Derby, complained after spotting him perched up a tree.

After that incident the EFL tightened its regulations regarding espionage appreciably. Nonetheless, Eckert’s advocates claim that, given he started last season as Southampton’s under-21s coach and became the manager after Will Still’s sacking in November, he had missed the EFL’s annual managerial summer rules refresher course.

View image in fullscreen ‘I would lie if I said this summer’s been easy,’ Eckert said last month. Photograph: Cody Froggatt/PA

Eckert, who began his career as a Germany national team analyst before moving into coaching at Cologne, RB Salzburg, RB Leipzig, Bayern Munich, Barnsley and Genoa, was only half-joking when he recently told reporters that the EFL handbook was his staple bedside summer reading. He also made contact with Gareth Southgate and visited the former England and Middlesbrough, manager, with the pair discussing English football culture and its zero tolerance for spycraft at length.

“I would lie if I said this summer’s been easy,” said Eckert last month. “I’ve asked the FA for forgiveness.” He has had unwavering support from Southampton’s board who made it clear they had no desire to sack him in the face of considerable dressing room hostility on the part offrom players who felt betrayed by ‘Spygate’.

With first-team hearts and minds since seemingly recaptured by the coach who led them so close to promotion last season, Southampton have won four and drawn two of their opening eight Championship games. Next up on Sunday is the visit of Portsmouth. South-coast derbies are invariably tense but Eckert’s reprieve may ensure he cuts an unusually relaxed figure in the technical area.

Sports.title: All aboard the Tuchel train? England camp has clear winners and losers
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel’s original idea had been for continuity. The England manager wanted to build on the positives from the World Cup and he was minded to stand by the vast majority of the players who had been a part of the journey to the semi-finals in North America over the summer. His squad for the four-match Nations League window and the beginning of a new international cycle would not be defined by radical change. What was it about the best-laid plans?

As Tuchel prepared to name his group in mid-September, he knew that he would be without a clutch of World Cup players because of injury. He then lost another handful after the announcement. Fast forward to the Czechia game at Wembley on Tuesday night – the final one of the quartet – and, after further withdrawals, Tuchel could count only 12 players who were available to him during the World Cup. He knows the train moves quickly in football, stopping for nobody. That flexibility is a prerequisite in his line of work. This felt like something else.

Tuchel and his staff were resolved to road-test an updated game model as they sought to move on from the devastation of the World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina. Again, nothing too radical because the principles were in place. They wanted to give the players greater freedom in terms of where they could roam on the pitch; encourage them to trust their instincts and take risks, all within a framework where covering for a teammate was fundamental. Tuchel would need some new players to execute it and, as he reflects on a positive window, in which defeat by Spain was followed by three wins, two against Czechia either side of the 7-0 dismantling of Croatia in Rijeka, he will feel he has found them.

There are always winners and losers from an international camp and maybe they are more pronounced on this occasion because of the timing; the sense of a fresh start, the desire to turn the page after Argentina. It was always going to be a tone-setter for the ultimate goal of Euro 2028 glory.

The biggest winners were Alex Scott and Lewis Hall, with Myles Lewis-Skelly getting an honourable mention. James Trafford pushed his claim to supplant Jordan Pickford as the first-choice goalkeeper, and then there was Trent Alexander-Arnold, ever tantalising, ever nuanced.

As for the losers, well, take your pick from those who were not present, with Tuchel making it clear that it would be harder for them. “It is always like this,” he said. “Everyone should be desperate to come because the train is rolling. Full credit to the players who bought in to that. We can only put our full energy into the camp and the players who are in camp. They make the camp special.”

View image in fullscreen Alex Scott (centre) caught Thomas Tuchel’s eye before being forced to withdraw with injury. Photograph: Sebastian Frej/Getty Images

Tuchel described Scott and Hall as “really excellent”. In the case of the former, Tuchel cannot contain his excitement. He does not want to. Scott did well when he came on as a 70th-minute substitute for his debut against Czechia in Prague and was very good from the start against Croatia, catching the eye with his smoothness on the half turn, his dynamic surges.

It was noticeable that when Tuchel’s assistant, Anthony Barry, spoke on Monday about fluid, hard-running midfielders to fit the team’s style, he name-checked three: Declan Rice and Elliot Anderson, who are well-established, and Scott. It is such a frustration that he aggravated a thigh problem against Croatia and is out for two months, which will rule him out of the matches in November against Croatia and Spain. Tuchel worked with Scott in November 2025 and at the pre-World Cup camp in Florida. “Alex came in here now and was on a completely new level,” Tuchel said. “He was super-strong.”

It was a positive window for Lewis-Skelly, who Tuchel counted on as a midfielder rather than a left-back for the first time. The 20-year-old started three of the games and came on as a 79th-minute substitute against Croatia. The worry was how he picked up bookings in both matches against Czechia; he is now suspended for the home game against Croatia. “I wasn’t aware of the yellow card,” Tuchel said of Tuesday’s one at Wembley, rather surprisingly. He knows about the need to stay out of red card territory.

Kobbie Mainoo is a potential loser from the emergence of Scott and Lewis-Skelly. Tuchel was at pains to sympathise with the Manchester United midfielder over the injury that forced his withdrawal, particularly after he did not play him for a single minute at the World Cup. But with Rice certain to return after an agreed rest this time this out, and James Garner in the frame, Mainoo has work to do. Ditto Jordan Henderson, who was not up to speed fitness‑wise after his broken arm at the World Cup.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Trent Alexander-Arnold made his mark after being brought back into the fold. Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty Images

Hall has taken his chance at left-back, stepping up after Nico O’Reilly played against Spain and was then forced to withdraw. Hall started in each of the subsequent games – “three top matches from him”, Tuchel said – and if he is plainly in possession of the shirt, he deserves to keep it in November. Which is bad news for O’Reilly and Djed Spence, who has not yet played this season.

Did Alexander-Arnold do enough at right-back after his surprise recall? He could not have done much more with his starting opportunities in both Czechia games. There was the lovely cross for Anthony Gordon’s breakthough goal in Prague and a driving, attack-minded performance at Wembley. Everybody knows what Alexander-Arnold can do; he showed it again and the argument remains that he must be included for his points of difference.

On the other hand, what does Tuchel do when Reece James, Tino Livramento and Spence are available? The manager has previously made it plain he considers all three to be ahead of Alexander-Arnold. He said he might have called up Ben White if he were fit and also has Jarell Quansah, even if the Bayer Leverkusen player would rather be considered in central defence. That was where Tuchel started him against Czechia at Wembley – ahead of Trevoh Chalobah and Jarrad Branthwaite.

Cole Palmer has found himself under an unforgiving spotlight after his withdrawal, particularly after Tuchel questioned whether he wanted to play for England. It looks a long way back for the Chelsea No 10 and the same is true of Phil Foden. Both were overlooked when Tuchel gave a late call-up to Morgan Gibbs-White, and neither looks an easy fit for this team’s aggressive style. “I don’t know [if they are],” Tuchel said. “That is the honest answer. They were not here. This team took another step and it’s always about the guys who are here.”

Tuchel has plenty to ponder before the November matches. He will hope to see John Stones recover his fitness and form at Inter. There is a belief that the centre-back’s move to Serie A, where the tempo is slower, can help him find his rhythm. Marcus Rashford will be expected to return; he has credit in the bank with Tuchel, even if Gordon has nailed down the starting spot on the left wing.

Can Noni Madueke stage a comeback on the right after being dropped? And what of the strikers in the Saudi Pro League, Ollie Watkins and Ivan Toney, who were also dropped? Tuchel now sees Jude Bellingham as the back-up No 9 to Harry Kane. He gave Dominic Calvert-Lewin only brief substitute appearances against Spain and Czechia at Wembley. The train hurtles on.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi’s Argentina career turned football into a sacred mystery | Marcela Mora y Araujo
Sports.content:
“What Argentina is doing in this World Cup is of a sacred order,” Brazilian writer Milly Lacombe posted at the height of the tide of anti-Argentinian sentiment during this year’s tournament. She was exploring the contradiction she felt around her support of Lionel Messi: “a player who is a God and a man who shakes Trump’s hand”.

Lacombe highlighted the importance of acknowledging the complexities around Messi and the Argentinian team. How is it possible that Messi was not speaking out against the racist incidents we all saw around the Argentina team, she asked. “That’s why it hurts so much to see someone with Messi’s power choosing to make himself small,” she wrote.

Much was made of Messi’s silence at the time. Then again, much has been made of his visible discomfort with words throughout his epic career. Journalist John Carlin once said that having interviewed Messi twice, he would decline a third opportunity, such was the challenge of getting the little giant to say anything of consequence. In 2010, Juan Sebastián Verón said he had never seen Messi as nervous as when he had to address his teammates for the first time as Argentina captain. In terms of public speaking, perhaps Messi’s most famous outburst was at the 2022 World Cup when he told a Dutch player to “go away”.

View image in fullscreen A giant number 10 shirt was displayed on the pitch before Messi’s farewell apperance. Photograph: Rodrigo Abd/AP

Despite this reticence, Messi has always meant something, even when he doesn’t speak. Messi and Argentina were treated as darlings when they won the World Cup in 2022. By the time the 2026 final ended in defeat to Spain, they had become villains.

“That’s why it’s important to understand that when Messi, in the middle of a game that was lost, looks at the sky, and then after that he turns the game around and smashed it, there is something very mysterious there. Right? That we can’t explain. That we just feel,” Lacombe said after Argentina’s semi-final victory over England this summer. “I started supporting England but by the end of the match I was weeping, surrendered to the commitment, the passion, the love that I saw the Argentina team pour on to the pitch. It’s only in that moment of intense passion that we reach the sacred.”

Not everyone surrendered to the sacred in the same way. The final against Spain lacked sublime power and opened the floodgates of vitriol from all corners of the globe. Argentinian fans were offended, hurt, defensive and aware they may have just seen Messi’s last appearance in an Argentina shirt. When he confirmed he would end his international career – his final appearance for Argentina came against Benin on Tuesday – a wave of grief and gratitude swept the nation.

View image in fullscreen An 18 yr old Lionel Messi grapples with Hungary’s Vilmos Vanczák and is sent off after 44 seconds on his Argentina debut. Photograph: Michael Mayhew/Getty Images/Allstar

Messi grew up in Barcelona’s youth system, and he was eligible to play for both Spain and Argentina. His debut for Argentina – in a youth match against Paraguay – set up a rush to ensure he pledged his allegiance to the country of his birth, before Spain could tempt him. He was already one of the Barcelona’s academy most promising stars, but he was little known in Argentina. His father, Jorge, wanted nothing more than for his son to represent Argentina, and sent videos to then-manager Marcelo Bielsa hoping to expedite the process. For years, Jorge endured an uphill struggle to consolidate the ties between Lionel and Argentina. Messi’s prowess, seemingly unstoppable in a well-oiled Barcelona system, did not come through at national level. For a long time, Jorge would ask his compatriots the same question. How can we get Argentina to love my son?

Now, as we start to write Messi’s football obituary, some of the most grievous incidents against him are resurfacing. There was the time when a panel of pundits stood in a minute’s silence in protest against Messi’s performances for his country. He was criticised for not singing the national anthem. We learned that before Argentina matches he suffered bouts of vomiting and diarrhoea. Diego Maradona mocked him, saying he was no leader (although he would later make Messi Argentina’s captain). And when the campaign to win over the nation stepped up and he gave interviews, his discourse was shockingly basic and he gave little away.

But Messi never gave up. He missed penalties, wept, and stood to take them again. “What characterized Messi in the national team is that he lost. He lost a lot. He’s constituted in defeat” Argentinian journalist Alejandro Wall says.

View image in fullscreen Adoring fans cheer for Messi before the match against Benin. Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/Reuters

But the vitriol more often came from the press than the people. When he quit the national team in 2016, a spontaneous show of love and desire swept the nation, and he reversed his decision. From then on, the Argentinian Football Association’s main priority mirrored that of Jorge Messi: finding a coach who could adapt the entire system to Lionel. It wasn’t easy.

Perhaps it was only after Maradona’s death in 2020 that the new Messi started to emerge. He walked taller, more confident and comfortable in his role as leader. In 2021, Argentina won the Copa América, and snippets of Messi’s pep talks to his teammates filtered out. He made simple statements in his unmistakable Rosario accent, aspiring the ‘s’ and not pronouncing most final consonants. His – and Argentina’s – achievements since then speak for themselves.

Tuesday’s farewell at the Monumental Stadium – much like that first youth game against Paraguay – had a rushed, improvised air. The Argentinian FA struggled to secure opponents, not wanting to share box office with another footballing power. Benin were mocked by some as unworthy, and even Lionel Scaloni made reference to a desire to face bigger opponents than Bolivia and Burkina Faso, the other teams Argentina played this window. Burkina Faso ended up sending an Under-23 side who arrived a few hours before the match, and the stadium was not filled to capacity. Ticket prices were extortionate, and diehard fans refused to fall for what they called “a scam”.

View image in fullscreen An electric atmosphere at Estadio Monumental. Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/Reuters

But against Benin they turned up in numbers. Earlier, Messi had picked up an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires, in a small and shabby ceremony in a back office of the Argentinian FA. Delicately produced homages to No 10 were aired. Social media posts full of hyperbolic emotion appeared. “Like Scheherazade, he mocked destiny match by match, to gift the Argentina people another day of his magic. The thousand and one nights of Lionel Messi with the light blue and white come to their end,” read one post. “Whoah, hold it! It’s 9am. I can’t start weeping yet” came a swift reply.

To paraphrase Wayne Rooney, the entertainment around the match was crap. There was a drawn out homage by Soledad Pastorutti, who sang the same number she had once performed with Maradona. A veteran of the Falklands/Malvinas War sang the national anthem, and then clad himself in the same flag that fell on the pitch in Atlanta. The terraces chanted against AFA president Chiqui Tapia in a beautiful chorus, which went some way to atoning for the drone show at the end, with adverts for an insurance company glittering in the sky.

But football is about redemption, and the night was redeemed. Benin actually put up a fight, bookended by the team’s captain gifting Messi a statue of a Dahomey Agojie, the group of women who fought against French occupation. Messi set up three of his team’s three goals and took a penalty. He didn’t miss.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi salutes his adoring fans after his final match for Argentina. Photograph: Roberto Tuero/ZUMA/Shutterstock

The cameras zoomed in on weeping faces but the sounds from the concrete terraces were decisively celebratory, relentless, trembling. It was football through and through. And Messi loved it. You could tell. He picked up the microphone and launched into a speech so articulate and confident that it merits a dissertation studying its every word. He addressed conspiracy theories surrounding the World Cup final: “Nothing odd happened. The match against England wore us out at an emotional level”. He warned of hard times to come but said team unity is the way through.

“We had the dream of fulfilling our dream,” he said, adding: “I don’t know, I’m talking more than ever. I don’t want to leave here. I love you”. And Argentina loves him back.

As Lacombe said, when Messi looks at the sky, then turns a situation around and smashes it, there is mystery. There is something sacred.

Sports.title: Robertson rant and the wrong system? Pocognoli’s Scotland start raises questions
Sports.content:
What is the general situation after four games?

Scotland are staring at a third-place finish in Group B1 of the Nations League, which will have repercussions for their seeding in Euro 2028 qualifying. More striking, though, was the general standard of performance over Sébastien Pocognoli’s first four games as manager.

Scotland were dismal for a half in Slovenia before a decent but scoreless recovery. They capitulated after an early sending-off against Switzerland, failing to register a shot on target in a meek 3-0 loss. North Macedonia were as poor an international team as Scotland have faced in recent times, rendering the 2-0 win in Skopje worthy of little more than a shoulder shrug. Pocognoli’s men rounded off this extended window by being played off the Hampden Park pitch by Slovenia. Andy Robertson, the captain, strikingly questioned the attitude of his teammates. There has been no new manager bounce.

Pocognoli was given only a two-year contract, which was odd given the pedestal he was placed on by the Scottish Football Association when hired in August. The likelihood remains host-nation status will secure the Scots a place in the next Euros, but the country cannot arrive at the event under the cover of darkness. The alarming nature of the performance against Slovenia – it really had no redeeming qualities – places a huge emphasis on November’s fixtures.

Are Scotland suited to the way Pocognoli wants to play?

It does not look that way. The manager deploys a three-man backline as routine, with an emphasis on pressing high and wingbacks being crucial to attacking phases. Scotland do not have an obvious two-man central defensive pairing, meaning they most definitely struggle when the number is increased by one. Time and again, they leave far too much space in behind and look woefully exposed. Counterattacks bypass Scotland’s midfield all too easily. Pocognoli’s Scotland are a dream to play against.

Success for the Scots under Steve Clarke came from being well-drilled, compact and difficult to beat. Unsexy perhaps, but effective. Playing with gay abandon is all well and good when having a level of security Scotland simply do not possess currently. Scotland allowed Slovenia to be just as menacing as Morocco and Brazil, top-quality opposition they faced at the World Cup. Pocognoli’s desired methods may be impossible to implement without day-to-day involvement with players. Ideology is fine when club football permits an overhaul of personnel.

When Scotland switched to a defensive four in the closing stages of the Slovenia clash, players appeared generally confused. This was a bad look for Pocognoli, who has insisted he is “flexible” in a tactical sense and disputed the idea he had a touchline row with Robertson. Scott McTominay’s return for the next set of fixtures would provide an iota of hope, were it obvious where the Napoli man fits in. The setup as is will not maximise the abilities of McTominay, John McGinn, Ryan Christie and Billy Gilmour.

View image in fullscreen Sébastien Pocognoli consoles Billy Gilmour after Scotland’s feeble defeat at home against Slovenia on Tuesday. Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty Images

Didn’t fans want a revolution?

A reality is Scotland have qualified for three of the last four major tournaments. Noise directed towards Clarke underappreciated the scale of his work. That said, after seven years, Clarke’s tenure had run its course.

The obvious move at that point was to turn towards a coach who had succeeded in tournament football with a similarly sized nation. With the level of available talent dropping or ageing, there was also a requirement for pragmatism and realism. Instead, Scottish FA officials spoke of a data-led search for Clarke’s successor, which led them to a coach who had never managed in international football before. Trying to be too smart by half? This team was not fundamentally broken, it just needed to progress.

Nobody of sane mind should insist upon Scotland morphing into the Ajax team of the 1970s. The baseline, created by Clarke, is now tournament participation. This summer’s World Cup was the latest example of how finals involvement positively alters attitudes within and outside Scottish football to an unparalleled level. That is the important thing. The rest is fluff.

There were 34,000 at Hampden for Slovenia’s visit; hardly disastrous in broader Nations League context but almost 20,000 short of capacity. The public are yet to buy into Pocognoli and the blue-sky vision sold by his employers.

How does Pocognoli handle Ben Gannon-Doak?

Some in Scotland would have us believe Gannon-Doak is the tartan equivalent of a young Ryan Giggs. The truth is that at 20 Gannon-Doak is a player who is lightly raced at club level and, at this point, looks unlikely to make a first-team impact at Bournemouth. He has searing pace and a directness that scares defenders, which is offset by woeful decision making. Whether these shortcomings can he improved upon very much remains to be seen.

What is clear is that Gannon-Doak cannot operate as a right wingback for Scotland against credible opposition. Deploying him there also denies a start to Aaron Hickey, who is undeniably one of Scotland’s best players. Gannon-Doak is a winger (as are Josh McPake and Findlay Curtis). Pocognoli’s first-choice method does not involve wingers. Something has to give.

View image in fullscreen Ben Gannon-Doak, pictured holding off Slovenia’s Erik Janza, is not a wingback. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

What is the wider scenario that Pocognoli is part of?

The Scottish FA suddenly has a chief football officer in Craig Mulholland, and a head of strategy, operations and performance in Graeme Mathie. The latter was plucked from the Scottish second tier and the former was present in the dressing room during Scotland’s Nations League fixtures. The move to insert this level of middle management carrying wishy-washy job descriptions is strange, not least when neither of the individuals in question can provide working examples of markedly improving the big picture with an equivalent nation. Meanwhile, the new Scotland Under-21s manager, Tony Docherty, who is fielding teams in the same formation as Pocognoli, last took charge of a plummeting Ross County.
