Mr Uwaleke said a renewed DFRRI-type programme should not reproduce past institutional arrangements but be redesigned as a community-centred rural productivity and infrastructure initiative.

He said the initiative should be jointly implemented by the federal, state and local governments, with clear accountability mechanisms and measurable outcomes.

According to him, these commitments must be translated into a coordinated national agricultural productivity programme with measurable targets, clear institutional responsibilities and adequate funding.

“Its priorities should include feeder roads, small-scale irrigation, rural electrification, water supply, produce aggregation centres, storage facilities, primary healthcare access and market infrastructure.

“Such a programme can accelerate grassroots development by connecting farming communities to markets, reducing transportation costs, improving access to agricultural inputs and creating employment through rural infrastructure projects.

“The emphasis should be on raising output per hectare, increasing multiple cropping, improving yields, reducing post-harvest losses and strengthening linkages between farmers, agro-processors and domestic markets,” he said.

Mr Uwaleke said the programme would provide a practical means of ensuring that economic recovery reached communities that had remained disconnected from the benefits of national growth.

“The emphasis must be on functional infrastructure and productive assets rather than politically distributed projects that have little lasting economic value,” he said.

Mr Uwaleke noted that beyond agriculture, the cost of energy remained a major constraint on domestic production.

He said manufacturers, small businesses and service providers continued to face high operating costs because of unreliable electricity supply and dependence on alternative energy sources.

The CMAN president said expansion of gas infrastructure, renewable energy, embedded generation and reliable grid supply must become integral components of the government’s prosperity agenda.

He said reducing energy costs would improve industrial competitiveness, encourage domestic production, reduce dependence on imported goods and create employment opportunities.

“The same logic applies to transportation and logistics.

“The completion of strategic roads, railways, ports and inland logistics infrastructure should be prioritised according to their economic returns and capacity to reduce the cost of moving people and goods.

“A well-connected agricultural or industrial production centre can generate substantially greater economic value than an isolated project with limited linkages to productive activity.

“Infrastructure investment must consequently be evaluated not only by the amount spent or kilometres constructed but also by its contribution to productivity, trade and employment,” he explained.

Mr Uwaleke said Nigeria needed a deliberate strategy to deepen domestic manufacturing, strengthen agro-processing, develop industrial clusters and encourage production of goods where the country had competitive advantage.

He noted that achieving this would require more than incentives and policy declarations.

The expert said it demanded reliable energy, efficient ports, affordable long-term finance, predictable taxation, effective trade facilitation and a stable regulatory environment.

Mr Uwaleke also called for stronger coordination between the fiscal and monetary authorities.

(NAN)

World.title: Poor record-keeping caused confusion over NAF crash manifest – Ex-SSS director
World.content:
A former Director of the State Security Service (SSS), Mike Ejiofor, has attributed the conflicting figures surrounding the number and identities of people aboard the Nigerian Air Force (NAF) aircraft that crashed in Ondo State to poor record-keeping.

Mr Ejiofor said proper documentation of passengers and crew members aboard the aircraft would have made it easier to establish the exact number of people on board and identify the casualties.

The NAF released the names of 25 people aboard the aircraft, rather than the 32 earlier reported by government officials.

Mr Ejiofor spoke on Arise Television’s Daybreak programme on Wednesday.

Commenting on the conflicting figures, he said the authorities should have been able to rely on the aircraft’s manifest to establish the identities of everyone on board.

“It goes again to the issue of data keeping; it would have been easier to get the manifest,” he said.

He said there was a possibility that some people aboard the aircraft might not have been included in the available manifest.

“I think they should rely more on the manifest of the aircraft if it was actually compiled from the people in the aircraft and their names were contained in a manifest,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“It’s a sad situation that this simple record-keeping can just be having conflicts.”

NAF recent aircraft crash

The NAF aircraft crashed on 5 October in a riverine swamp in the Igbokoda area of Ondo State.

According to the information provided by the authorities, the ATR-42 military aircraft, with tail number NAF 931, was on a routine maritime patrol and transport mission from Benin City to Lagos when air traffic controllers lost contact with it.

The NAF said all 25 people on board – 20 passengers, mostly military personnel, and five crew members, died in the crash.

The wreckage was located in a dense, muddy swamp opposite a local naval base. Recovery efforts have reportedly been hampered by the terrain and the fact that much of the wreckage became submerged in water and mud.

President Bola Tinubu declared three days of national mourning and ordered an investigation into the cause of the crash.

The incident has also renewed concerns over the safety and maintenance of military aircraft in the country.

‘Investigate NAF aircraft operations’

Mr Ejiofor said the crash should prompt a broader examination of the Nigerian Air Force’s aircraft fleet, including the maintenance history and operational condition of its aircraft.

He described the frequency of military aircraft crashes as a concern that should be investigated thoroughly.

“What is the state of maintenance of all these aircraft? How long have they been serviced? From records we have, there have been over 10 crashes in the last 10 years,” he said.

“We should look into the general operations of the Air Force.”

He also cited the 21 May 2021 crash in which Ibrahim Attahiru, then chief of army staff, and other military personnel were killed.

Mr Ejiofor said the recurring incidents warranted a comprehensive review of military aviation operations rather than investigations being limited to individual crashes.

Crash site poses rescue challenge

On the search and rescue operation following the latest crash, Mr Ejiofor said the difficult terrain had posed a significant challenge to rescuers.

He said the proximity of the crash site to military and police facilities would ordinarily have raised expectations of a swift response, but the swampy terrain complicated the operation.

“The terrain posed a very serious challenge, and as we speak, the forces of the aircraft have not been recovered yet. So, there’s no hope that there will be any life,” he said.

He, however, cautioned against blaming those involved in the rescue operation, given the conditions at the crash site.

Mr Ejiofor also cautioned against drawing conclusions about what caused the loud sound reportedly heard before the aircraft crashed.

He said it was too early to determine whether the aircraft exploded before hitting the ground or whether the impact itself produced the sound.

“For me, these are speculations,” he said.

“It’s possible the impact on crashing was the deafening noise, it might not.”

He added that an explosion could also have occurred before impact, potentially contributing to the scattering of debris and body parts.

“It’s also possible that there was an explosion before the impact, which led to the dissemination and finding of body parts,” he said.

He stressed that the cause of the crash could only be established after a proper investigation.

“So, until the investigation is complete, we can’t be specific about whether it was an explosion in the air or the impact on the ground,” he said.

World.title: Plane Crash: Aiyedatiwa visits site, says aircraft’s main body yet to surface, human parts recovered
World.content:
Search operations continued on Wednesday at the site of the crash of the Nigerian Air Force plane at Igbokoda, headquarters of Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State. Still, divers could not locate the main body of the aircraft.

The divers, comprising the Police, Navy and locals, including members of the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), only managed to bring out some human body parts as well as pieces of the aircraft.

Ondo State Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa disclosed this to journalists during an assessment visit to the crash site.

Mr Aiyedatiwa visited the site alongside personnel of the Nigerian Navy and Nigerian Air Force, divers, the South-west Director of the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Director of the State Emergency Management Agency and residents who had participated in rescue efforts since Monday.

The ill-fated ATR-42 aircraft, which was carrying Nigerian Air Force personnel on a special mission from Benin to Lagos, crashed at Igbokoda on Monday morning.

NAF authorities said 26 people were on board the aircraft at the time it crashed.

According to the governor, no survivors had been found, noting that only parts of bodies, clothes and jackets belonging to Air Force personnel and broken aircraft parts were recovered and preserved for further investigation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the main body of the aircraft had not been sighted as it was believed to be submerged in the swamp.

Mr Aiyedatiwa, from the local government area where the crash occurred, explained that the difficulty of accessing the site prompted him to direct the Ministry of Works to deploy two amphibious machines, popularly known as swamp buggies, to open wider access through the waterways.

He said the machines had enabled rescue teams to move bigger boats closer to the crash site and were being used to excavate the soil in search of other parts of the wreckage or the main body of the aircraft.

The governor further said the aircraft had still not been sighted as of the time of his visit. At the same time, Navy personnel and local divers continued searching the deeper sections of the area for possible bodies and the cockpit.

Mr Aiyedatiwa said only the pilot could have explained the cause of the crash, adding that the occupants were believed to have died.

He said the swamp’s nature and depth could have caused the aircraft to become deeply submerged in the mud.

“From construction experience and analysis of this area, for you to get to refusal level, it’ll get to about 30 metres deep,” he said, adding that the aircraft could have gone completely into the mud.

He said jet fuel was flowing into the water, polluting the area with aviation fuel.

He said he was grateful the aircraft did not crash in the middle of the community, adding that it would have been a major catastrophe.

According to him, residents who witnessed the incident said the aircraft appeared to be coming down with a sound suggesting a bad engine and was almost landing within the community.

He said the pilot managed to manoeuvre the aircraft away from the community before it landed about 200 metres away and went straight into the swamp.

The governor said only the pilot could have explained the effort made to manoeuvre the aircraft away from the community.

Mr Aiyedatiwa also sympathised with the families of the deceased and the Nigerian Air Force, describing the victims as able and young Nigerians who had signed up to defend and protect the territorial integrity of the country.

He, however, said that based on what had been seen at the crash site, he doubted whether any of the victims could return to life.

“May their souls rest in peace,” he prayed.

Mr Aiyedatiwa, however, urged the search and rescue teams to intensify efforts to get out the remaining parts of the aircraft and the bodies of the victims.

Earlier, the Commander of the Nigerian Navy Forward Operating Base, Igbokoda, Andy Alemongwa, briefed the governor on the progress of the search-and-rescue operation.

Also on Wednesday, the Flag Officer Commanding, Western Naval Command, Abubakar Mustapha, and the Air Officer Commanding, Logistics Command, Nigerian Air Force, Abubakar Suleh, inspected the crash site of the Nigerian Air Force ATR-42.

Mr Mustapha, a rear admiral, conveyed the appreciation of the Chief of Defence Staff, Olufemi Oluyede, a general, and the service chiefs to the Ondo State Government, communities, emergency agencies and other stakeholders for their support since the incident occurred.

He urged stakeholders to remain calm and continue to cooperate with the various agencies involved in the recovery operation.

At the site, the team assessed the situation and provided technical guidance to facilitate the timely recovery of the submerged aircraft and its contents.

As part of the recovery efforts, the team began an underwater survey using side-scan sonar equipment to map the crash site and determine the submerged aircraft’s position.

The sonar survey is expected to help divers and other technical personnel locate the aircraft and plan subsequent recovery operations, including deploying a swamp buggy to facilitate excavation in the difficult terrain.

World.title: 2027 Polls: ‘84% intend to vote, but only 41% committed’ – Yiaga survey
World.content:
A new voter intention survey by Yiaga Africa has revealed a wide gap between Nigerians’ stated intention to vote in the 2027 general elections and their actual commitment to participating in the polls.

The survey found that while 84 per cent of respondents said they were likely or very likely to vote in the 2027 elections, only 41 per cent of that group said they were certain and committed to voting.

The findings were presented in the third edition of Yiaga Africa’s National Voter Intention Survey (NVIS 3.0) at a policy roundtable on voting intentions ahead of the 2027 general elections in Abuja on Wednesday.

The survey was designed to assess voter interest and participation and identify factors that could encourage or discourage Nigerians from taking part in the elections.

According to Yiaga Africa, 2,470 Nigerians aged 18 and above across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory participated in the September 2026 survey.

Of the respondents, 2,066 were interviewed by telephone, while 404 were interviewed face-to-face, particularly in rural communities.

The Senior Manager and Head of Knowledge Management and Learning at Yiaga Africa, Safiya Bichi, said the mixed approach ensured that people without access to telephones, especially those in rural communities, were not excluded.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Over 2,400 people were surveyed. We used a mixed method where we used telephone lines and traditional surveys to reach out to people and administer the survey questions,” Ms Bichi said.

She said the survey was intended to provide a broader picture of Nigerians’ attitudes towards the 2027 elections.

Ms Bichi said the 84 per cent intention to vote recorded in the latest survey did not necessarily translate into a firm commitment to participate in the election.

“84 per cent of citizens said they intended to vote, but only 41 per cent are committed to vote in this election,” she said.

She explained that a significant proportion of those who said they intended to vote had not yet decided which candidate they would support.

According to her, 44 per cent of the 84 per cent who said they intended to vote had not yet settled on their preferred candidates.

This, she said, presents political parties and candidates with a large pool of voters who could still change their preferences before the election.

She also said between six per cent and 10 per cent of respondents were either disinterested or undecided about participating in the election.

The latest figure represents an increase in overall voter intention compared with the first two rounds of the survey.

Yiaga Africa said 77 per cent of respondents indicated that they were likely to vote in the first NVIS, conducted in December, while the figure dropped to 73 per cent in the second survey before rising to 84 per cent in the third round.

However, the survey showed that the proportion of respondents who were “very likely” to vote has continued to decline.

According to the organisation, 52 per cent of respondents in the first survey said they were very likely to vote. That figure fell to 48 per cent in the second survey and 47 per cent in the third.

Ms Bichi said the difference suggested that although more Nigerians expressed an intention to vote, their certainty about actually participating in the election remained a concern.

Insecurity threatens participation

Insecurity emerged as one of the most significant threats to voter participation.

The survey found that 61 per cent of respondents feared that violence could prevent them from voting.

The concern was particularly pronounced in the North-East, where 78 per cent of respondents identified violence as a potential barrier to voting.

The survey also found that 82 per cent of respondents were very concerned that insecurity could affect the conduct of the elections.

The findings point to a dual concern among voters: fear of violence during the electoral process and doubts about the ability of security agencies to protect voters.

Only 48 per cent of respondents said they trusted security agencies to protect their votes during the elections.

Ms Bichi said improved security remained the strongest factor likely to motivate Nigerians to participate in the 2027 elections.

According to the survey, 83 per cent of respondents said improved security would motivate them to vote.

Another factor, 38 per cent of respondents identified as better logistics, while 20 per cent cited stronger candidates.

Ms Bichi said security and the quality of candidates had remained among the major factors influencing voter participation across the three rounds of the survey.

Confidence in INEC falls

The survey also revealed declining confidence in the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

Only 34 per cent of respondents said they were confident in INEC ahead of the 2027 elections.

This is down from 45 per cent in each of the first two rounds of the NVIS.

Confidence in INEC was particularly low in some regions. Yiaga Africa said 62 per cent of respondents in the South-east expressed a lack of confidence in the electoral commission. In comparison, the North-East recorded 62 per cent in another measure cited during the presentation.

The survey also found that Nigerians had greater confidence in some technological components of the electoral process than in the institution administering the election.

Forty-nine per cent of respondents said they trusted election technology, including accreditation and the IReV results-transmission system, compared with the 34 per cent who expressed confidence in INEC.

Ms Bichi said the finding suggested that Nigerians were increasingly placing their trust in electoral technology rather than solely in the institutions responsible for conducting elections.

Trust in electoral process becomes partisan

Yiaga Africa also found a relationship between citizens’ assessment of the current government’s performance and their confidence in the electoral commission.

The survey found that 54 per cent of respondents approved of the current government’s performance, while 71 per cent rated the state of the economy as poor or very poor.

Ms Bichi said confidence in INEC appeared to have taken on a partisan dimension.

She said respondents who rated the current government’s performance highly were also more likely to express confidence in INEC. In contrast, those dissatisfied with the government’s performance tended to have lower confidence in the electoral commission.

This, she said, suggested that public trust in the electoral process was not merely institutional but was increasingly influenced by political perceptions.

Low confidence in judiciary

The judiciary also recorded low levels of public confidence in its ability to resolve electoral disputes.

The survey found that 63 per cent of respondents were not confident that the judiciary would resolve electoral disputes fairly and effectively after the elections.

The South-South recorded the highest level of distrust, with 81 per cent of respondents in the region expressing a lack of confidence in the judiciary’s handling of electoral disputes.

The finding adds another layer to concerns over public confidence in Nigeria’s electoral process, from voting and security to the electoral commission and the post-election dispute resolution system.

Desire for change drives voter intention

The survey also examined why Nigerians intended to vote.

The desire for change in leadership emerged as the leading motivation, with 49 per cent of respondents identifying it as their main reason for voting.

Only 20 per cent identified civic duty as their motivation, while 16 per cent pointed to specific candidates.

Ms Bichi said the findings suggested that candidates themselves were not currently the primary motivation for participation.

Rather, the desire for a change in leadership appeared to be the dominant factor influencing voter intention.

Vote buying remains a concern

The survey also highlighted the continuing influence of vote buying on Nigeria’s electoral process.

Nineteen per cent of respondents, about one in five people surveyed, said they received money as an incentive to vote for a particular candidate in an election.

The prevalence was higher in some regions, with 32 per cent of respondents in the North-West saying they had received money to vote for a specific candidate.

Young people also featured prominently in the findings, with 24 per cent of young respondents saying they had received money to vote for a candidate.

The findings suggest that despite ongoing electoral reforms and efforts to curb inducement, financial incentives remain a significant feature of voters’ experiences.

The survey recorded a significant increase in public awareness of electoral reforms.

Only 24 per cent of respondents were aware of the electoral reform process during the first NVIS conducted in December.

The figure increased to 37 per cent in the second survey conducted in March and rose sharply to 62 per cent in the third survey.

Yiaga Africa attributed the increase to growing public awareness following the passage of the 2026 Electoral Act.

Among the reforms respondents were aware of were changes relating to accreditation and the electronic transmission of election results.

Young people less likely to vote

Despite the prominence of young Nigerians in the country’s electorate, the survey found that younger respondents showed weaker intentions to vote than older Nigerians.

Only 40 per cent of respondents in the younger age group indicated that they were likely to vote.

In contrast, 64 per cent of respondents aged 61 and above indicated that they were likely to participate.

The finding suggests a significant participation gap between younger and older voters and raises concerns about political parties’ and electoral stakeholders’ ability to mobilise young Nigerians ahead of 2027.

The survey also found a gender gap in voter intention, with 65 per cent of men indicating a likelihood to vote compared with 57 per cent of women.

INEC responds

Responding during the panel session, Victoria Eta-Messi, director of the Voter Education and Publicity Department at INEC, acknowledged the concerns around public trust and voter participation but defended the commission’s efforts to improve the electoral process.

Ms Eta-Messi said continued focus on the 2023 elections without recognising improvements made since then was concerning.

“The fact that people just keep holding on to 2023 rather than seeing the small steps that we’re making is a bit worrisome,” she said.

She, however, acknowledged that INEC still had significant work to do to increase participation and restore public confidence.

She cited the recently concluded Osun election as an example of improvements the commission was seeking to build on.

According to her, INEC had been concerned about the Osun election because of the attention it would attract as a test of the commission’s preparations ahead of 2027.

She said the commission was encouraged by the conduct of the election, particularly improvements in the deployment of personnel and materials.

Ms Eta-Messi said INEC was also working to improve its infrastructure and logistics, while engaging transport unions, including the National Union of Road Transport Workers and the National Association of Road Transport Owners, to address challenges experienced during previous elections.

She said training of INEC staff and ad hoc personnel was also being strengthened to ensure that officials understand the electoral process and perform their duties effectively at polling units.

Technology and logistics

The INEC official said the commission was also working to ensure that technology was deployed appropriately during elections while maintaining human safeguards.

She said technology would not be allowed to operate without checks and controls, stressing that human oversight would remain part of the electoral process.

She also identified logistics as one of the areas requiring continued attention.

According to her, the commission’s experience during the Osun election showed that better planning could improve the movement of personnel and electoral materials and ensure that polling units opened on time.

Need for grassroots mobilisation

Ms Eta-Messi said improving electoral participation would require greater engagement with Nigerians at the grassroots.

She said a significant proportion of the electorate lived outside major urban centres and that electoral stakeholders must therefore use available platforms to reach citizens in local communities.

She said INEC was engaging organisations and institutions that could assist in voter education and mobilisation, including the National Orientation Agency (NOA).

World.title: Afrilition and the prophesy of an African renaissance, By Adéwálé Àjàdì
World.content:
Afrilition is a call to service to be the generation that is willing to sacrifice comfort so that posterity will stand in excellence. Like the story of Joseph, prophecy is not determinism but a call to duty and commitment in faith so that our vision becomes our fate.

Afrilition expresses ancestral promise and affirmation, and it inevitably strays into a prophetic voice, not just as a spiritual invocation but also as critical engagement with trends and patterns. For me, as a writer, this is not new territory. In the early 2000s, I wrote a piece for Vanguard newspaper based on my experience of a Venezuelan film titled Sequestro Express. It dealt with kidnapping that had become endemic in this oil-rich but deeply divided society. It awakened something in me, and I wrote to warn that kidnapping on a mass scale was coming to our beloved Nigeria if we did not address the social cracks urgently. The comment section was devastating to my ego, as responses mocked and attacked me; they especially seemed to suggest that living abroad dislocated me from understanding Nigeria. Well, we have watched kidnapping replace armed robbery as Nigeria’s violent pathology. Join the Premium Times WhatsApp Community For Quick Access To News and Happenings Around You. Open in WhatsApp The thing about prophecy is that only God sees all and is always right; even with the highest gift, we prophesy only in part. Afrilition as part prophecy is showing early signs of alignment. This last week, the IMF published the top 20 countries with the largest GDP based on Purchasing Power Parity (PPP). The report has two African countries ranked 18th and 19th, respectively: Egypt and Nigeria. PPP ranking provides a better reflection of each country’s true market size, production volume, and domestic purchasing power, without exchange rate distortion. In line with Afrilition‘s prediction, the trend towards economic transformation is emerging. IMF further predicts that Nigeria will be the sixth largest contributor to Global Economic Growth in 2026 by driving 1.5 per cent of all new economic activity in the world.

Some African institutions are acting in very visionary ways, especially in processing African mineral wealth and developing industrial capacity to change patterns from being producers of raw and primary commodities to adding value through industrial processes and producing secondary and finished goods. Kenya has banned all unprocessed minerals, starting September 2026, whilst constructing three local gold refineries. Zimbabwe added to its restrictions on raw lithium concentrate, the extraction of antimony and tungsten in September. Both Guinea and Ghana have prohibited the export of unrefined gold, with stricter raw gold export regulations in Guinea. Malawi and Botswana have also implemented bans on critical transition minerals like cobalt, lithium, manganese, and rare earth elements. There is the boom in agro-processing and its effect on import substitution, like the ongoing effort of Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire to translate their 60 per cent of world cocoa production into processing chocolate, with a 2030 plan to process 80 per cent of their own cocoa beans locally. Ethiopian coffee is going through something similar, and so is the West African cashew.

The Dangote case study is worthy of a standalone, as the level of intention to transform here is a force of true Pan-African imagination. In 2003, at the end of the Obasanjo administration in Nigeria, the outgoing government offered that Nigeria’s moribund refineries in Port Harcourt and Kaduna be sold to a consortium that included Dangote. There was a major public outcry that this was the worst kind of cronyism. Editorial after editorial depicted this proposal as state capture. In my own family, this fuelled a major disagreement between my youngest brother and me. He saw it as part of my glorification of Obasanjo because it seemed, in those days, that he could do no wrong in my sight (things have since changed completely). My brother’s position had a lot of merit, and so did the editorials because, in a privatised public business, the questions of true value will never end. Had Dangote taken over the Nigerian government refineries, he would have had to go through business by attrition. Today, he has built the largest refinery on the continent and is expanding it towards the largest in the world. He has also broken ground on another refinery for East Africa, while the wind of war has benefited his refinery, so that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz put wind beneath his business wings. The emergence of these patterns and policies is in line with Afrilition. These are just the beginnings, and the battle to keep Africa as an extractive provider of primary commodities will enter a new and more sophisticated phase beyond the blatant violent destabilisation we see in many corners of the continent. The most egregious of which is in Sudan and the DRC Congo.

There is the boom in agro-processing and its effect on import substitution, like the ongoing effort of Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire to translate their 60 per cent of world cocoa production into processing chocolate, with a 2030 plan to process 80 per cent of their own cocoa beans locally. Ethiopian coffee is going through something similar, and so is the West African cashew. The emergence of these patterns and policies is in line with Afrilition. These are just the beginnings, and the battle to keep Africa as an extractive provider of primary commodities will enter a new and more sophisticated phase beyond the blatant violent destabilisation we see in many corners of the continent. The most egregious of which is in Sudan and the DRC Congo. The dreams that Joseph told his brothers did not say they were not stars themselves, but their own insecurity led the brothers to nearly kill him and eventually sell him into slavery. Over the next few decades, there will be many tests of African will to transform and realise its civilisation. Despite African excellence not being to dominate others, this will not stop them from doing all in their power to maintain their chokehold. They will try to keep Africa as an extractive and consumer- or importation-dependent space. Afrilition is a call to service to be the generation that is willing to sacrifice comfort so that posterity will stand in excellence. Like the story of Joseph, prophecy is not determinism but a call to duty and commitment in faith so that our vision becomes our fate. Stay Ahead with Premium Times

World.title: CJN charges judges to uphold integrity matching beauty of new industrial court’s headquarters
World.content:
Chief Justice of Nigeria (CJN) Kudirat Kekere-Ekun called on the judges of the National Industrial Court of Nigeria (NICN) to uphold integrity to match the beauty of the court’s new headquarters complex, which she inaugurated on Wednesday.

“Let its imposing physical presence be matched by integrity, independence, competence, discipline, and fidelity to the law,” she said during the inauguration of the complex in Abuja.

She expressed confidence that the building would be an enabling environment for the court to discharge its duties and contribute meaningfully to the development of labour and industrial jurisprudence.

The building inauguration took place as part of the ocassion marking the commencement of the NICN’s new 2026/2027 legal year.

The President of the NICN, Benedict Kanyip, expressed the court’s commitment to strengthening capacity to discharge dignity and that the courtroom is accessible to all persons who seek justice.

Like the CJN, he noted that buildings “do not dispense justice and technology does not replace judicial wisdom” but only support efficiency.

Emphasising human roles in advancing cause of public good, Mr Kanyip said, “Infrastructure does not guarantee public governance.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He affirmed the NICN’s commitment to ensuring integrity and impartiality remain guiding principles.

“Fairness must remain at the heart of our decisions. With respect for the policies of the rule of law must remain absolute,” he said.

He noted that the NICN exists to provide a peaceful and lawful environment for the growing industrial and human industries, protect rights and uphold lawful obligations.

The building

Wednesday’s inauguration serves as the climax of the construction project which the former and pioneer president of the NICN, Babatunde Adejumo, started in 2010.

The building has four floors with seven courtrooms and one ceremonial court.

It also boasts 11 judges’ chambers, three of which are designated for visiting judges. It also houses the president and heads’ chambers, judges’ library, chief registrar’s office and a conference room.

The basement has a parking lot with capacity of 35 cars along with stores and archives. The ground floor of the building has several offices.

The Chairman, Sunsplash Business Systems Limited, George Alonge and the quantity surveyor, Sunday Makinde, who led the construction, were present at the inauguration.

‘Beautiful building can’t deliver justice’

Speaking at the inauguration on Wednesday, the CJN said the building “represents many years of vision, planning, commitment, and perseverance…a practical response to the realities of the court’s present and future workload.”

She commended both the former and incumbent presidents of the NICN for their foresight and vision. The former president, Mr Adejumo, was in attendance.

She said the building stands as a reminder that “institutional development is a continuum.”

“One administration may conceive an idea, another may advance it, and yet another may bring it to completion,” the CJN said.

She however said the facility comes with responsibilities.

“A beautiful building cannot by itself deliver justice. The true measure of this edifice will ultimately be found in what takes place within its walls,” she said.

She said that the completion of the building should not be the end of responsibility, as she called for proper maintenance and preservation to ensure the edifice continues to serve the court effectively for generations to come.

The Minister of Justice and Attorney General of the Federation, Lateef Fagbemi, was represented at the event by the Acting Director of Civil Appeals of the Federal Ministry of Justice, Tijani Gazali.

Other prominent figures at the event included the Chief Judge of the Court of the Federal Capital Territory, Husseini Yusuf, the President, Customary Court of Appeal of the FCT, Stanley Lawal; President of the Court of Appeal, Monica Dongban-Mensem, and former CJN Mahmoud Mohammed, Walter Onnoghen.

New legal year speech

In his new legal year speech, Mr Kanyip noted that the NICN would embrace technology where necessary and ensure that the confidence imposed in us by those who use our services is justified through our broader position and our commitment to the rule of law.

Reflecting on the past 2025/2026 legal year, Mr Kanyip disclosed that 2,236 cases were disposed of.

He said the NICN aims at full digitalisation of the court process, expansion of its judicial infrastructure and improved welfare of its staff; he prayed for an improved budget for the NICN to actualise this.

He also disclosed that the National Judicial Council has recommended an NICN judge, Sanusi Kado, to the Court of Appeal.

The AGF, represented by Mr Gazali, commended the NICN for its structure and urged that the “responsibility is to build on the foundation to strengthen the court process, expand access to justice, and continue the possible use of technology, while ensuring that every worker and employer who comes before the court receives a fair, efficient, justified decision.

The CJN also said that the new legal year ceremony is an opportunity to reflect on the responsibilities that accompany judicial office.

“Judicial office is a great privilege, but it is also a profound responsibility. Every judge must remain conscious that the authority of the court is the right of the Constitution and the law, and that the confidence which the public places in the judiciary must be held up fresh every year.”

She acknowledged that the volume of cases can be demanding but reminded the judges that pressure “must never become an excuse for impatience, discourtesy, or inadequate attention to the matters placed before the court.”

The CJN said the judges should always remember that every case represents people, businesses, and livelihoods.

She also acknowledged that the workplace is changing with new forms of employment, digital platforms and remote agreements.

She said that while artificial intelligence could help in research, judges should always verify, as AI is susceptible to errors.

World.title: Whose archive, whose history? Reclaiming the African past, By Toyin Falola
World.content:
At its deepest level, therefore, “Whose History?” is a question about power. Who has the power to record history? Who has the power to preserve it? Who has the power to classify it? Who has the power to interpret it? Who has the power to teach it? And who has the power to define what the future generations will remember? These are not theoretical queries. They shape how societies perceive themselves and how they envision their future. In other words, the historical archive is also a political site since the ability to control memory can affect one’s identity.

I was impressed by the youth-dominated audience that attended my lecture on archives on 6 October, hosted by the G.A.S. Foundation in Lagos, as part of the MOWAA in Residence fellowship. Space does not allow me to speak elaborately on this public lecture, which attracted significant questions and concerns.

Before engaging with the history in an archive, it is first necessary to come to terms with the history of the archive. In other words, the question is not one of ownership alone. It is, more broadly, a question of power, memory, representation, evidence, silence, and authority. The temptation on approaching an archive looking for Africa’s history is to see the archive as nothing more than a repository of facts. But an archive is never a mere storehouse of facts. An archive is always a construction of history, a choice of what someone has found significant enough to collect, preserve, categorise, and pass on. And it is not an innocent construction.

An archive always reflects its historical context, institutions, technologies, politics, and structures of power. Every piece of documentation has an author, an institution, a purpose, an audience, and an historical context. A colonial report, missionary correspondence, government memo, newspaper, court document, photo, or museum inventory does not provide us with the entire past. It provides us with a representation of the past. For the African scholar, it would be wise to ask not only the question, “What does this document tell us?” but also the questions, “Who is the author, why was the document produced, and what was the structure of power at play here?” This is important because history can never be totally disconnected from the environment that produces it.

This problem is more important when dealing with the colonial archive. Colonial administrations collected immense amounts of data on African societies. Such information included taxation, agricultural practices, education, labour relations, migration patterns, religion, politics, conflicts, movement of population, and resistance. This material cannot be substituted by anything in reconstructing African history. However, it was primarily collected within administrative structures, the primary goal of which was to govern African populations. Africans were often seen in these documents as subjects of classification, measurement, administration, and control, rather than authors of their own history. Words like “native”, “tribe”, “custom”, “chief”, “primitive”, and “civilised” were not neutral terms. They were part of the terminology used by colonial powers to render African societies comprehensible and governable. In this way, colonial sources can tell us a lot about Africa, but also about colonial imagination of Africa.

It is for this reason that the scholarship of African studies, and historians like me, is relevant to anyone interested in the use of African archives. In my previous analysis of the colonial archives of Nigeria, I have made points that we should not approach the colonial archives just as a repository of data but as a product of a certain knowledge and power system. This treatment of the colonial archives in conjunction with other alternative perspectives shows the need to consider the official archives together with other forms of African historical memories such as oral history, indigenous systems of thought, rituals, chronicles, among others. It is not about discarding the colonial archive but considering it within a wider evidentiary world.

This demands, as often pointed out, reading against the grain, which is to do more than grasp the obvious meaning of the document and uncover the voices, experiences, political consciousness, and history hidden behind its language. A colonial official may term a people’s demonstration as a “disturbance.” But then the historian needs to ask himself, disturbance to whom? What caused such disturbance? Is it because of taxation, alienation of land, labour abuse, political marginalisation, religious conversion, or protest against the new administration system? Perhaps the colonial language converted politics into administration. And perhaps the language of the official hides the political consciousness of the people whom he talks about. The archive will reveal much more when its assumptions, contradictions, silence, and omissions are properly considered. At times, what a document fails to say could be just as historically important as what it says.

We must therefore rethink what we mean by an archive. The archive is not simply a room filled with files. A family album can be an archive. A traditional ruler’s palace can contain an archive. A photograph can preserve a history absent from government correspondence. Songs can act as a repository for political memories that span generations. Monuments represent a society’s understanding of its history. Museum objects hold information regarding technology, religion, aesthetics, social organisation, and identity.

This approach to methodology is also directly related to the wider concerns with regard to the sources and methods of African history. Previous works like Sources and Methods in African History: Spoken, Written, Unearthed, edited in collaboration with Christian Jennings, are useful because they combine various types of evidence in the construction of African history. This approach is important in many ways. It cannot be that African history can be constructed on the basis of the documentary record of the colonial administrations alone. Every archive always has its silences. Thus, the issue is not only about what is being stored but who has been silenced as well. Where are the voices of women whose lives were not deemed historically significant? Where are the rural people who could not access the institution of writing? Where are the workers, migrants, artisans, children, minorities, dissidents, religious groups, and common people? What became of the history of people who could not write and whose papers were not seen as valuable enough for storage? The absence of a certain community in an archive does not necessarily mean that the community has not played a historic role. It is possible that the priorities of the institution have led to it.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

We must, therefore, resist the perilous inclination to mistake the lack of evidence for evidence of lack. This is where the question of oral history becomes important. African societies have preserved knowledge across generations through oral traditions, genealogies, praise poetry, songs, proverbs, rituals, performances, religious practices, storytelling, and collective memory. The inability to record an event in written form does not mean that the event disappeared from historical consciousness. Orality can preserve dimensions of African experience that official archives never captured. Here, analysis of indigenous knowledge and oral traditions in Nigeria becomes useful.

First, we must focus on the oral traditions as an important source of historical information and indigenous memory, which may be treated as an archive. Consequently, it becomes obvious that African historical studies need to treat the very knowledge systems which were used by African societies to remember and transmit their past. Nevertheless, oral history cannot be idealised. Memories are rather changeable; people often forget, misinterpret, reconstruct, and even transform their memories in accordance with the current needs. Some events become important for families, while other events are neglected. Communities tend to construct competing versions of the same event. Political considerations shape memory, just as institutional considerations shape written documents. The solution here is not to substitute oral tradition for written archives but to put them in dialogue. Contradictions between official documents and oral tradition should not be considered as problems at all. They could turn out to be productive points for historical analysis.

We must therefore rethink what we mean by an archive. The archive is not simply a room filled with files. A family album can be an archive. A traditional ruler’s palace can contain an archive. A photograph can preserve a history absent from government correspondence. Songs can act as a repository for political memories that span generations. Monuments represent a society’s understanding of its history. Museum objects hold information regarding technology, religion, aesthetics, social organisation, and identity. Buildings, fabrics, recordings, movies, maps, court documents, family archives, and even digital materials can turn into historical evidence. The expanded idea of the archive relates directly to questions about the limited ideas about what counts as legitimate knowledge and delves into other types of archives of memory, speech, imagery, pictures, materiality, and native intellectual tradition. It is important to make such an intervention not only because of its political significance but also due to the methodological one. If knowledge takes on many shapes, then the historian needs to develop the capacity to recognise them.

The goal of researching African archives is to give back agency to African history. In other words, Africans were not just the targets of colonialism, governed subjects, and studied people. Africans were thinkers, diplomats, traders, politicians, entrepreneurs, intellectuals, priests, artists, farmers, institutional builders, negotiators, and resistors. Hence, the study of African history is not just about the impact of colonialism on Africa but also about what Africans did in response to colonialism…

The question of archives eventually becomes a question of ownership. Much of the history and culture of Africa exists beyond the continent in European and North American museums, libraries, universities, archives, and private collections. These items from Africa’s past include documentation, manuscripts, photographs, ethnological artefacts, and more that have travelled through a process of colonial extraction and academic collecting. This creates difficult questions. Who owns a document produced during the colonial rule? Who owns an artefact removed from an African community? Who has the right to classify indigenous knowledge? Which group has the authority to categorise indigenous knowledge? Which group has the authority to characterise African cultural materials? Which group has the authority to decide on the return, digitisation, restriction, or exhibition of objects?

Digitisation brings about a further complication into the picture. Digital technology can enable scholars, students, journalists, filmmakers, and communities in Africa to gain access to materials that might not have been previously accessible to them. It can preserve materials that would otherwise fall apart and enable researchers to gain access to materials that might be miles away from them. Digitisation, however, does not necessarily settle the problem of control. Who controls the servers? Who controls the access? Who owns the digital materials? Who creates the metadata? In which language should an African material be described? Does digitisation equal restitution, or will it be just another form of control? Africans, therefore, have to be participants in the process of archiving practices in the future and not merely users of digitised materials.

The historian, therefore, has to be not just a documentarian but an interrogator of documents. Who produced this source? When was it produced? Under what circumstances? For whom? What vocabulary does it employ? What political interests shaped it? What other sources confirm or contradict it? What voices are absent? What does the document reveal unintentionally? What does the document show us accidentally? These sorts of questions make us methodologically humble. We enter the archive prepared not only to confirm something but to complicate our assumptions. Good archival research is not about finding documents that will confirm our thesis. Great archival research allows the evidence to change, improve, and even disprove our thesis.

The goal of researching African archives is to give back agency to African history. In other words, Africans were not just the targets of colonialism, governed subjects, and studied people. Africans were thinkers, diplomats, traders, politicians, entrepreneurs, intellectuals, priests, artists, farmers, institutional builders, negotiators, and resistors. Hence, the study of African history is not just about the impact of colonialism on Africa but also about what Africans did in response to colonialism, about what institutions and ideas existed in Africa before colonialism, and about how they envisioned their futures. In other words, it is for this reason that the archive must not be confined within the walls of public buildings. Historical knowledge must move beyond the university to schools, museums, communities, media; to professionals such as documentary filmmakers and authors; and, most importantly, to the youth. Archival documents can be turned into exhibitions, documentaries, web pages, educational materials, community histories, and dialogues. It is about transforming archival research from a scholarly endeavour to dialogue across time.

At its deepest level, therefore, “Whose History?” is a question about power. Who has the power to record history? Who has the power to preserve it? Who has the power to classify it? Who has the power to interpret it? Who has the power to teach it? And who has the power to define what the future generations will remember? These are not theoretical queries. They shape how societies perceive themselves and how they envision their future. In other words, the historical archive is also a political site since the ability to control memory can affect one’s identity.

Toyin Falola, a professor of History, University Distinguished Teaching Professor, and Jacob and Frances Sanger Mossiker Chair in the Humanities at The University of Texas at Austin, is the Bobapitan of Ibadanland.

World.title: Cardiologist warns military personnel of hypertension, heart disease risks
World.content:
A military cardiologist, Life Ajemba, has warned that hypertension, prolonged stress, and inadequate sleep could increase the risk of cardiovascular disease among serving military personnel and veterans.

Mr Ajemba, a major-general, said hypertension remains one of the most common cardiovascular conditions among serving personnel and military retirees.

Speaking in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria on Wednesday in Abuja, he urged military personnel and veterans to prioritise their heart health through regular medical checks, physical exercise, healthy diets and adequate rest.

He cited studies which showed that hypertension accounted for 15.31 per cent of cases treated among mainly military retirees between 2015 and 2020.

He also referenced another study which found a hypertension prevalence of 34.3 per cent among military personnel.

He noted that major risk factors included alcohol consumption, tobacco smoking, family history of cardiovascular disease and being overweight.

According to him, the demanding nature of military service could also increase cardiovascular risks due to physical stress, psychological trauma, irregular schedules and inadequate sleep.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Military duties affect heart health through a combination of extreme physical stress, psychological trauma and environmental exposures that increase the risk of cardiovascular disease,” he said.

The military cardiologist explained that prolonged stress could increase the release of hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol, leading to increased heart rate and blood pressure.

He added that sleep deprivation, anxiety and other psychological pressures could further increase the risk of hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart attack and stroke.

Mr Ajemba stressed the importance of regular medical screening among military personnel, saying early detection could help identify silent conditions such as high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol levels and elevated blood sugar.

He said routine medical checks could include blood pressure and heart rate monitoring, blood tests, lipid profiles, electrocardiograms (ECGs), chest X-rays, and echocardiography where necessary.

“Early detection ensures that soldiers receive treatment while remaining fit for duty, preventing medical evacuation and safeguarding their long-term health,” he said.

He also encouraged military personnel to maintain regular physical exercise, saying fitness helped reduce blood pressure, improve heart efficiency and increase resistance to operational fatigue.

Mr Ajemba, however, advised personnel to combine physical fitness with healthy eating, adequate rest and avoidance of smoking and excessive alcohol consumption.

He said maintaining a healthy lifestyle could help military personnel reduce cardiovascular risks and remain fit both during active service and after retirement.

(NAN)

World.title: Nnaji advocates increased funding for education
World.content:
By Alumona Ukwueze

NSUKKA — Former Minister of Power, Prof. Bart Nnaji, has called for increased funding of education at all levels, saying adequate investment in the sector is critical to building a globally competitive economy in the 21st century.

Nnaji made the call on Wednesday in Nsukka while delivering the University of Nigeria, UNN, 66th Founders’ Day Lecture, titled, “Grappling with 21st Century Development Challenges through Higher Education in Nigeria.”

He said Nigeria could not achieve sustainable economic development without substantial investment in education to strengthen institutions, promote research and drive technological innovation.

The former minister urged governments at all levels to increase funding for education and promote strategic partnerships between universities and industries.

According to him, such partnerships would strengthen collaboration between the academic and business sectors while bridging the gap between classroom knowledge and the skills required in the workplace.

“I urge government at all levels to increase investments in education because records have shown that leading nations in economy and technology invest adequately in education.

“With adequate investments in education, universities will not only produce graduates but also become centres of innovation, research and technological advancement capable of providing solutions to the country’s economic and developmental challenges,” he said.

Nnaji, who is also Chairman of Geometric Power Group, stressed the need to prioritise Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics, STEM, education, noting that the future of the global economy increasingly depended on technological competence, innovation and the ability to develop home-grown solutions.

He urged Nigerians to believe in themselves and have confidence in the younger generation, saying Nigerian youths possessed the talent and intellectual capacity to compete favourably with their counterparts globally if given the necessary opportunities and support.

Nnaji also stressed the importance of competence and capacity in leadership, saying those entrusted with public responsibilities must possess the knowledge, ability and character required to deliver positive results.

“Nigeria needs leaders who will think strategically, take difficult decisions and deploy available resources effectively for the benefit of the people,” he said.

He, however, said Nigeria’s development challenges could not be addressed by government alone, urging universities, industries, professional bodies and other stakeholders to collaborate in developing the human capital required for national transformation.

Nnaji commended UNN for sustaining the Founders’ Day Lecture, noting that its founder, Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe, envisioned the institution as a world-class university with global standards and a mandate to provide comprehensive education for Nigerians.

He expressed appreciation to the university for finding him worthy to deliver the 66th Founders’ Day Lecture.

The Chairman of the occasion and 13th Vice-Chancellor of UNN, Emeritus Prof. Bartholomew Okolo, said the university’s founding was anchored on a vision to establish an institution capable of attaining the highest standards of academic excellence.

Okolo said the founding fathers of the university conceived a bold vision and mission that remained relevant to Nigeria’s development aspirations.

The former vice-chancellor commended the current administration of the university, led by Prof. Simon Ortuanya, for its infrastructure transformation and efforts to improve the physical and academic environment.

In his remarks, the Vice-Chancellor of UNN, Prof. Simon Ortuanya, said the Founders’ Day Lecture was instituted to commemorate the establishment of the university and honour the vision of its founder, Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe.

Ortuanya said the annual lecture provided a platform for intellectual discourse on national and global issues, while promoting the ideals of the university’s founding fathers, encouraging scholarship and critical thinking, and reflecting on the role of the university in Nigeria’s socio-economic development.

He said the best way to honour the founding fathers was not merely to celebrate their achievements but to sustain and advance the vision upon which the university was established.

“Let us honour the founding fathers by finishing what they began,” Ortuanya said.

World.title: AEDC expands digital channels for customer services
World.content:
By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja

ABUJA — The Abuja Electricity Distribution Plc, AEDC, has expanded its digital service channels with the launch of its MyPower Mobile and Web Apps to enable customers access and manage electricity services remotely.

The platforms bring key customer services into a single digital ecosystem, allowing customers to purchase electricity tokens, pay bills, report power outages and other service issues, as well as lodge and track complaints without visiting AEDC offices.

Customers can also use the platforms to monitor their energy consumption, access bills and payment receipts, manage multiple accounts and meters, and update their personal information digitally.

A statement by the company on Wednesday said the launch, which formed part of its Customer Service Week activities, was part of AEDC’s broader digital transformation programme aimed at improving customer experience.

Speaking at the launch, the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of AEDC, Engr. Chijioke Okwuokenye, said the initiative was designed to give customers greater control and convenience in their interactions with the company.

He said: “Our customers are at the heart of everything we do. As their needs and expectations evolve, we must evolve with them.

“The MyPower Mobile and Web Apps are significant steps in that direction, using technology to give our customers greater control over how they interact with AEDC and access the services they need.”

Okwuokenye said AEDC remained committed to improving its customer service and building an organisation that was more responsive, accessible and aligned with customers’ expectations.

The Chief Operating Officer of AEDC, Engr. Blessing Ogbe, said the digital platforms reflected the company’s commitment to continuously improving the customer journey.

“For us, this launch is another step in how we are redefining the way we serve our customers. We are building a culture where customer feedback informs how we design our processes, improve our channels and deliver our services,” she said.

Ogbe said the company would continue to listen, learn and innovate to ensure that its services kept pace with customers’ expectations.

As part of the digital rollout, AEDC also introduced a staff verification feature that enables customers to confirm the identity of company personnel before granting them access to their premises.

The company said customers who preferred mobile access could use the MyPower Mobile App, while those using computers or mobile browsers could access the Web App and enjoy similar services.

World.title: Mental health experts demand urgent action on Nigeria’s youth crisis
World.content:
Mental health

….As 4th Vanguard summit opens Friday

By Sola Ogundipe

Nigeria’s youth mental health crisis will come under sharp scrutiny as leading psychiatrists, public health experts and advocates press for stronger action on substance use, suicide, social isolation and the growing mental health pressures linked to social media and technology.

The 4th Vanguard Mental Health Summit on Friday October 9, at the Civic Centre, Victoria Island, in Lagos is expected to focus attention on the widening gaps in mental healthcare for young Nigerians, particularly the need for earlier intervention, accessible services and stronger support systems.

The event is themed “Advancing Youth Mental Health in Nigeria,” with “Mental Health in a Digital Age: Navigating Social Media, Technology and Wellbeing” as its sub-theme.

Lead presenter, Dr. Veronica Oluyemisi Nyamali, President of the Association of Psychiatrists in Nigeria and Chief Consultant Psychiatrist at the Federal Neuro-Psychiatric Hospital, Yaba, will speak on mental healthcare, addiction and suicide prevention.

Also speaking is Prof. Taiwo Lateef Sheikh, Professor of Psychiatry and Psychopharmacology at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, and former

President of the Association of Psychiatrists in Nigeria. His work includes

suicide prevention, mental health advocacy and policy.

Prof. Mashudat Bello-Mojeed, Professor of Psychiatry and Public Health and Chief Consultant Child Psychiatrist at the Federal Neuro-Psychiatric Hospital, Yaba, will address child and adolescent mental health, while Prof. Afekhide Ernest Omoti, 33rd President of the Nigerian Medical Association, will bring a broader healthcare perspective.

The addiction discussion will feature Dr. Daniel Ikpechukwu, a US-based substance abuse and behavioural health counsellor, and Dr. Ayantunde Kayode Ayankola, Senior Consultant Psychiatrist in Drug and Addiction Treatment and Rehabilitation at Neuropsychiatric Hospital, Aro.

The panel will include Dr. Tolu Ajomale, Director, Special Projects and Mental Health, Lagos State Ministry of Health; psychiatrists Dr. Olufunmilayo Akinola and Dr. Olufemi Oluwatayo; a legal practitioner, Ayo Adebusoye, Secretary-General, Nigeria Network of NGOs; and Deborah Omage, a mental health policy advocate and lived-experience leader. Ayankola will serve as lead panelist.

The discussions will examine the intersection of youth mental health with substance misuse, digital pressures, social isolation, family challenges and limited access to professional care.

World.title: David Silva comes out of retirement at 40 to join Hong Kong club Sha Tin
World.content:
By Adegboyega Adeleye

Former Manchester City and Spain midfielder David Silva has come out of retirement at the age of 40 to return to professional football with Hong Kong Premier League club Sha Tin.

Silva, who retired in 2023 after suffering an anterior cruciate ligament injury during pre-season training with Real Sociedad, is set to link up with the Hong Kong side and work towards making his debut.

The former City playmaker won the 2010 World Cup and two European Championships with Spain, while claiming four Premier League titles during a decade at Manchester City.

He won 11 major honours with City and scored 60 Premier League goals, earning a statue outside the club’s Etihad Stadium.

“I’m so excited to go to Hong Kong and enjoy the local culture, the food in Sha Tin and, of course, football in Hong Kong,” Silva said in an Instagram video.

Sha Tin said Silva would arrive in Hong Kong to settle in, join squad training and build up his match fitness before making his debut.

“David Silva will be in Hong Kong soon to settle in, link up with squad training, and build up to peak match fitness before making his pitch debut,” the club said.

Sha Tin are currently eighth in the Hong Kong Premier League after four matches and are scheduled to face Hong Kong Football Club on Sunday, October 18.

World.title: FBI arrests 18-year-old over alleged mass shooting plot at Mall of America
World.content:
FBI operatives

US authorities on Wednesday charged a man who allegedly planned a mass shooting at a shopping mall in Minnesota in support of the Islamic State group.

The FBI arrested Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, after he bought an AK-47 rifle and ammunition from an undercover agent in a sting operation that foiled his apparent plot.

“This individual allegedly obtained a weapon he hoped to use in a mass casualty attack in support of ISIS, but this FBI arrested him and put a stop to his plans,” said FBI Director Kash Patel.

Mohamud, from Richfield, Minnesota, allegedly intended to kill 30 to 60 people at the nearby Mall of America — a venue he apparently targeted as he claimed it was Jewish-owned.

He is accused of sharing his intentions with an FBI source in hundreds of messages exchanged since 2024, including a selfie-style video whereby Mohamud pledged his allegiance to IS.

Mohamud allegedly said he wanted to emulate other IS-inspired attacks such as the 2016 Pulse Nightclub Shooting in Florida and the 2025 Bondi Beach shooting in Australia.

He is said to have identified October 24 for his planned shooting — saying it would target Asians and other non-Muslims during a planned “Hmong Arts Celebration” at the mall.

“As alleged in the criminal complaint, Mohamud took substantial steps to plot to murder innocent people in the name of ISIS,” said Daniel Rosen, US attorney for Minnesota.

Mohamud is charged with one count of knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition in order to commit a federal crime of terrorism. He appeared before a federal judge on Wednesday.
