World.title: Africa: World Cotton Day - The Real Value of Africa's Cotton Comes After the Harvest
World.content:
World Cotton Day should measure more than output. It should ask how much manufacturing, employment and African-owned value the continent creates from every bale it grows.

A cotton boll is light enough to sit in the palm of a hand. The economy wrapped around it is not. Before cotton becomes a shirt, a uniform, a designer collection or a roll of industrial fabric, it can pass through farms, ginneries, spinning mills, weaving plants, dye houses, garment factories, logistics companies, retailers and digital marketplaces. At each stage, value is added. Across much of Africa, too many of those stages still happen elsewhere.

That is the contradiction World Cotton Day should bring into focus. Africa produced about 7.5 per cent of the world’s cotton in 2022, according to the Cotton to Cloth World Cotton Day data pack. Yet estimates compiled in the same document show that most African cotton leaves the continent before it is transformed. The precise share varies by source: UNCTAD places raw-cotton exports at 70 per cent, UNESCO cites an International Cotton Advisory Committee estimate of 81 per cent for sub-Saharan Africa in 2022, while the World Trade Organization estimate is higher still. The methodologies differ, but the industrial message is remarkably consistent: Africa grows cotton more successfully than it converts cotton into prosperity.

The imbalance becomes clearer at the other end of the chain. Drawing on the World Bank’s World Integrated Trade Solutions database, UNESCO reports that Africa exports about $15.5 billion worth of textiles, clothing and footwear each year but imports $23.1 billion, leaving a $7.6 billion deficit. This is not simply a trade statistic. It describes factories that could have been operating, skills that could have been acquired, brands that could have been built and incomes that could have circulated through African economies.



Raw cotton is valuable. What happens after the harvest is more valuable still. Ginning separates fibre from seed. Spinning turns fibre into yarn. Weaving and knitting create fabric. Dyeing, finishing, cutting, sewing, branding and retailing multiply the commercial possibilities. The African Development Bank estimates that ownership of the cotton value chain can generate a 600 per cent increase in economic value. That figure explains why the central question is not whether Africa should grow more cotton, but whether it can retain more of the value created from the cotton it already grows.

Benin offers an early indication of what the shift can look like. Cotton farming accounts for roughly 12 to 13 per cent of the country’s economy. The emergence of the Glo-Djigbe Industrial Zone has enabled about 30 per cent of Benin’s cotton to be processed locally, with annual output estimated at seven to ten million finished garments. Faki Adje, the zone’s deputy general manager, has said the wider effort to activate the cotton value chain could support 300,000 formal industrial jobs by 2030. These are ambitions, not guarantees, but the direction matters: the cotton field is being linked deliberately to the factory floor.

That link changes the development equation. A farmer’s productivity still matters, but so do electricity tariffs, water, freight costs, machinery finance, technical training, quality standards and the reliability of customs systems. Cotton policy cannot stop at agriculture ministries. It must reach finance ministries, trade authorities, power utilities, universities, logistics operators and the private investors who decide whether a mill is commercially possible.

The opportunity is also social. Cotton provides income to an estimated 3.5 million African farmers, although only about 17 per cent are women. Further down the chain, women make up between 70 and 90 per cent of the continent’s formal garment workforce. That contrast should shape policy. If value addition expands without deliberate attention to ownership, pay, skills and progression, women may remain concentrated in the least secure parts of the chain. If it is designed well, cotton industrialisation can widen women’s access not only to jobs, but to management, enterprise and capital.

The market is no longer hypothetical. Clothing and footwear sales in sub-Saharan Africa were valued at about $31 billion in 2020. Online commerce is widening the route to consumers: the share of active e-commerce shoppers in Africa rose from 13 per cent in 2017 to 28 per cent in 2021, reaching an estimated 334 million users. For African designers and manufacturers, digital distribution can shorten the distance between workshop and wardrobe. But a marketplace cannot compensate for an absent production base. The product still has to be made competitively, consistently and at scale.

Scale is where the African Continental Free Trade Area becomes central. A complete textile ecosystem need not be duplicated in every country. Cotton grown in one market can be ginned or spun in another, woven elsewhere, cut and sewn where specialised capacity exists, and sold across the continent. The advantage lies in connecting capabilities. Yet intra-African trade in textiles and apparel is valued at only $2.7 billion, about 8 per cent of continental imports. The AfCFTA is projected to lift intra-African trade by 11 per cent, but tariffs are only part of the obstacle. Slow borders, incompatible standards, costly transport and fragmented payments can erase the advantage of regional production.

Close 

World Cotton Day should therefore be less a ceremonial tribute to a crop than an annual industrial audit. Is Africa processing a larger share of its fibre? Are mills operating closer to capacity? Are farmers earning more predictable incomes? Are women progressing through the value chain? Are African manufacturers supplying African retailers? Are designers building brands that can compete at home and abroad? Are governments removing the costs that make local production uncompetitive?

Cotton is grown as a primary cash crop in 37 of Africa’s 54 countries. That reach gives the continent a foundation few industries enjoy: raw material, farming knowledge, an existing workforce, creative talent and a large consumer market. What remains uneven is the machinery that joins them together.

The cotton field should not be treated as the end of an export story. It is the beginning of an industrial one. The true measure of success will not be the number of bales Africa sends abroad, but the amount of skill, enterprise, manufacturing and wealth it builds before a single garment reaches the customer.

World.title: Kenya: The Researchers Building Kenya's Cotton Industry From The Seed Up
World.content:
At Kirinyaga University, researchers are testing whether Kenya can produce quality Bt cotton seed locally. The trials could help improve supply and lower costs, but taking the research to farmers will require commercial investment and support across the cotton value chain.

Inside a laboratory at Kirinyaga University in central Kenya and on nearby fields, researchers are investigating a question that could shape what farmers plant in future: can Kenya produce its own Bt cotton seed?

Their work aims to establish whether the seed, currently imported, can be produced locally as Kenya seeks to strengthen its cotton industry.



“The experiment is about more than producing seeds. It is about generating the evidence needed to determine whether a process can work locally before it is taken to farmers and commercial producers,” says Dr. David Kabata, one of the researchers involved.

According to Kabata, the trials started in September 2025 and seed from the trial plants is now ready for laboratory testing. The tests will assess whether the seed is true to type, viable and healthy, and retains the intended Bt trait.

Grace Wambui, the trials’ field assistant, says the process began when the team received approved and certified Bt cotton seed from Mahyco. They received seed for both male and female parent plants, which they planted on separate demonstration farms according to the trial requirements.

“With these trials we are trying to establish two things. First, whether it is possible to produce high-quality BT cotton seeds locally, and the second one is to see if cotton can become a perennial crop. We want to see if cotton plants can be retained for subsequent seasons and still remain productive instead of planting new seeds every season,” says Dr. Kabata.

According to Wambui, workers were trained to select suitable female plants for seed production using a sticky/non-sticky test. They took young cotton bolls from the female plants and rubbed them against the backs of their hands. Plants whose bolls felt sticky were considered unsuitable and uprooted, while those with non-sticky bolls were retained.

At the flowering stage, workers hand-pollinated the female plants to support seed production.

Kabata says the laboratory results will guide the next stage of research, whether the locally produced seed meets the required quality standards or falls short.

“If the seeds don't perform as expected, the team plans to identify what may have affected their quality and refine the production process before conducting further trials. The objective is not simply to produce seed once, but to establish a reliable process for producing quality cotton seed locally,” adds Dr. Kabata.

The research comes as Kenya seeks to revive its cotton industry, with access to adequate and affordable seed central to efforts to expand production. Kabata says local seed production could reduce costs if the trials succeed.

“If we are able to produce the seeds here, it means that the price can go down by half,” says Dr. Kabata.

Local production could also give Kenya greater capacity to align seed supply with farmers’ planting requirements. However, the Agriculture and Food Authority (AFA) cautions that producing seed locally will not automatically make it affordable. Prices will depend on the efficiency and scale of the production and distribution system.

Dr. Paul Chege, a crop scientist and biosafety expert, says local production could also help the country build seed reserves and maintain sufficient stock as farmers seek to expand production.

According to AFA, demand for Bt cotton seed is increasing as Kenya expands cotton production and promotes improved varieties. The authority expects demand to grow further as more farmers adopt Bt cotton and the area under cultivation increases.

Supply, however, has not always been sufficient to meet potential demand. Kenya depends on imported certified Bt cotton seed, with delays associated with government procurement sometimes disrupting farmers’ access.

“Lack of a local seed production and supply system is one of the major constraints affecting cotton production and expansion in Kenya. Emphasis should be on strengthening local production, multiplication, distribution and availability of Bt cotton seed, while ensuring that farmers have access to seeds in adequate quantities and before the planting season,” reads a statement from AFA.

Chege says local seed production alone will not resolve the challenges facing cotton farmers. Other parts of the value chain also need investment.

In the short term, he says, Kenya needs to strengthen extension services tailored to cotton production, revive existing ginneries and establish new ones to ensure farmers’ harvests can be processed.

He also advocates support for cottage industries to create jobs and enable more people to benefit from cotton production beyond the farm.

“Local production of Bt cotton seed is one of the critical factors that can revive the cotton industry by bringing down the cost of production and improving the quality of the produce, but it should not be viewed in isolation; it is not a silver bullet. Sound extension, proper soil and water management, mechanization and other agronomic practices must also be adhered to,” says Dr. Chege.

According to AFA, local seed production requires a system that connects research to farmers and, ultimately, finished products.

That means developing suitable cotton varieties, producing sufficient quality seed, testing and certifying it, and distributing it in time for planting. Farmers also need support to grow the crop successfully, while processors need the capacity to gin the harvested cotton and supply industries making textiles and clothing.

Close 

If effectively implemented, such a system could provide a more sustainable foundation for expanding cotton production and strengthening links between researchers, farmers and processors.

At Kirinyaga University, the researchers are working with an already approved and certified variety rather than developing a new one. This could shorten the route to supplying farmers if the locally produced seed meets the required quality and performance standards.

Kabata says commercial seed companies will need to take the work forward if the trials yield positive results. The university’s role is to establish whether quality seed can be produced locally and generate evidence to guide the next stage. It cannot produce seed on a commercial scale.

“This is a research production centre, so our main goal is, first of all, to do research and know whether it is possible to produce these seeds locally or not. From there, the other part we can play is to train people on how to produce these cotton seeds wherever they are,” he says.

Moving beyond the university’s demonstration farms will therefore require commercial seed companies and other producers to invest in larger-scale production and distribution.

Kabata is also calling on other researchers to pursue similar work and on the government to support institutions investigating ways to strengthen Kenya’s cotton industry.

World.title: Somalia: Beyond Irro's U.S. Visit - Next Steps for Washington-Hargeisa Relations
World.content:
Addis Abeba — President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi 'Irro' spent nearly two weeks in the United States from 5 to 19 September 2026, engaging in Washington and New York to press Somaliland's case for deeper international engagement. His program includes discussions with lawmakers, policy institutions, and engagement with the Somaliland diaspora. The visit gave Somaliland access to audiences that matter in American foreign-policy debates, but access by itself is not a policy outcome

Read Travel Guides For Somaliland, the more important questions are what follows the meetings and whether political attention converts into sustained relations with Congress, policy institutions, and American business. Can discussions about the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden lead to practical cooperation? And can Somaliland make an economic case that stands alongside its long-running argument for international recognition?

Discover morenewsNewsRead Daily News Since re-declaring independence from Somalia in 1991, Somaliland has built its own governing institutions and held a series of elections while continuing its long-running campaign for international recognition. For decades, however, that effort has not resulted in formal recognition by any UN member state. This situation changed on 26 December 2025, when Israel became the first UN member state to formally recognize Somaliland. The decision also generated strong opposition. The African Union reaffirmed its support for Somalia's sovereignty and territorial integrity, while Somaliland rejected the recognition



Follow Politics Somaliland has also maintained an official representative office with Taiwan since 2020. Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced the mutual establishment of representative offices in July 2020. This cooperation is in the areas of fisheries, agriculture, energy, health, education, and information technology. These relationships have increased Somaliland's external profile, but they have not removed their wider diplomatic dispute over its status.

Building Somaliland's case in Washington

A central event in the Washington Programme came when Irro delivered a keynote address at the Hudson Institute on 14 September, 2026, marking his first official U.S. visit since winning the November 2024 presidential election. During the event, President Irro framed Somaliland's value around regional maritime security, the strategic port of Berbera, and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb strait amid rising Red Sea tensions and Houthi threats.

Access by itself is not a policy outcome."

The port city of Berbera is situated on the Gulf of Aden, across from Yemen and near the maritime pathway that leads to the Red Sea. Continuing insecurity around the Red Sea has demonstrated how quickly regional conflict can affect commercial shipping and global trade. Recent attacks on commercial ships illustrate how rapidly the instability in these waters can influence international trade.

Discover moreNews subscription serviceInvestigative journalism reportsDaily news updatesCurrent events analysisRead NewspapersBreaking news alertsRead Local NewsBrowse MagazinesEthiopia election coverageBuy Maps Somaliland can point to Berbera, its coastline, and its strategic location. But geography alone will not build a partnership. Hargeisa also needs to show where practical cooperation could work, whether in trade, logistics, maritime affairs, or other areas of shared interest.

Irro also used the visit to strengthen contact with Capitol Hill. On 19 September, he met Senator Ted Cruz. According to Somaliland's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the discussion covered recognition, strategic cooperation, security, economic cooperation, and regional stability.

Senator Cruz had already made his position public. In August 2025, he wrote to President Donald Trump urging U.S. recognition of Somaliland, pointing to its position on the Gulf of Aden, relations with Taiwan, and possible security and economic cooperation. His position represents the view of a U.S. senator, not a change in U.S. recognition policy.

Congressional engagement with Somaliland also predates this visit in 2022; the Somaliland Partnership Act was proposed to require a review of aspects of the USA-Somaliland relationship, including security cooperation; it did not itself provide U.S. recognition of Somaliland.

The opportunity lies in what comes afterwards. Somaliland needs regular contact with lawmakers, congressional staff, and policy institutions. Those relationships have to continue when there is no presidential delegation in Washington.

From strategic interest to commercial reality

Security formed another part of the Washington program. On 17 September, Irro met with representatives from the Atlantic Council and the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. The Somaliland Foreign Ministry said the discussions covered the Horn of Africa, the Gulf of Aden, shipping lanes, international trade, and strategic cooperation.

The timing is understandable. Conflict in Yemen and attacks on commercial vessels have pushed Red Sea security higher on the international agenda. Somaliland sits beside this increasingly important maritime corridor. That gives Berbera both commercial and strategic relevance.

Somaliland should use this interest, but security should not become the entire basis of its relationship with Washington. Security priorities change. Trade, investment, technology, education, and business links can give the relationship a broader base that lasts beyond the current security concern.

This may be the harder test. Somaliland regularly promotes Berbera, livestock, fisheries, minerals, energy, and infrastructure as areas with economic potential. Getting those sectors discussed in Washington is useful. Getting companies to invest is another matter.

An American company considering it would first want a clear answer to practical questions--how easy is it to register and license a business? - Can the contract be enforced? - What taxes apply? - How are commercial disputes handled? -Can profit and capital be transferred? -And is there reliable information about the local market?

If the U.S. visit leads to interest from American business, Somaliland needs to be ready with credible information, clear procedures, and projects that investors can properly assess.

There is a difference between saying Somaliland has fisheries, minerals, or a strategic port and presenting a commercially workable opportunity. Diplomacy can open the door. The business environment will determine whether investors walk through it.

On 23 September, people from Somaliland, as well as those who support their cause, assembled in front of the United Nations Headquarters in New York City (Dag Hammarskjöld Plaza), asking for global recognition of their country. Somaliland's Foreign Ministry reported the rally as a public call for international recognition.

The gathering took place during the UN General Assembly high-level week. It was a diaspora-led public advocacy event rather than an official united national event, but it gave Somaliland supporters in North America a visible platform at a time when diplomatic and media attention was concentrated on New York.

Diplomacy can open the door. The business environment will determine whether investors walk through it."

The following day, Irro appeared at the Council on Foreign Relations, where the announced discussion focused on Somaliland's recognition bid and the regional security landscape. The two events served different purposes; the rally sought public visibility, while the CRP meeting placed Somaliland's arguments before a foreign-policy audience.

Somalia remains central to the equation

Somalia rejects Somaliland's claim to independence and maintains that Somaliland forms part of Somalia. The African Union and United Nations have also continued to affirm Somalia's sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity, even after Israel recognized Somaliland in December 2025. The United States has likewise stated that its policy has not changed. Washington's approach therefore sits within a wider set of interests involving its relationship with Mogadishu, counterterrorism, maritime security, and regional stability in the Horn of Africa. Somalia does not recognize Somaliland as an independent nation; therefore, Somalia views Somaliland as being a part of Somalia. The UN briefing also recorded Somalia's rejection of Israel's recognition decision.

Close 

For Hargeisa, this means making more than a historical argument for recognition. It also needs to explain how closer international engagement with Somaliland would fit within the wider region. That question will remain part of the debate.

Conclusion: What happens next?

A presidential visit can secure meetings and create attention. It cannot do the follow-up.

Congressional offices need continued engagement. Policy institutions need reliable contacts in Hargeisa. Investors need clear information. Business inquiries need timely answers. Security discussions will also need to move from general interest to specific areas of cooperation.

The diaspora also has the potential to contribute. Somalilanders across North America work in business, education, technology, and many other fields. Their professional networks can help build trade links, attract investment, support research, and connect people and institutions instead of primarily being organized to advocate for recognition.

The real test of Irro's visit will therefore come later.

Six months or a year from now, are the relationships built in Washington still active? Have business discussions moved forward? Are U.S. companies looking seriously at opportunities in Somaliland? Have any of the meetings led to practical cooperations?

Those questions will tell us more than the number of meetings held in September.

President Irro's visits gave Somaliland a larger audience in Washington. That is useful, but it is only a beginning.

Somaliland has spent years trying to get its case heard. Now it has to give Washington a reason to keep listening. AS

Editor's Note: Zakarie Mohamed Abdi serves as a senior advisor at Somaliland's Ministry of Trade and Tourism. He can be reached at Zakarieabdi2009@gmail.com

World.title: Africa: U.S. Backs Stronger AU-UN Role in Africa Conflicts, Supports UN Financing for AU-Led Missions
World.content:
Nairobi — The United States has backed a stronger African Union-United Nations partnership to address conflicts across the continent, saying a UN framework for financing AU-led peace operations could provide a useful tool in responding to Africa's security crises.

U.S. Representative for UN Management and Reform Ambassador Jeffrey Bartos told the Security Council that closer AU-UN coordination was particularly important in Sudan, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and the Sahel, where conflicts and militant violence continue to threaten regional stability.

"Coordination and partnership between the UN and AU can help achieve peace, security, and prosperity in Africa," Bartos said.

Washington specifically pointed to UN Security Council Resolution 2719, which provides a framework for UN financing of Security Council-authorised, AU-led peace support operations.



Bartos said such missions could strengthen the AU's role in resolving conflicts on the continent while drawing on UN support and resources.

"The deployment of a peace operation under UNSCR 2719 will strengthen the AU-UN partnership and leverage the AU's comparative advantages to addressing conflict in Africa," he said.

The United States, however, said the mechanism should be applied selectively, with any operation kept small, time-bound and focused on clearly defined objectives.

Washington said it would assess on a case-by-case basis where the framework could be most effectively used.

The remarks come as the AU and UN seek closer coordination over some of Africa's most persistent conflicts.

On Sudan, the United States called for an immediate end to the fighting and backed efforts by the AU and UN, alongside other members of the Quintet, to promote an inclusive political dialogue.

Bartos also said the United States was considering measures to support efforts to end the Sudan conflict, including expanding the existing Darfur arms embargo to cover the whole country.

On eastern DRC, he said the AU and UN should continue supporting U.S.- and Qatar-led peace efforts aimed at ending the conflict.

The United States also condemned terrorist attacks, including drone attacks, in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, saying African leadership and AU-UN cooperation were essential to confronting insecurity in the Sahel and West Africa.

World.title: Somalia: Somalia Says Al-Shabab Amniyat Chief Killed in Nisa Operation
World.content:
Mogadishu — Somalia's intelligence agency said a former head of al-Shabab's Amniyat security wing was killed in a planned operation carried out with international partners in the southern town of Jilib.

The National Intelligence and Security Agency, or NISA, identified the man as Bashir Ahmed Haji Nunow and said he was killed during the operation on Oct. 1, 2026.

NISA said Nunow led the militant group's Amniyat unit between 2016 and 2024. The agency said he operated under several aliases, including Geescadde, Fanax, Gardhuub and Ali Dheere.

The agency accused Nunow of playing a senior role in planning and carrying out attacks against Somali civilians. It specifically linked him to several major attacks in Mogadishu, including the Oct. 14, 2017, bombing at the Soobe intersection.



NISA also attributed the Ex-Control Afgooye attack and the attack known as Soobe 2 to Nunow, along with assaults targeting hotels and other locations around Mogadishu's Lido Beach.

The agency said the operation formed part of a wider campaign to pursue senior al-Shabab figures accused of directing attacks and maintaining the networks used to organise militant operations.

NISA said the killing could disrupt al-Shabab's leadership and the networks responsible for planning and executing attacks. It did not provide details on how Nunow was killed or whether other people were killed or wounded in the operation.

Al-Shabab, an al-Qaida-linked militant group, has waged an insurgency in Somalia for more than a decade and continues to carry out attacks despite military operations by Somali forces and their international partners.

The Somali government has increasingly focused on targeting the group's senior leadership and disrupting its command, intelligence and financial networks as part of efforts to weaken the insurgency.

World.title: Africa: How Africa Can Capture More Value From Its Cotton
World.content:
column

As World Cotton Day approaches on 7 October, Africa has an opportunity to consider how its cotton industry can contribute more to agricultural development, employment and economic growth. The opportunity extends far beyond producing and exporting raw cotton.

Africa's cotton industry has significant potential to support agricultural development, employment and economic growth. Yet the opportunity extends far beyond producing and exporting raw cotton.

Building a stronger, more resilient sector requires attention to the entire value chain – from farmers and ginneries through to spinning, textile manufacturing, clothing and, ultimately, consumers.

South Africa's experience offers practical lessons in supporting farmers, promoting sustainable production, protecting fibre quality and strengthening links between growers and downstream users.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

A strong cotton value chain starts with farmers who can produce consistently, sustainably and profitably. Farmer development must therefore go beyond access to seed and markets. Training, mentorship, technical support and knowledge-sharing can strengthen both production and business management.

South African cotton farmer Frans Malela illustrates what can be achieved when these opportunities are combined with determination and a willingness to learn. Malela began farming in 1984 on four hectares while working full-time in Johannesburg. He later moved into commercial cotton production, expanding his operation to more than 200 hectares.

His practices include crop rotation, soil management, integrated pest management, good harvesting practices and field hygiene. His yields increased from approximately 800 kg of seed cotton per hectare to 1.2 tonnes, reaching an exceptional three tonnes per hectare in 2021/22.

Malela also shares his experience through farmers' days, demonstrations and research trials, while his operation provides seasonal employment for approximately 40 people. His story shows how farmer development can improve productivity and fibre quality while spreading knowledge and creating employment within farming communities.

Sustainability and fibre quality go hand in hand

Sustainability is increasingly important throughout global agricultural and textile supply chains. Good agricultural practices are also fundamental to producing consistent, high-quality fibre.

Cotton fibre characteristics such as length, strength and micronaire – a measure reflecting fineness and maturity – directly influence spinning performance and fabric quality. Production, harvesting, storage and ginning practices therefore affect the value of cotton lint.

Cotton SA's South African Cotton Standard (ZACS) provides a practical framework for responsible production, bringing together farm management, environmental stewardship, people and economic viability.

Good agricultural practices support fibre quality from the beginning of the crop cycle. Appropriate land preparation and timely planting encourage uniform development. Locally adapted cultivars, effective weed and pest management, and appropriate nutrient and crop protection programmes support mature, strong fibre.

Quality protection continues during and after harvesting. Clean picking, appropriate storage and careful transport help prevent contamination and moisture damage. Clean ginneries and well-maintained equipment further minimise contamination and mechanical damage.

Sustainability, quality and profitability should therefore be pursued together. Good practices can protect natural resources, improve fibre quality and strengthen the commercial value of the crop.

Making sustainability measurable

ZACS shows how sustainability principles can be translated into a structured, measurable process.

The standard rests on four pillars – Management, Environment, People and Socio-economic – covering continuous improvement, water stewardship, soil health, responsible crop protection, labour practices, worker protection, economic viability and resilience.

Participants complete a self-assessment, followed by an internal review and a farm or ginnery visit. External verification takes place before certification, providing a mechanism to monitor performance and encourage improvement.

The programme is being tested under South African cotton production conditions through a three-year pilot. Malela has joined as a leader farmer, contributing to discussions and sharing his crop rotation system with other smallholder farmers.

For Africa, ZACS offers an example of how locally relevant standards can turn sustainability objectives into practical action at farm level.

Connecting farmers to the textile industry

Another major opportunity lies in strengthening links between cotton production and downstream textile manufacturing.

Producing more cotton does not automatically mean retaining more economic value within a country or the continent. When cotton is exported as lint and processed elsewhere, much of the value generated through spinning, textile production, garment manufacturing and retail is captured outside the producing country.

South Africa has experienced this challenge, highlighting the need to develop capacity beyond the farm gate. Initiatives such as the South Africa Cotton Mark show how locally produced cotton can be connected more visibly to manufacturers, retailers and consumers, supporting efforts to retain more value locally.

The processing gap is particularly pronounced in West and Central Africa. The World Trade Organization reported in March 2026 that around 98% of cotton from the region is exported as raw fibre, highlighting the opportunity to expand regional processing and manufacturing.

Close 

Retaining more value within Africa

Capturing this opportunity requires investment in spinning, weaving, knitting, dyeing, finishing and garment manufacturing, alongside the infrastructure, skills, finance and markets needed to make these industries competitive.

Regional cooperation could allow countries to develop complementary strengths, rather than each establishing every stage of the value chain independently.

Value addition must also benefit farmers. Stronger relationships between growers and downstream users, quality-based incentives, sustainability premiums, traceability and longer-term supply arrangements can help ensure that benefits reach producers.

There is no single solution to strengthening Africa's cotton sector. Farmer development, sustainability, fibre quality, processing capacity, manufacturing and market access are interconnected.

South Africa's experience shows the value of bringing these elements together: supporting farmers, applying practical sustainability standards and connecting local cotton with manufacturers and consumers.

The journey from farm to fashion is an opportunity to strengthen African agriculture, create employment, develop skills and ensure that a greater share of the value generated by Africa's cotton remains within the continent.

Erica Vogel is Senior Quality Control Officer at Cotton SA.

World.title: South Sudan: South Sudan Rejects Claims of Foreigners' Expulsion Order
World.content:
Nairobi — South Sudan has moved to dispel reports that foreigners have been given seven days to leave the country, with Juba County Caretaker Commissioner Kalisto Lado Faustino Nyigilo saying the government remains open to legally resident foreigners but wants them to stay out of small-scale retail businesses.

Lado made the clarification on Tuesday following reports circulating on social media claiming that he had ordered foreign nationals to leave South Sudan.

He said the reports were false and that he did not have the authority to expel foreigners from the country.

"The Commissioner has never said that, and it's even not the mandate of the Commissioner to actually evacuate people or to send people out of South Sudan," Lado said.



He said South Sudan welcomes foreigners who enter the country legally for business, residence, humanitarian work and other legitimate activities.

"Our policy is welcoming. We are welcoming everybody from any country who want to come to be with us in South Sudan," he said.

However, Lado maintained his position that foreign nationals should avoid small-scale retail trade in Juba, including boda boda operations and the sale of everyday food items.

He said foreigners should instead invest in wholesale businesses, companies, factories and other ventures capable of creating jobs for South Sudanese.

Lado said his earlier remarks were aimed at protecting economic opportunities for local youth and women rather than discriminating against foreigners.

He questioned the growing involvement of foreign nationals in boda boda operations, asking what opportunities would remain for South Sudanese youth if foreigners dominated the sector.

He similarly raised concern over foreign women engaging in small-scale food vending, including selling chapati, potatoes, onions and tomatoes.

Lado rejected claims that his position amounted to a ban on foreign investment or hostility towards foreigners.

"There is nothing about sending of foreigners out of South Sudan. There is nothing about prohibiting foreigners from business. There is nothing about hating foreigners," he said.

He instead urged foreign investors to bring substantial capital into the country and establish industries and companies that could employ South Sudanese.

Lado also addressed the ongoing removal of roadside businesses and structures in Juba, saying the county was not conducting indiscriminate demolitions.

He said the exercise was intended to clear roads, remove garbage and relocate businesses operating on road reserves to designated areas.

Close 

"We are not demolishing structures. We are organising the road, taking garbage out of the road and sending those who are putting their booths on the road to be in the rightful places," he said.

Lado urged foreigners living in Juba to remain calm, saying those who obey South Sudanese laws had nothing to fear.

"Our foreigners who are here, be peaceful. No fear, no worry, unless if you commit any crime," he said.

World.title: Kenya: The Symbolism Behind Raila Odinga's Pentagon-Shaped Mausoleum
World.content:
Nairobi — The unusual pentagonal shape of the late former Prime Minister Raila Odinga's mausoleum at Kango ka Jaramogi in Bondo was deliberately chosen to reflect a key symbol associated with his political life.

The Kenya Defence Forces officers involved in guiding President William Ruto and other dignitaries through the facility during its handover to the Odinga family have explained the thinking behind the design.

Samson Malaki said the five-sided structure draws inspiration from the raised fist that became one of the most recognisable gestures associated with Odinga.

According to Malaki, the fist was not intended as a gesture of confrontation, but as a symbol of strength and a call for Kenyans to come together.



He said the five fingers of the raised hand informed the decision to adopt a pentagonal form for the mausoleum.

"In as much as he was raising that particular fist, he wasn't raising that fist in defiance, but he was raising that fist to call people to unity. It is five, which represents a pentagon, and it's actually what informed the design of this mausoleum," Malaki explained.

The design also establishes a visual connection between Raila's final resting place and that of his father, the late Jaramogi Oginga Odinga.

While Jaramogi's mausoleum has six sides, the structure housing Raila's remains has five. Mr Malaki said the architects deliberately worked with the two geometric forms to create a sense of continuity between the neighbouring structures.

"The Jaramogi Mausoleum is actually hexagonal in shape. The Raila Mausoleum is pentagonal in shape. And for the purposes of that architectural harmony, we tried to play around with the geometry of Jaramogi Mausoleum, which is hexagonal, and we came up with the Raila Mausoleum, which is pentagonal," he said.

The explanation adds a political dimension to what might otherwise appear to be an architectural choice.

The number five has featured at important moments in Odinga's political journey, most notably during the build-up to the 2007 General Election.

'Pentagon'

The term "Pentagon" became synonymous with the Orange Democratic Movement's senior leadership in the run-up to the 2007 presidential nominations.

It referred to a group of five prominent politicians who were positioning themselves for the party's presidential nomination before the contest at Kasarani.

Odinga eventually secured the ODM ticket, with the other members of the group supporting his presidential campaign as the party entered the 2007 General Election.

Close 

Nearly two decades later, the pentagon has acquired a different meaning at his final resting place.

The symbolism of the five-sided mausoleum, according to its designers, links Mr Odinga's familiar raised-fist gesture with the broader theme of unity that defined much of his political messaging.

The structure therefore serves not only as a burial site but also as an architectural representation of elements associated with his public life.

Its pentagonal form stands alongside Jaramogi's hexagonal mausoleum, creating what the KDF officer described as a deliberate architectural relationship between father and son.

World.title: 'Glad to see it': Super Bowl champion Bruce Arians rips out-of-control NFL refs after two suspensions
World.content:
NFL officials were suspended after separate incidents occurred involving players in two different games this past weekend, and one former Super Bowl-winning head coach was a bit "surprised" by what happened.

Bruce Arians, who won the Super Bowl alongside Tom Brady and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers as the team’s head coach in 2021, knows that things can get heated with referees on game days.

However, under the new collective bargaining agreement between the referees and the NFL, the league has the right to take action when they deem a line was crossed – no matter which side did so.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The NFL suspended line judge Jeff Seeman for 2 games and referee Adrian Hill for 1 game due to "unprofessional conduct toward a player." For Seeman, he was seen in a late-game exchange with Arizona Cardinals star Trey McBride, where he clearly mouthed a couple obscenities toward the tight end, who had been frustrated over an unflagged contact play on third down.

As for Hill, he got frustrated after Miami Dolphins running back Ollie Gordon blocked Vikings' linebacker Eric Willson into him, which knocked the official to the ground. Hill stood up and confronted Wilson immediately face-to-face before ordering him to go back to the huddle.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"This kind of behavior from an official towards a player is unacceptable," NFL Players Association Executive Director JC Tretter shared on social media. "Players are consistently held accountable when the roles are reversed. We expect the NFL to hold officials to the same standard."

Arians saw the altercations as well, and he gave OutKick his take on it during a recent interview.

"I did see it and I am surprised a little bit because there was never accountability before," he said, while also highlighting his work with Novartis and early prostate cancer screenings for their new initiative. "Under the new collective bargaining agreement with officials, there’s a lot more accountability and I’m glad to see that.

"I’ve had many, many run-ins with the referees. I’m legendary in that part, you know. They’d come over [and say], ‘Please, just don’t spit on me, coach.’ I’d be hollering and screaming at them. But, yeah, it’s a great thing I think."

As he said, Arians had dust-ups with officials during his lengthy tenure in the league, but that’s something seen on game days all the time. He was surprised, however, to see it occur with players, who usually let the coaches do the yelling for him.

"I was surprised it was more with a player than a coach, because coaches can go way overboard," Arians explained. "But I think that’s a very, very important thing that the NFL now has control."

It seems the league didn’t want to handle this behind the scenes, but rather sent a broader message with these two suspensions: acts like this by officials won’t be tolerated moving forward.

Arians believes that is the right balance to have in the sport.

World.title: Iowa city council meeting erupts after former member opens meeting with satanic prayer and 'Hail Satan'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A city council in Iowa erupted after a resident opened a meeting with a satanic prayer on Tuesday.

Before the meeting of the Ottumwa City Council began, former council member Matt Dalbey opened with an invocation to the "dark father" to "embrace the Luciferian impulse to eat of the tree of knowledge" before ending with a "Hail Satan" declaration.

After the council recited the Pledge of Allegiance and took roll, New Life Center pastor Rick Bick interrupted the meeting to demand pushback against Dalbey's invocation.

LUTHERAN MINISTER AND HOUSE CANDIDATE UNDER FIRE AFTER RECOUNTING HER PART IN SATANIST COUPLE'S WEDDING

"Let's just reverse this curse that was put on our city. That ending with 'Hail Satan' or 'Hail dark god,' that's not welcome here," Bick insisted.

Though City Council member Cara Galloway told Bick to save his comments for public discussion, Bick demanded immediate action.

"It needs to be done now," Bick said. "I appreciate what Ms. Galloway is saying, but that was a curse put on the city. When he said 'Hail Satan' ... most of you know that, and we need to just stop and reverse it."

In response, Ottumwa Mayor Benjamin Foote requested 30 seconds of silence to allow for prayer or reflection and overruled Galloway's efforts to move forward with the meeting.

Reacting to the controversy, Foote told Fox News Digital, "This is not a reflection of our community. As the Mayor of my hometown in Iowa, I know the people of Ottumwa, and the invocation read at the start of Tuesday’s meeting does not represent the faith or the values of families who call this city home."

SWING STATE MAYOR SUED AS CITY’S MUSLIM HOLIDAY DISPLAYS IGNITE RELIGIOUS-FAVORITISM FIGHT

After the meeting concluded, Galloway gave additional comments on the matter, repeating past concerns she had about establishing invocations at city council meetings that could lead to more conflicts.

"Opening with an invocation means allowing viewpoints that may not reflect our own, and responding to someone's invocation is a slippery slope to putting a financial liability on the taxpayers and allowing for others to object or respond," Galloway said. "And this is exactly why I had concerns about having an invocation when we first talked about it, and I think I even specifically referenced that having someone from the Church of Satan or a prayer about Satan when we talked about that, that this could happen, and we would need to allow it."

"I just want to remind us that again, sometimes things are said that we may not agree with ... and while you're allowed to do the moment of silence and that kind of thing too, I think we've opened ourselves up for others to object or respond to others' invocations," she continued. "And we need to remember that we are up here to be neutral and allow viewpoints because we've opened up invocations."

According to a report by the Ottumwa Courier, the city adopted an invocation policy in January. The policy says it does not endorse any faith or religous denomination but is intended "to acknowledge and express the City Council's respect for the diversity of both organized and unorganized religious denominations, as well as other faiths, belief systems, or the lack thereof, represented and practiced among the citizens of the City of Ottumwa."

SUPREME COURT SHOWDOWN LOOMS OVER ST MICHAEL STATUE BLOCKED FROM PUBLIC SAFETY BUILDING

In a private message, according to the Ottumwa Courier, Dalbey, who is a member of The Satanic Temple of Iowa, said that the prayer is commonly used by the temple "but has nothing to do with the belief in a satanic deity."

In a comment to Fox News Digital, council member Bill Hoffman described leaving the room once the prayer was invoked and returning for the Pledge of Allegiance, though he defended Dalbey's right to say what he believes.

"I'm a Christian man with Christian values. That doesn't mean I don't want to observe his First Amendment right. It just means that I want to use my rights not to observe that," he said.

Hoffman added that he expects the invocation policy to be discussed in the future and that the council did not condone the content.

World.title: Cleveland Guardians stay alive in ALDS, deny White Sox clinch at home
World.content:
The Chicago White Sox last clinched a postseason series at home when Jiggs Donahue and George Davis helped the South Siders defeat the Chicago Cubs in Game 6 of the 1906 World Series.

More than a century later, the White Sox came up short Thursday in their bid to clinch a spot in the American League Championship Series on their home field, falling to the Cleveland Guardians 7-3 in Game 3. The Guardians haven't made it to what is effectively the MLB's playoffs semifinals since 2005.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The White Sox entered the potential ALDS-clinching game with a 2-0 series lead and struck first when catcher Kyle Teel doubled to right field, driving in the game’s first run.

WHITE SOX RIDE ANOTHER DRAMATIC COMEBACK WIN TO BEAT GUARDIANS AND TAKE COMMANDING 2-0 ALDS LEAD

The Guardians recorded two triples in a postseason game for the first time in franchise history. They became the first major league team to accomplish the feat since the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 1 of the 2024 World Series.

Adell, Ramírez, Bailey and Brayan Rocchio each had two of the team’s 11 hits — a complete turnaround for the AL Central champions after they managed just three runs and seven hits in the first two games of the series combined.

Chicago won its first four games in a surprising postseason appearance after going 60-102 last year. It was backed by a frenzied crowd of 40,590 for the franchise’s first home playoff game since 2021, but there wasn’t much for the fans to cheer in the final innings.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Parker Messick is scheduled to start for Cleveland in Game 4 on Thursday.

Wednesday marked Chicago’s first home playoff game since 2021 and another milestone in a surprising season. The White Sox had lost a combined 324 games over the previous three years.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Critical House race that could decide control of Congress hits home stretch as GOP rep warns what's at stake
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

PRAIRIE CITY, Iowa — Iowa's 1st Congressional District is shaping up to be one of the closest races in the country as Republicans try to hold their razor-thin majority in the House, and Fox News Digital spoke to Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks about her pitch to keep the seat in GOP hands and what Democrats taking back control would mean.

"Common sense over crazy. This is just common sense over crazy communism," Miller-Meeks told Fox News Digital about her opponent, former Democratic state Rep. Christina Bohannan, who Miller-Meeks said is "perfectly in alignment" with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

Miller-Meeks accused Bohannan, who the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) has labeled a "DEI queen," of supporting progressive priorities during her time in the Iowa House that aren't in line with where the majority of Iowa voters stand.

"My opponent has not supported law enforcement, she tries to hide where she is on open borders, she has voted against every single tax cut while she was an Iowa legislator and said that the working family's tax cut was dangerous and would get rid of all of it," Miller-Meeks said. "Then she talks about in her campaign ads supporting tax cuts for the middle class. She also supported keeping boys in girls sports and boys and girls locker rooms."

HOUSE GOP BILL MOVES TO CLOSE WHISTLEBLOWER GAPS EXPOSED BY MINNESOTA MEDICAID FRAUD SCANDAL

Miller-Meeks, who spoke to Fox News Digital at a Department of Agriculture roundtable talking to farmers about their needs and the Trump administration's efforts to lower burdensome farming regulations, said that over the next month until the election her campaign will continue to "make sure that we're serving Iowans, that were out meeting with constituents answering their questions, coming before them and being available and doing the great constituent work that we've always done and showing the contrast."

The incumbent congressman touted her record of working to bring in a massive steel mill in recent months, creating manufacturing jobs, helping farmers through ethanol and biodiesel policies, improving water quality and supporting conservation.

DEM IN KEY SWING RACE MISSED NEARLY HALF HER STATE HOUSE VOTES WHILE TAKING TAXPAYER SALARY: 'NO SHOW'

Voters across the country, including in Iowa, have expressed frustration with the economy, the cost of gas and diesel, and the Iran War, and while Miller-Meeks acknowledged the concerns, she's making the case that putting Democrats back in power isn't the answer, as they would roll back the work that has been done by Republicans.

"There'll be no relief coming," she said. "They already said that they would get rid of all those policies."

Miller-Meeks said the Democratic Party as a whole has moved further left and will attempt to "get rid of" Republican-led measures she credited with making U.S. steel production more competitive and benefiting states like Iowa.

"Our bill on opening up energy production here in the United States did bring gasoline prices and diesel prices down at the first of the year," Miller-Meeks explained, adding that if Republican policies had been put in place during the Biden administration "we would have already had more biodiesel, which would have helped bring down diesel prices."

The congresswoman argued Republicans will fight to preserve policies that lower energy, housing, healthcare and prescription drug costs, create jobs and root out fraud, waste and abuse that cost taxpayers millions.

"It's not just making prices affordable, but it's also increasing wages and increasing jobs and good-paying jobs," she said. "We have certainly done that with the policies that we've put in place that the Democrats would get rid of."

WATCH: BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT CALLED IOWA A 'BACKWATER' OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES BAN

Miller-Meeks also mentioned several proposals she led targeting fraud in government programs following the Feeding Our Future scandal, which raised many questions about accountability among state leaders. The Medicaid Whistleblower Protection Act would establish federal protections nationwide for Medicaid workers who report early warning signs of fraud, and the WALZ Act would require the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General to open investigations into any program that sees a 10% or greater increase in total payments over any six-month period within a fiscal year.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Tackling corruption inside the government, inside government agencies, or in members of Congress or the administration, we're gonna continue to do that and work to serve Iowans and the American people," she said.

This will be Bohannan’s third time running for Congress against Miller-Meeks after narrowly losing by less than a percentage point in 2024. The race is rated a "toss up" by Cook Political Report, reflecting Democratic momentum and broader headwinds facing Republicans in a midterm election shaped by President Donald Trump’s approval ratings and economic concerns.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Bohannan defended her positions, writing Miller-Meeks' "siding with drug companies, data centers, billionaires and party leadership at every turn" is "self-serving."

"What's crazy is pretending to represent your constituents when you're bought and sold. I'll always put Iowa first--that's common sense," Bohannan said.

World.title: Driver opens fire on strangers along major US interstate, tells cops he ‘had to kill people today’
World.content:

An Iowa man accused of opening fire on passing vehicles along an interstate and wounding a woman allegedly made a chilling admission to police after his arrest, according to court documents.

Andrew Darrick Tanaka, 27, of West Des Moines, faces four counts of attempted murder in Monday afternoon's shootings along Interstate 35 in Warren County, according to the Iowa Department of Public Safety.

After being taken into custody, Tanaka allegedly told law enforcement, "I had to kill people today," according to a criminal complaint and affidavit filed Tuesday in Warren County District Court.

The incident began around 3:31 p.m. Monday when authorities received multiple 911 calls reporting gunfire along the northbound lanes of I-35.



VIDEO SHOWS IOWA ROAD RAGE SUSPECT SURRENDER AFTER POLICE ORDER HIM TO DROP GUN

Tanaka was driving a black Chevrolet Equinox when a woman driving a black BMW passed him on the interstate, according to the affidavit. The BMW then passed a Subaru Outback.

Investigators allege Tanaka caught up to the Subaru and fired at least two rounds through the driver's side window, striking the woman behind the wheel in her left shoulder.

He then allegedly caught up to the BMW and fired another round through its driver's side window.

Tanaka continued north before rear-ending a gray Nissan Altima carrying two people, according to the affidavit.



APPARENT ROAD RAGE DRIVER APPEARS TO THREATEN MOM ON CAMERA AS 3-YEAR-OLD CRIES IN BACK SEAT

When the Nissan's occupants stopped to check on him, Tanaka allegedly got out of his vehicle with a handgun and fired at least one round into the car's windshield.

Deputies from the Warren County Sheriff's Office, officers from the West Des Moines Police Department and Iowa State Patrol troopers responded to reports of gunfire near mile marker 56.

Officers found the wounded woman and several vehicles that appeared to have been struck by gunfire. The woman was taken to a hospital with injuries that authorities said did not appear to be life-threatening.

Police later found Tanaka along the interstate after his vehicle became disabled after the collision.



POLICE SWARM MICHIGAN SHOPPING CENTER AFTER 'SIGNIFICANT' SHOOTING INCIDENT; AT LEAST 2 DEAD

He was standing on the shoulder of the highway holding a handgun when officers arrived, according to the affidavit. Tanaka was taken into custody without further incident.

The shootings prompted authorities to shut down the interstate for several hours while investigators processed the scene.

Tanaka was booked into the Warren County Jail on four counts of attempted murder.

World.title: Diet soda vs water: Study reveals which beverage is better for weight loss
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Diet drinks containing sugar substitutes were found to be as effective as water for supporting weight loss in overweight or obese adults, according to a two-year randomized trial.

The study, led by the University of Liverpool, England, included 493 participants ranging from 18 to 65 years old, all of whom had a body mass index (BMI) between 27 and 35 (overweight or obese).

Half of them received 22.3 ounces of water each day, and the other half received the same amount of soda with non-nutritive sweeteners (about two cans) for a 104-week period.

YOUR BRAIN MAY BE TRICKING YOU INTO LIKING ARTIFICIAL SWEETENERS, STUDY FINDS

The group assigned to NNS drinks could choose from a variety of diet sodas, low-calorie fruit drinks and flavored waters. The primary sweeteners used were aspartame, acesulfame potassium and sucralose.

After two years, people drinking diet beverages had lost about 10.6 pounds, while those drinking water lost about 8.2 pounds.

People in both groups kept off a meaningful amount of weight for two years, even during the last year when they no longer had regular weight-management support, the researchers stated.

Both groups lost inches around their waists and hips and reduced body fat, with no meaningful difference between people drinking diet beverages and those drinking water.

POPULAR ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DANGEROUS HEART RISK

Additionally, total cholesterol remained within the healthy range in both groups.

The findings were published in the British Journal of Nutrition.

"The study does not show that diet beverages themselves caused the weight loss," Alix Turoff, a registered dietitian in New York City, told Fox News Digital.

"Everyone in the study was participating in a structured weight-management program that included nutrition counseling, behavioral support and physical activity recommendations."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Turoff, who was not involved in the study, noted that the main value of including diet beverages comes down to substitution — "not that these beverages have a magical metabolic effect."

Notably, the study compared diet beverages with water — rather than with sugar-sweetened drinks — making it a test of whether the sugar substitutes themselves appeared to hinder weight-loss efforts.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"If someone normally drinks 250 calories of regular soda and switches to zero-calorie soda, then they’re saving calories," she added.

The dietitian emphasized that these findings don’t mean water and diet soda are nutritionally identical.

"The study did not find significant between-group differences in hunger or sugar intake at the end of the trial, which is relevant because one common concern is that artificial sweeteners may increase appetite or lead to compensatory eating," Turoff said.

"I would still recommend water as the primary hydration choice, but I don’t think people need to be afraid of diet drinks because they think they will automatically prevent fat loss or cause weight gain."

CLICK HERE TO 

There were some limitations with the research, including that it was conducted at one location in England. Race and ethnicity data were not collected, which limits the generalizability of the findings.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Only 220 of the 493 participants who started treatment completed the 104-week assessment. The second-year extension was also voluntary, meaning those who continued may have been more motivated or more likely to stick with the program, Turoff noted.

While the trial was funded by the American Beverage Association, the study authors stated that the association did not participate in the study design, data analysis or interpretation of the results.

World.title: DNC sues administration over taxpayer-funded pro-Trump TV ads
World.content:
The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration Wednesday over its taxpayer-funded s that portray President Donald Trump in a favorable light, alleging the ads violate federal laws on government spending and propaganda.

The DNC cited a measure Trump signed into law this year that says funds appropriated by Congress can’t be used “for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States not heretofore authorized by Congress.”

The lawsuit also cites the Anti-Deficiency Act, which bars spending government money that hasn’t been appropriated by Congress, and the Purpose Statute, which says taxpayer funds can be used only for the specific purposes approved by Congress.

The DNC said the administration’s use of taxpayer dollars for “campaign-style s” deprived Democrats “of a fair electoral process by adding public funds to the resources available to support Republican candidates.” The use of public funds places Democratic candidates at an electoral disadvantage, it argued.

The watchdog group Common Cause filed its own suit making similar legal arguments, alleging the administration had violated appropriations statutes.

The ads, launched last month, sparked criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, many of whom questioned their legality.

Trump reversed course Monday, announcing on Truth Social he would no longer use government funds for the ads and saying he and his PAC, MAGA Inc., would foot the bill moving forward, instead. He didn’t say whether the government would be reimbursed for the ads that already ran.

Reached for comment on the lawsuits, the White House pointed NBC News to Trump’s Truth Social post. The Department of Homeland Security and the Office of Management and Budget, which are named as defendants in addition to Trump and the White House, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit.

Since Trump’s announcement, several of the ads have continued to run with the disclaimer that they were paid for by the U.S. government.

Asked by NBC News whether those were paid for before or after Trump pledged to cover the costs, the White House wouldn’t say either way.

A person familiar with the ads said that the ad buy for the spots, placed before Trump’s Monday announcement, will end this week. Afterwards, the person said, outside groups will begin paying for the ads.

NBC News has reported that a $20 million contract was awarded to a Maryland firm for the ad campaign. AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm, estimated that at least $10 million had been spent to air the ads through Monday.

Attorneys for the DNC asked a federal judge in Washington to find that the administration acted unlawfully “by developing and airing the propaganda ads using Congressionally appropriated funds” and to prevent it from using those funds to develop and air the ads in the future.

DNC Chair Ken Martin condemned the administration for using taxpayer dollars as Americans struggle with a rising cost of living.

“Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes,” he said in a statement Wednesday.

Omar Noureldin, Common Cause’s senior vice president of policy and litigation, said in an interview with NBC News Wednesday that the group is bringing forth the suit “because we want to make sure that no president, regardless of party, can hijack public funds to fund political self-promotion without congressional approval.”

“It appears that the $20 million that had been contracted for this has not all been spent yet, and so they will continue to run ads paid for by taxpayer dollars, and so we think we need to stop that now, and not another dollar of taxpayer dollars should be spent on these ads,” Noureldin said.

The federal money for the ads came from funds intended for Customs and Border Protection, an arm of DHS. NBC News reported that CBP leadership was cut out of the decision to run the ads.

Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, said last week that the ads didn’t merit FCC review, arguing that they weren’t “anything at all out of the ordinary.”

The White House has defended the ads by calling them “clearly not political” and claiming they were about “reminding Americans to love their country.” It has also pointed to other administrations’ use of public safety announcements.

World.title: Florida poll: Republicans lead in the races for governor and Senate
World.content:
Republican Byron Donalds holds a 7-percentage-point advantage over Democrat David Jolly in the Florida governor’s race, according to a new NBC South Florida/Telemundo Station Group poll, while Republican Sen. Ashley Moody is up by 10 points in her matchup against Democratic challenger Angie Nixon.

Donalds, a congressman from the southwest corner of the state, is at 48% in the poll, compared with Jolly’s 41%, in a race in which Donalds has had a commanding financial advantage. (That advantage is just inside the poll’s margin of error, but Donalds has the edge in most of the range of possibilities.)

Moody is at 50% in the Senate race, compared with 40% for Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America-aligned candidate who got into the general election after a surprise primary victory over Democrat Alexander Vindman in August.

The results come amid broad Democratic optimism about the 2026 elections, with public polling showing the party making races in some typically red states into competitive contests this year. This poll suggests limits to that apparent momentum in other places.

The poll also took a snapshot of the state’s hugely influential bloc of Hispanic voters, largely congregated in South Florida. In 2024, Donald Trump won Hispanic-heavy Miami-Dade County by roughly 11 points, a significant reversal in a part of the state that had long been Democratic-leaning. Joe Biden won the county by 7 points in 2020.

But now, Florida Hispanic voters — including large Cuban, Nicaraguan, Honduran and Colombian populations — appear to be swinging back away from Trump, even as other high-profile Republican candidates hold comfortable leads among Hispanic voters.

Donalds holds a 48%-43% lead over Jolly among Hispanic voters, according to the survey, while Moody is up 47%-40% over Nixon. Trump’s job performance rating, however, is underwater, with 49% disapproving of his job performance, compared with 45% who approve.

Overall, 48% of all Florida likely voters approve of Trump’s job performance and 48% disapprove.

Before Trump’s gains among Florida’s Hispanic population in 2024, Democrats had generally won the demographic in the state by comfortable margins. Democrats argue that recent special election victories in Florida show the party has already started winning back the Hispanic vote, in part because of Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policy. Unhappiness with prices and the cost of living has also affected Trump’s ratings among Hispanic voters.

“In legislative races in Florida, we have seen huge swings,” Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, told NBC News last week, speaking of the committee’s efforts in Florida House races. She said that on immigration, Trump and his party broke a promise “to go after the worst of the worst.”

By far the most important issue identified was inflation and the cost of living, with 30% saying it is likeliest to influence their votes. In both the overall sample and the sample of Hispanic voters, “direction of the state or country” (17%) was the second most important issue. The broader polling data put “immigration enforcement” as the third most important issue (16%), while the Hispanic sample put property taxes (13%) as the third most important issue. Immigration enforcement was the fourth most important issue among Hispanic voters (12%).

Questions about the Trump administration’s push to allow local and state policy to cooperate with federal immigration officials fell along party lines.

Among all voters, 85% of Republicans support the policy, compared with 18% of Democrats and 44% of those identified as independent voters who supported the harsher immigration enforcement tactics.

Property taxes have also been front and center in Florida during the midterms.

The state Republican Party and term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis support a ballot measure, known as Amendment 3, that would increase property tax exemptions to the first $250,000 of a home’s value by 2028. The exemption cap is currently $50,000.

In the poll of all Florida voters, 55% back the amendment, 26% oppose it, and 19% are undecided. Nearly three-quarters (74%) of Republicans supported the idea, compared with 36% for Democrats and 43% for independents.

The overall survey questioned 625 registered voters, all of whom said they were likely to vote in the November elections. They were interviewed over the telephone by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research Inc. from Sept. 28 to Thursday, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The same time frame and methods were used to survey 400 Hispanic registered voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 5 percentage points.

World.title: Republican John James seeks some distance from Trump in Michigan governor debate
World.content:
Republican Rep. John James on Tuesday sought to put some daylight between himself and President Donald Trump as he debated his opponent in the Michigan governor’s race.

Democratic nominee Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, repeatedly tried to tie James to Trump during the hourlong showdown, saying he had failed to stand up to Trump and wouldn’t do so as governor, either.

James, who was boosted by Trump’s endorsement in his GOP primary campaign, pointed to the Iran war and tariff policy as issues over which he has disagreements with Trump.

“I’ve stood up to the president many times. I’ve said that I can agree with the president without worshipping him. I can disagree without attacking him, and I always put Michigan first,” James said.

James said he believed the conflict in Iran needed to end “quickly, as in yesterday,” echoing comments he made last month. James, who has voted against several resolutions in the House that sought to end the Iran war, also said he wants to “use whatever checks and balance power that we have to bring this war to a swift conclusion.”

His comments in his first debate with Benson in the key battleground state come as polls show voters nationally continuing to sour on Trump’s handling of the Iran war and the cost of living as the midterm elections draw closer.

Benson attacked James for voting against the Iran war powers resolutions while blaming high gas prices on the conflict.

“I struggle with that vote,” James said of the war powers resolutions votes. “I’m a combat veteran. I have been to war. She has not. I understand what war means, and so I voted to protect the troops and to fund them while they were in harm’s way.”

Benson pointed out that her husband served in the Army.

“Military spouses serve also, congressman,” she said.

Benson sought to link James to Trump’s tariff agenda, saying she dubs them the “John James tax,” while James said he had pushed back on the Trump administration’s tariffs against Canada.

“I’ve actually called out the administration specifically, talking with the trade ambassador and saying that we must get back to the table, stop acting like children and negotiate a reciprocal, fair and mutually beneficial arrangement to make sure that we can bring our jobs back and protect our industry,” James said.

James, who promised in July to “back law enforcement, end sanctuary city policies” and “cooperate with federal immigration authorities to remove criminal illegal immigrants,” seemed to soften that stance Tuesday, saying he does not see a need for ICE presence in Michigan.

“We’re going to be cooperating with federal law enforcement as well as our communities. We’re going to make sure that we’re prioritizing violent offenders, and we’re going to make sure that we enforce the law,” he said. “Frankly, I don’t believe we’re going to need ICE presence in the state of Michigan, because we are going to be enforcing the law.”

James tried to tie Benson’s record to that of term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

Asked by moderator Rick Albin of NBC affiliate WOOD of Grand Rapids to point to a decision about which Whitmer did not listen to Michiganders, Benson did not cite a specific policy but said, “Where I think we need to listen to the people ... is a way to improve our Department of Health and Human Services.”

The candidates also clashed over data centers amid a growing public backlash to them, each accusing the other of profiting from them. Benson accused James of having voted for policies friendly to data centers while holding stocks in them, and James accused Benson’s family of profiting from one center’s construction. Benson denied that her family had profited from them, while James said any data center-related stocks he owns were held in broad mutual funds.

The nationally watched Michigan Senate race, in which the Democratic candidate, Abdul El-Sayed, is running against GOP former Rep. Mike Rogers, did not come up Tuesday. Republicans in particular have been eager to tie El-Sayed, a progressive, to other Democratic candidates in competitive races.

Neither candidate mentioned that race or tried to tie the other to either Senate nominee.

Democrats are looking to keep Michigan’s governorship in their party’s hands after Whitmer’s two terms in office. Trump carried the state by just over 1 percentage point in the 2024 presidential election. NBC News characterizes the race as leaning toward Democrats.

Benson and James are scheduled to debate again on Oct. 15.

World.title: Cornell students hold sit-in over alleged 2024 fraternity assault
World.content:
ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University students began a seven-hour sit-in Wednesday in solidarity with Jane Doe, the woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity nearly two years ago.

“Seven hours for the seven hours she endured. Seven hours of solidarity. Seven hours demanding change,” a coalition of Cornell student groups said in a post on Instagram ahead of the demonstration.

Roughly 80 students had gathered inside a campus dining hall named for Pulitzer Prize-winning author Toni Morrison by around 3 p.m. Outside the building, students displayed posters bearing slogans such as “Justice for Jane Doe” and “Stop Protecting Rapists.”

The organizers said the sit-in is part of “Zero Day,” an “economic blackout calling on students to disrupt business as usual by not attending class or spending on campus.”

The protest illustrates the tense mood on the Ivy League campus following Jane Doe’s allegations that she was sexually assaulted and plied with drugs Oct. 19-20, 2024. She filed a civil lawsuit against the university and seven fraternity members last month, leading to renewed national attention on sexual misconduct and collegiate Greek life.

Three of the accused men have publicly denied the allegations through attorneys.
