World.title: She got Trump's $500 check for health insurance. To her, it's a 'political stunt'
World.content:
She got Trump's $500 check for health insurance. To her, it's a 'political stunt'

toggle caption i Sue Julian

Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news on the midterms.

Ellen Allen has mixed feelings about the check from the U.S. Treasury and letter from President Trump that arrived at her house near Charleston, W.Va., on Monday.

"I just can't believe it; I mean, that's crazy," says Allen, who's the executive director of a small nonprofit called West Virginians for Affordable Health Care. She says, in her opinion, sending out these checks is a "political stunt."

NPR first spoke to Ellen Allen in the summer of 2025. She was 63 years old at the time and knew she needed coverage from Healthcare.gov even as generous federal subsidies for her premiums were ending. She has a serious eye condition and needs expensive drops to preserve her vision. She advocated for the Republican-controlled Congress to extend the subsidies. It didn't. She ended up using retirement savings to pay $1,967 every month for her premiums from January through August, 2026.

Sponsor Message

Then her birthday came; she turned 65 and was eligible for Medicare. "I was ready at midnight — the first day I could apply, I did," she laughs.

A second check on the way?

Allen chose traditional Medicare, which means she could soon be getting another check from the U.S. Treasury. Last week, President Trump announced that $90 checks will be sent to 20 million people enrolled in Medicare.

"The $90 is — I mean, that's just nothing," Allen says. In her work, she talks to people about healthcare costs all over West Virginia. "People aren't going to be fooled by this," she predicts. "People are hurting. People are feeling the cost of healthcare all year long."

"If they wanted to do something meaningful, they would work on affordable healthcare instead of just sending out checks every now and then," Allen says.

Both checks are directed to select groups. The $500 checks mailed by the Trump administration last week were only sent to people who live in one of the 30 states that use Healthcare.gov for their insurance marketplace. They also make more than $64,000 annually for an individual, which is too much money to qualify for subsidies. These are people, like Allen, who were likely to be hard hit when Congress failed to extend the extra financial help put in place under President Joe Biden.

Sponsor Message

The $90 checks that will be sent to Medicare beneficiaries are only going to certain people enrolled in Medicare Part B. People in Medicare Advantage plans, which are managed by insurance companies, will not get checks.

Can Trump do that?

The checks are hitting people's mailboxes just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The text of a letter sent along with the money touts the Trump administration's efforts on health policy and criticizes the Biden administration.

"This reads like electioneering," says Kathleen Clark, professor of legal and governmental ethics at Washington University law school in St. Louis, Mo. "This reads as though it's intended to influence votes. That is prohibited by law."

Specifically, it would violate the Hatch Act, "the statute that prohibits using federal power and money to influence partisan political elections," she explains. It may also be a use of funds that's unauthorized by Congress.

The money for Healthcare.gov enrollees is from fees insurance companies paid to participate in the marketplace, and the money for Medicare beneficiaries is from a general improvement fund. Neither of these funds has been used for direct payments to enrollees before.

"It looks like a pretty desperate effort to, in essence, bribe the recipients of this letter to vote in gratitude to Trump in the upcoming midterm elections," she adds.

An empowered executive branch

The checks and letters are arriving in people's mailboxes, whether they're legal or not. Clark notes the Supreme Court has enabled Trump's illegal actions many times in the past. "So, of course, he feels empowered to go ahead and do this," she says.

The White House did not respond directly to NPR's questions about electioneering, whether the action is a violation of the Hatch Act or if it is a "political stunt," as Allen put it.

"This is an out-of-touch criticism," Trump administration spokeswoman Allison Schuster wrote in an email. "Americans were overcharged for the operation of the Obamacare exchange, and President Trump returned their hard-earned money. This President will never stop enabling Americans to take control of their health by implementing policies that put money back in their pockets."

Sponsor Message

'Half a tank of gas'

Some Republicans in recent years have advocated for giving more money directly to people rather than to health insurance companies, although the party has yet to settle on a particular approach.

In any case, sending these checks is unrelated to that effort, says Joseph Antos, senior fellow emeritus at the conservative think tank American Enterprise Institute. There's nothing that requires people to use this money for their health.

"From the perspective of the average senior citizen, when they get a $90 check, it's money," he adds, referencing the forthcoming checks for Medicare beneficiaries. "You can go out to McDonald's and buy probably two hamburgers and a shake for $90 [and] maybe buy a half a tank of gas."

A widening trust gap, poll says

A few weeks from the midterm elections, voters say they are struggling with health costs and want candidates to address them, according to a poll released Tuesday by the nonprofit health research organization KFF.

"The cost of healthcare is what's going to be front of mind as they're casting their votes in November," says Ashley Kirzinger, director of survey methodology for KFF. "And what we are seeing is that the Democratic Party has the advantage overall among all voters on which party voters trust to handle healthcare, but they also have the advantage among independent voters, and that's a really important voting bloc for midterm elections."

She says there is "a widening gap" between the Democratic Party and Republicans when it comes to which party voters trust to handle health costs. "It was just a 10-point margin back in April, and now we're seeing it to be a 20-point margin," she says. The poll found 22% of voters trust Republicans on the issue, compared to 42% who trust Democrats.

Where's the credit for GOP candidates?

Antos, of AEI, calls the Trump administration's decision to send out these checks "inexplicable." He describes the move as politically strange, since a Republican administration that disparages Obamacare is investing more money into it, and "unreasonable from a fiscal standpoint," because of the growing national debt.

Sponsor Message

He also notes that most Americans won't be getting these checks. "How about the average, lower-income worker who has employer coverage?" he asks. "They're not getting anything. Why is that? Is that fair?"

He is doubtful the move will have a political benefit for Republican candidates. "For one thing, Trump is not saying that your local congressman did this for you, Trump is saying he did it for you," Antos says. "I don't get it, and I don't see any advantage to anybody, including Donald Trump."

Despite her mixed feelings, Ellen Allen of West Virginians for Affordable Health Care is planning to deposit the $500 check she just received. "I'm not going to send it back," she says. "I'm going to put it in my health savings account and keep working towards healthcare for all."

World.title: 'Canada is not our enemy': Michigan Republican Senate candidate breaks with Trump on trade war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Republican candidate in a pitched battle for Michigan's open Senate seat is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to end the trade war with Canada.

Mike Rogers released a new 30-second ad criticizing the tariffs while sitting in a sports bar with a Labatt beer, a Canadian brand popular in border states like his.

"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not on our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Rogers says in the ad, as an image of the Ambassador Bridge, which connects Windsor and Detroit, appears on screen.

"As Michigan's senator, I'll bring both parties together to lower your prices. That's job No. 1," Rogers says in the spot.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office later Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump was dismissive of the ad, recasting Rogers's trade war message.

"Well, I viewed it as though he wanted Canada to make a deal," Trump said.

"We don't want them to make cars for us.... It's a long story, but they've been ripping us off. Canada has been ripping us off for many, many years and they're not going to rip us off anymore," he said.

WATCH | Reporter asks Trump about Rogers: Trump reacts to anti-trade war ad from Republican candidate | Duration closed caption 0:45 U.S. President Donald Trump was asked by a reporter about a new ad from Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers that called for an end to the trade war with Canada. Trump said he 'viewed it as though [Rogers] wanted Canada to make a deal' and repeated his claim that Canada has been taking advantage of the U.S. for 'many, many years.'

About-face for Rogers

This is an about-face for Rogers, who earlier had endorsed the tariffs Trump levied on Canadian goods.

In an interview with Fox News this summer, Rogers said Trump's trade policy designed to "reindustrialize" the U.S. was "huge for us ... all of these things are really positive."

He said Canada wants to sell hundreds of thousands of cars into Michigan and that should be "absolutely unacceptable" because those exports "undercut the people who build cars and car parts."

"The Canadians have not been good partners on this," he said.

WATCH | Trump adviser warns Canada against election interference: 'You will pay': Trump adviser warns Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:54 White House trade adviser Peter Navarro warned Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterm elections in border states such as Maine and Michigan by lobbying against the Trump administration's tariffs. Navarro said Canada would 'pay even more dearly' for doing so.

Rogers has long been closely associated with Trump. When the U.S. president endorsed Rogers earlier this year, the candidate said he was "thrilled" to receive it.

"Together, President Trump and I will unleash a great revival in the state of Michigan," he said at the time of the endorsement.

Tariffs unpopular in U.S.: polls

Rogers's break with the president on Canadian trade policy comes as polls suggest Trump's tariffs are deeply unpopular in the U.S.

Only 26 per cent of Americans surveyed for a Politico poll late last month said levying tariffs on Canadian goods was the right thing to do.

LISTEN | Canada's choices: Front Burner 23:47 Should Canada have taken the U.S. deal?

Rogers is also trailing his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, in most public opinion surveys. After the ad was released, El-Sayed said Rogers "must have had one too many of those Labatts."

"You cheer-led this tariff war from the beginning and you’re flip-flopping now because your poll numbers are in free fall. Donald is the reason we’re in a trade war. And he’s the reason you’re running," he wrote in a social media post.

Canada, U.S. auto industries deeply intertwined

The Canadian and U.S. auto sectors have one of the most deeply intertwined cross-border manufacturing relationships in the world.

Canada does not "undercut" the U.S. industry, as Rogers describes; rather, it supplies critical parts used in assembly plants throughout the U.S.

Some of those components cross the border a half-dozen times or more because these sectors are so integrated after decades of free trade, with Canadian plants specializing in particular parts and powertrains.

WATCH | How tariffs are affecting our auto industry: How are tariffs affecting Canada's auto industry, really? | Duration 2:28 Car parts can cross international borders six, seven or even eight times before ending up in a vehicle. But amid a trade war, as both Canada and the United States raise tariffs up to 50 per cent, it's getting more expensive — and complicated — to build cars. The CBC's Acton Clarkin breaks it down.

It's a relationship that experts say has helped the North American auto market compete against low-cost overseas manufacturers.

Plus, Canada is a huge customer for what American auto plants churn out every year. About three-quarters of all vehicles sold in Canada are imported, with the majority coming from U.S. plants in Michigan, Indiana and Texas.

Dearborn, Mich.-based Ford has been the No. 1 vehicle brand in Canada for years, with the American-made F-Series being hugely popular among Canadian consumers.

And, despite Republican claims that Trump's tariff policies are boosting industrial employment, data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics compiled by the Economic Policy Institute shows that some 62,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost since Trump took office for his second term in January 2025.

World.title: Canada yanks sponsorship of disinformation conference discussing U.S. as a threat
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government has withdrawn sponsorship of a European disinformation conference that includes panels discussing the U.S. government as a foreign interference risk.

Samantha Lafleur, a spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada (GAC), said the government took issue with the framing of some panels at the event organized by EU DisinfoLab, a non-profit based in Brussels.

The conference features panels about the U.S. as a source of "foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI)," a phenomenon where foreign governments or actors on their behalf manipulate information to confuse, divide or mislead the public and erode confidence in institutions.

GAC — Ottawa's diplomatic arm — Lithuania's Foreign Ministry and the European External Action Service were initially listed as supporters of the annual conference largely attended by researchers and civil society organizations.

The government of Canada logo was covered up on signs spotted around the anti-disinformation conference. (Submitted)

As the gathering got underway in Vilnius, Lithuania, on Wednesday, their names were covered up on signs spotted around the conference, according to photos shared with CBC News. As of writing, the French government remains a sponsor.

In a statement to CBC News, GAC did not deny that it had concerns with describing the U.S. as a foreign interference threat.

"Following changes to the framing of several panel discussions, GAC decided to revise its participation in those sessions at the EU DisinfoLab 2026 conference," wrote Lafleur.

She did not respond to questions about particular changes GAC took issue with or whether the U.S. raised concerns.

According to the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, the description of Wednesday's panel discussing how to push back on the U.S. as a foreign interference threat appears to have been unchanged since Sept. 9.

GAC no longer chairing Arctic panel

A GAC official also pulled out of chairing a session on disinformation in the Arctic scheduled for Thursday, said presenter Ben Shultz with the American Sunlight Project.

The panel proposes to talk about Greenland and "growing evidence that the United States has, in specific Arctic contexts, operated as a FIMI actor."

Shultz shared the initial plan for the panel from months ago, which includes talking about the U.S. as a foreign interference actor.

He called three governments withdrawing a "shock" and questioned whether they were pressured.

"Thankfully every speaker has still shown up, which is awesome, and I think a testament to the resolve of the research community. But it's definitely put a bit of a damper on the atmosphere," he said in an interview.

The European External Action Service, the EU's diplomatic service, said in a statement it asked to have its logo removed from the material associated with the conference "in view of the content of the programme."

Asked if it was related to the U.S. foreign interference panel, an EU spokesperson repeated that the EEAS logo was removed because "organizers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU."

Neither Lithuania's Foreign Ministry nor the conference organizers responded to a request for comment.

Canada's withdrawal comes the same week the Globe and Mail reported that some people involved in campaigning for Alberta independence had met on both sides of the border with U.S. entities.

CBC News previously reported that some of those meetings took place in U.S. State Department offices in Washington, D.C., last year.

GAC's move also comes as the country is embroiled in an often bitter and personal trade dispute with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration.

Lafleur said Canada "remains firmly committed to addressing the challenge of disinformation and misinformation" and that Global Affairs Canada officials "look forward to engaging with partners and stakeholders on efforts to counter disinformation."

World.title: Don't support Trump tariffs then blame Stelco job cuts on 'act of God,' Joly warns Cleveland-Cliffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's industry minister said Wednesday Stelco Holdings Inc. cannot use the trade war to justify cutting jobs it committed to when it bought the Hamilton-based steel plant, particularly when the head of its U.S. parent company has publicly backed steel tariffs.

Mélanie Joly told reporters that the chief executive of U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs has supported steel tariffs and therefore cannot characterize the company's plan to lay off up to 500 workers due to tariffs and market pressures as beyond its control.

"He's in favour of these U.S. tariffs against steel," she said, referring to Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves' public support of American steel tariffs.

"They cannot say that this is now an act of God or force majeure."

If the company does not respond to the federal government's demand for a plan outlining how it will meet all of its commitments, including maintaining more than 1,500 jobs, Ottawa will pursue enforcement action, Joly said.

"They need to comply," she said. "If not, we will use the full force of the law."

Canada gave U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs the green light to purchase Stelco back in 2024 under the Investment Canada Act.

Canada's approval of that takeover was contingent on the new owner maintaining the number of union jobs and the majority of non-union positions, Joly said.

She sent a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon on Monday demanding a plan outlining how Cleveland-Cliffs intends to comply with all of the undertakings it made to Ottawa when it acquired Stelco, including its jobs commitment.

Ottawa has not yet received a response from Stelco on the letter, Joly said.

Meanwhile, she distinguished Stelco's planned job cuts from recent layoffs and plant disruptions in the auto sector, saying Cleveland-Cliffs made legally binding employment commitments when it acquired the steelmaker.

"These obligations are binding."

World.title: Lawyer accused of fraud says bad cheque didn't hurt the bank
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The fraud trial for a suspended Ontario lawyer ping-ponged back and forth Tuesday on whether TD Bank had suffered any harm or risk of loss as a result of a bad cheque the lawyer wrote.

Nicholas Cartel, a class-action and litigation specialist, is on trial on a single count of fraud over $5,000 relating to a $300,000 personal cheque he wrote in 2023, which prosecutors allege was done to help cover up the financial collapse of his and his wife’s law firm. That cheque bounced five days after being deposited into a TD bank account belonging to the law firm.

In the second day of testimony in provincial court in Toronto, a witness representing TD was grilled by both the defence and prosecution about what harm, if any, the bank incurred as a result. Proving fraud under the Criminal Code requires proving that someone either suffered a loss or was exposed to a risk of economic deprivation.

“There was no negative balance at the end of the day?” Cartel asked TD employee Tonya Cole in cross-examination.

“That’s correct, yes,” Cole replied.

Prosecutors Megan Rauser, left, and Dihim Emami converse outside court at the end of the first day of Cartel's criminal trial. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

Cartel has not denied he wrote the bad cheque for $300,000 on a personal account at RBC — which he maintains was a joint account with his wife, Singa Bui. But he says his wife, not he, deposited the cheque to the TD trust account of their firm, Cartel & Bui LLP. And then she was the one, he says, who immediately after obtained a $2.2-million certified cheque from TD to send to a client of the firm.

Prosecutors allege the certified cheque couldn’t have been issued without the top-up from the $300,000 deposit, because the law firm’s trust account was already in shortfall. Bui had been embezzling money from it for years, according to her own evidence in a separate civil case.

When Cartel’s personal cheque from RBC bounced five days later, TD had to go into his firm’s trust account and take out the $300,000.

Prosecutor Dihim Emami focused on that in his re-examination of Cole.

“It's fortuitous that this account had funds subsequent for TD to recover their $300,000, correct?” he asked. “If this account was depleted … or for a whole host of reasons other influxes of money didn't come in, TD might never have recovered that amount, correct?”

“That's possible, yes,” Cole said.

Home buyers and sellers left in lurch

The collapse of Cartel & Bui LLP in December 2023 left more than 25 home buyers and sellers in southern Ontario in the lurch for amounts ranging from $66,000 up to $2.16 million, in the case of one couple — money they had either transferred to the firm's trust account to buy a home or were expecting in payouts after selling their home.

Bui has admitted in lawsuits against her and Cartel that she started pilfering money from the firm’s trust account as far back as 2014 to fund the couple’s "luxury lifestyle," in a Ponzi-like scheme where incoming funds from new clients would cover for amounts she had stolen. She and Cartel bought two Toronto homes for $6 million total, sent their children to private school, took "luxurious vacations" and, she said, “decorated our home and office with elegant furnishings and expensive art.”

Cartel has long maintained he didn’t know about the embezzlement until December 2023, but a Superior Court judge overseeing more than 15 lawsuits against the couple and their former law firm has questioned those claims, saying at one point in June 2024: “Did she pay for nice gifts for you? Did you buy a car that she paid for? Did she pay mortgage payments? How can you not know, when you're living with her and you've got a home together and you've got children together, where $6 million went?"

The judge later sent both Cartel and Bui to jail, for 30 days and 20 days respectively, for contempt, ruling that they "have taken active steps to hide their finances and to frustrate the court."

Now-disbarred real estate lawyer Singa Bui leaves a Toronto courthouse in October 2024 after being sentenced to 30 days in provincial prison for civil contempt of court. The sentence was later reduced to 20 days. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

A Law Society of Ontario ruling in April 2024 suspending Cartel from practising law commented that “while it is conceivable that Ms. Bui acted alone and that Mr. Cartel had no knowledge or involvement, there are good reasons to believe otherwise,” including that various of Cartel’s explanations were “difficult to accept.”

Bui has since been disbarred while the Law Society’s disciplinary case against Cartel has yet to come to a final hearing.

Bogus signatures

In his criminal trial, Cartel is representing himself after a falling-out with his former defence lawyer Richard Posner.

Court records from a separate case, where Cartel challenged Posner’s invoices, show Posner criticizing Cartel for being “arrogant and patronizing” toward staff at Posner’s firm. Posner also told Cartel he was “completely uncomfortable” with Cartel’s wish to interact mainly over email “given the tenor of your writing.” Cartel had made claims in emails to Posner's firm that, among other things, the prosecution in his case had drafted a fraudulent document to pressure Cartel into agreeing to certain facts ahead of trial.

Cartel, in turn, accused Posner of “deliberate willful blindness” to documents that would supposedly help exonerate him. He also said Posner’s assistant “forced condescending, unsolicited opinions of culpability onto” him.

In another email, Posner states that if Cartel is going to testify in his own defence, it will take “a few days” to coach him because “without extensive preparation, Mr. Cartel will not present well as a witness.”

The dispute between them also reveals that Cartel put together documents that contained bogus signatures of another lawyer, George Tsimiklis. The signatures appear on the witness line of two affidavits Cartel swore in his dispute with Posner.

“Although the document bears my signature … I did not sign it either in person or electronically, and I did not authorize Mr. Cartel or any other person to affix or reproduce my signature on it,” Tsimiklis says in his own sworn statement filed in the case.

Cartel says the documents were only in draft form and he never intended them to be submitted to court.

Tsimiklis was a colleague of Cartel and has previously witnessed affidavits for him and represented Cartel’s wife, Bui.

Cartel told CBC during a break in his trial on Monday that he emailed the documents to a court clerk but only as drafts and he wasn’t formally filing them. He blamed the clerk for misunderstanding instructions and placing the affidavits with the bogus signatures into the court file.

Asked how the signatures got onto his affidavits in the first place, Cartel claimed it happened because different pages from different documents got compiled together by the court clerk, including some pages that had Tsimiklis’s genuine signature from past filings.

That explanation, however, doesn’t square with the fact that Tsimiklis’s bogus signatures don’t appear on their own page but rather at the bottom of the newly created affidavits.

Cartel is currently suing CBC, Toronto Life magazine and the Toronto Sun newspaper for their coverage of his and his wife’s ordeals.

His trial is scheduled to resume in November.

World.title: Teen accused in school sword attack praised Nazis, talked about mass murder plans, court hears
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story contains references to violent crime and racially motivated attacks.

In the months leading up to a sword attack at a Brandon, Man., high school, a teen wrote in a notebook about "invaders" of Canada — specifically Black and Muslim immigrants — and his mass murder plan.

That's according to an agreed statement of facts presented in court Tuesday, as the trial for the boy began unexpectedly ahead of schedule in Brandon's Court of King's Bench. The day was originally scheduled for a pretrial hearing.

The now 17-year-old, who can't be named under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, pleaded not guilty to nine charges related to the June 10, 2025, attack at Neelin High School in the southwestern Manitoba city, including three charges of attempted murder.

He's also charged with aggravated assault, two counts of assault with a weapon, wearing a disguise with intent and two counts of possessing a weapon for a dangerous purpose.

As the charges were read out, the boy became emotional, prompting the judge to ask him if he needed a break.

The 2025 attack left a fellow 15-year-old student — who is Black and whose family is originally from Nigeria — with major injuries, in what police have previously described as a racially motivated crime.

Details of the attack were revealed in court in an agreed statement of facts read by federal Crown prosecutor Hugh Crawley.

Just after 10 a.m. on the morning of the attack, the accused, then a Grade 10 student, told a friend on the phone that he was going through with the plan he'd been formulating for months.

WATCH | Teen wrote about 'invaders,' mass murder plan, court hears: Teen accused in Neelin High School sword attack pleads not guilty | Duration closed caption 1:56 A teenager charged in a sword attack at Neelin High School in Brandon, Man., in 2025 pleaded not guilty on Wednesday to nine charges, including three counts of attempted murder. Court heard that the 17-year-old boy, who can't be named under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, allegedly wrote in a notebook about "invaders" of Canada — specifically Black and Muslim immigrants — and his mass murder plan in the months leading up to the attack.

Shortly after 1 p.m., he entered the school wearing black pants and a black trench coat, with a concealed sword and steak knife. He went to a washroom and put on a black "plague" face mask, which featured a long, beak-like nose and covered most of his face.

He then entered the east hallway of the high school, which has about 380 students in grades 9 to 12.

The victim, a fellow student, stopped to tell the teen he liked the costume. They spoke for a few seconds before the accused stabbed the other teen multiple times in his shoulder, chest, stomach, thigh and arm.

The victim — a 15-year-old Grade 10 student — grabbed at the sword to try to prevent the attack, which severed one of his fingers and cut others.

That victim ran away, with the accused following, then ducked into the administration office.

Brandon community cadets are seen outside Neelin High School in Brandon on Tuesday, June 10, 2025. (Chelsea Kemp/CBC)

He passed by the principal, Baseswa Nundu, who thought the victim was playing a joke. Soon after, the accused spotted the principal and chased him down the hall.

Nundu ran into a nearby classroom and held the door closed. The accused stabbed at a small glass window by the door, narrowly missing Nundu's eye.

The accused then walked down the hallway past several Caucasian students and didn't react, the agreed statement reads. He saw another student, identified in the statement only as B, and started chasing that student with his sword above his head.

A Caucasian teacher stopped the accused and was unharmed.

According to the agreed statement of facts read by Crawley, the accused entered a classroom and asked if there were "any blacks." The students told him no and the accused left.

'Why didn't you shoot me?'

By this point — about five minutes after the accused had entered the school — the principal had ordered a lockdown and the hallways were largely empty.

Seven minutes after the teen entered the school, Brandon police officers arrived. Nearly the entire Brandon police service was sent to the school, the statement of facts says.

The accused asked police to shoot him in the head and refused to drop the sword, the statement says.

Police used a Taser on him twice before he was taken into custody.

Once in custody, the teen shouted, "Why didn't you shoot me?" and "I wanted you to shoot me."

The teen "told every officer he encountered that he was intoxicated," according to the agreed statement of facts, but officers said he showed no signs of this.

WATCH | Teen arrested in June 2025 after sword attack at Brandon school: More bloodshed intended in Brandon high school sword attack: police | Duration 2:09 A 16-year-old boy accused of attacking and seriously injuring another student with a sword at Neelin High School in Brandon, Man., intended to hurt more people, but was stopped by the swift action of school staff and officers, police say. Community members have left chalk messages of support for students and staff on the sidewalks outside the school.

In a videotaped interview with police, played in court Tuesday, the boy told detectives he'd been planning the incident for months and he'd gotten the sword from his home, saying it belonged to his sister. He said he practised with it in the bushes in his yard.

When pressed on his motive, he said he wanted to "go out with a bang" and hoped that would garner praise from certain people.

He admitted to being inspired by a 2015 case in Sweden where a man dressed in black and armed with a sword killed three immigrants before being killed by police.

In the interview, the teen told detectives he didn't attack Caucasian kids in the classroom because they were white.

He also used the term "invaders" to describe people he believed move to Canada but hate the country and do monstrous things to Canadians, the agreed statement of facts says.

"The accused told police the only thing that went different from his plan was that he was not killed by officers," the statement says.

Journal entries praised Nazis

A day after the attack, Brandon police combed through the accused's home.

In it, they found several cardboard weapons, in the shape of guns and swords, in the teen's room.

A black notebook with journal entries dating back to mid-2022 had several entries celebrating Hitler and the Nazis, and others supporting Texas's right to patrol its borders.

The notebooks also contained references to Black and Muslim immigrants, whom he called "invaders," the statement of facts says.

A Feb. 5, 2022, entry spoke of a hatred for Muslims, saying "with a gun, I'd spree kill as much … as I can."

A journal entry written 12 days before the Neelin school attack detailed a "mass murder" suicide plan.

Crown prosecutors say a phone seized during a search of the teen's home contained a file that they plan to argue was the beginning of a manifesto he wrote. (CBC)

Police also seized a tablet and phone belonging to the accused that had files about school shootings, including the 1999 shooting in Columbine high school in Colorado.

In the months leading up to the school attack, there were thousands of searches on the accused's phone for domestic terrorism, specific incidents of violence and targeted acts of racially motivated violence.

One search included average police response times in Brandon.

The phone contained 14,538 photos, including many of guns and other weapons, Hitler and other Nazi imagery, plus some pictures of himself giving a Nazi salute with cardboard weapons.

Several documents on his phone had titles referencing Hitler, white supremacy and school attacks. The phone also had several manifestos written by white nationalists.

Crown prosecutors also said the phone contained a file that they plan to argue was the beginning of a manifesto written by the accused.

Video footage from inside Neelin High School, which has over a dozen video cameras, according to the statement of facts, are expected to be shown in court during the trial.

The accused has been in custody since his arrest. His trial is scheduled to resume in June 2027.

World.title: U.S. army moves to execute man convicted in 2009 deadly Fort Hood rampage by firing squad
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The former U.S. army officer convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad in December in what would be the first U.S. military execution in more than 65 years.

Acting secretary of the U.S. army Adam Telle said in a social media post that army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan will be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood. This followed news from the Pentagon that U.S. President Donald Trump had approved the execution.

The announcement stunned an attorney who had represented Hasan in a civil case, and raised concerns among experts on military law about whether the army followed its mandated process for setting an execution and notifying a prisoner they've been condemned to death.

It also sparked questions about how a firing squad would be assembled and what procedure it would use. The last time the military executed someone by firing squad was shortly after the Second World War.

Here's a look at the military execution process and how experts say this case may proceed.

A man and child lay flowers and a balloon outside the front gate of the Fort Hood Army Post in Fort Hood, Texas following the shooting rampage which left 13 people dead in 2009. (Jessica Rinaldi/Reuters)

Who would form firing squad

Telle confirmed in his post on X that Trump had approved the execution on Oct. 2, starting the clock in army regulations that requires an execution date to be set no sooner than 60 days and no later than 150 days after that approval.

Telle also noted that the execution would be carried out by firing squad, but did not offer details of where on base the execution would take place, what personnel would be a part of that squad or what procedure they would follow.

The Associated Press asked both Pentagon officials and the army for more details, but those requests were declined. A message to the army seeking comment on the potential procedural issues was sent Wednesday.

The procedures for execution in army regulations do not contain specific protocols for particular methods of execution. Experts said in previous iterations of the firing squad — nearly 80 years ago — one shooter would be given a blank so they all could plausibly believe they had not fired the fatal shot.

The execution could be delayed

Hasan, an army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups, shouted Allahu akbar — Arabic for "God is greater" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.

He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims — a defence a military judge barred him from presenting during his trial. Hasan made almost no effort to defend himself in court, telling jurors when he acted as his own counsel that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had "switched sides."

"What happens now, is if Dr. Hasan decides he wants to resist execution, he can go to federal civilian court for a Habeas Corpus petition … and that can last years," said Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.

Habeas Corpus is a legal procedure whereby an incarcerated person can challenge the lawfulness of their imprisonment.

"It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions," Fidell said.

Trump resumed the federal death penalty after an informal moratorium during previous administrations. The federal government executed 13 people between 2020 and early 2021, contributing to making Trump the most prolific execution president in over 130 years.

Military executions rare

Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system and executions even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kan., and the last execution that took place there was a hanging in 1961.

John Galligan, a retired colonel and a former military judge, represented Hasan in civil matters. The attorney said Wednesday that he's limited on what he can talk about, but called the rush to conduct the execution "horrific."

Galligan, who spoke with Hasan on Wednesday, said he believes the army regulation to have the facility's army commandant notify Hasan, accompanied by a chaplain and a Trial Defence Service attorney or civilian counsel if possible, was not followed. Galligan said that, according to Hasan, there was no legal counsel present.

"For the life of me, I don't know what they are trying to accomplish in such a rush fashion … and by trying to conduct this execution at Fort Hood, when he has such medical issues," Galligan said, raising questions about how Hasan, who is paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair, would be transported to Fort Hood.

How South Carolina conducts firing squads

Before Hasan's execution was set for Fort Hood, there was speculation the army might reach out to one of the handful of states that have recently reinstated the firing squad for use in executions — particularly South Carolina or Utah, where they've renovated facilities and established protocols.

South Carolina has killed three prisoners by firing squad in the past 18 months, the only such executions in the U.S. in the past 16 years.

It's unclear if the army will borrow from the state's protocol, but it sets out for three volunteer shooters to stand 4.6 metres from the condemned prisoner, who is strapped to a chair. A medical professional uses an X-ray to find the prisoner's heart and place a target over it. A hood is placed over the prisoner's head after his final words, and a shade is lifted so the shooters can see their target.

All three shooters have live ammunition and fire at the same time with no verbal warning for the condemned prisoner.

South Carolina spent about $54,000 US to renovate its death chamber for the firing squad.

World.title: NASA's Curiosity rover takes striking image of dawn on Mars
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

NASA has released a striking image of dawn on the Martian surface taken by its Curiosity rover, showing sunlight bathing ‌jagged crags formed billions of years ago as the car-sized vehicle continues to explore Earth's planetary neighbour.

Curiosity landed in 2012 in Gale Crater near the Martian equator, and since 2014 has been climbing Mount Sharp, a five-kilometre-tall mountain rising from the crater floor.

The image was taken by the six-wheeled rover's Mastcam camera about ​an hour after the sun rose above a landscape featuring wind-carved ​cliffs in the distance.

"The bright craggy peaks in the distance are a rock layer that is quite different in appearance from all the layers the rover has driven through so far," said planetary scientist Ashwin Vasavada of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, the Curiosity project scientist.

NASA believes that some kind of wind-blown sediment landed in the crater from nearby volcanic activity. Once it hardened into rock, "eons of wind carved ‌up the rock layer into ridges called yardangs," Vasvada said.

The yardang layer most likely formed about three billion years ago, around the same time as the rest of the mountain, according to Vasavada. This layer spans about 16 ⁠kilometres across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp.

But the layers appears to have been added on later, he said.

"It's above what geologists call an ‌unconformity: a gap in time where previous layers eroded down before new layers were deposited on top."

Rover making gradual ascent up mountain

The rover on its gradual ascent up the mountain has gained upwards of nearly a kilometre in elevation, the most ever climbed on Mars, according to NASA.

Mount Sharp is built of layers, each recording a ​period of the planet's geological past. In studying these layers, scientists have learned more about bodies of water — lakes and streams — that long ago covered this region, at ⁠a time when Mars was wetter and warmer than the cold and desolate place it is today.

Vasavada said NASA hopes ⁠Curiosity will reach the yardang layer in 2027 or 2028, at which time it will use its instruments to ⁠scrutinize ⁠the geology there.

Curiosity has been studying the ​geology and climate of Mars and examining whether it once bore conditions conducive to harboring microbial life. It is one of two ​NASA rovers operating on Mars. The ⁠Perseverance rover is currently traversing the margins of Jezero Crater in the northern hemisphere.

Curiosity's new image of Martian dawn is certainly otherworldly.

"This scene has a wildness that reminds me of a road trip through Monument Valley, Arizona. You can almost feel the silence and the endless open space under the sky," Vasavada said.

"But as familiar as that sounds, the sky is orange and the sunrise has shades ⁠of blue. It's like Earth, but ‌it's definitely Mars."

World.title: Student-led protests have thrown France into chaos. Here's what's happening
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

France has been thrown into crisis as student-led protests erupted across the nation, calling for better conditions for learning and for the government to address a decade-long staffing shortage.

Protests began at a Paris-region high school in mid-September, soon growing into a nationwide movement. More than 250,000 people took to the streets on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, the Interior Ministry said, in the demonstration's biggest day yet. (Organizers put the number higher, at 450,000.)

The rallies have led to widespread school disruptions, arrests and violence, with police deploying tear gas and other riot-control weapons against crowds of mainly teenagers — angering their parents and teachers and prompting them to participate.

It represents the latest test for outgoing President Emmanuel Macron. His prime minister Sébastien Lecornu addressed the nation on Wednesday night, pledging to introduce new measures by the end of the month. A platform for students to voice grievances, launched on Tuesday, has already received some 40,000 submissions.

Here's a look at what we know so far about the protests — and how they became so widespread.

Protesters hold a banner reading 'Rostand angry, Rostand supportive' during the protest in Caen, France, on Oct. 6. (Guillaume Saligot/AFP/Getty Images)

Why are they protesting?

Many high school students say the state of their learning environment is poor, from decaying infrastructure to a lack of personnel. More than half of all schools are short-staffed this year, according to a survey conducted by a secondary school teachers’ union.

The shortage has affected public education in France for close to a decade. The chronic failure to replace absent teachers or hire substitutes means students can miss hundreds of hours of instruction.

They are fed up with overcrowded classrooms, as well, which have increased to an average of 25 to 30 students a class.

Students also describe dilapidated buildings, pest infestations — including cockroaches and rats — and uninsulated classrooms severely affected by temperature shifts, particularly during recent heat waves.

“In the summer, it's 35 degrees,” said Rudy Cuvilliez, who studies in the Paris suburb of Pantin. “And we're, like, 30 to 35 students in every class, so it's unbearable!”

Rudy Cuvilliez, who studies in the Paris suburb of Pantin, holds up canisters from tear gas he says police fired earlier in the day on Oct. 6. (Kyle G. Brown/CBC)

Students and their supporters have taken to the streets for weeks because they feel the government is doing too little, too late. The Education Ministry will receive an additional €1.2 billion in funding next year, but it will not be enough, according to opposition parties , who say the amount barely keeps up with inflation.

Why is the state of schools so poor?

The French state spends more on education than on any other ministry, but it has not kept up with a sharp increase in the youth population, expected to peak in 2028.

The movement originated in the suburbs of the greater Paris region — areas historically underserved and facing significant growth. There are considerable regional disparities, with Île-de-France spending less than any other region in the country.

Schools in higher-income areas benefit from parents’ contributions, while those in underprivileged areas often lack resources.

WATCH | Students say education system is underfunded: Why thousands of high school students in France are protesting | Duration 1:43 Police fired tear gas and water cannons at protesters blockading French high schools — as students, teachers, parents and unions took to the streets against what they say is underfunding of the education system. Rights groups and students have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government ‌has responded to the demonstrations with riot police and says the movement has been hijacked by outsiders and morphed into urban violence.

Meanwhile, administrative and contracting procedures can be complex, meaning that even repairs that have been financed can take a long time to carry out.

As for personnel, teachers are not valued as they once were — entry-level salaries were more than double minimum wage in 1980; now, they are only just above the minimum.

“The government has not really made an effort to make the profession attractive," said Agnès Van Zanten, a senior research professor emeritus at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research, "such as by raising salaries, for instance.”

What do the students want?

Many want to see large-scale recruitment of teachers, school nurses and teaching assistants. Students, particularly in the banlieues, or economically deprived suburbs, call for urgent repairs and renovations to school buildings.

Recent educational reforms have resulted in longer school days, often extending from 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m., which many find onerous.

But students should be careful what they wish for: The French school day is so long in part to compensate for lengthy school vacations — some 16 weeks compared to the European average of 14. Shortening school days may mean fewer holidays.

A protester in Paris holds a sign that says, 'Is the revolution reserved for history classes?' in French on Oct. 6. (Kyle G. Brown/CBC)

What keeps other students awake at night is “Parcoursup,” a national web platform where high schoolers can secure a place in a higher education institution. Students can list up to 10 schools of preference, with their marks and test results included in their applications.

How they are assessed, however, is a bit of a mystery, with critics calling for the repeal or overhaul of the process.

It was among the topics raised by students meeting with the national education minister last week, but they reached no agreement, and school blockades resumed.

Wracked by weeks of student protests and an increasingly broad base of support, the French government is now trying to rush through a number of reforms.

What disruptions have the protests caused?

Since the movement began last month, hundreds of schools have been blockaded. And while the majority of protests have been peaceful, some have been marred by vandalism and violence. Police have made more than 5,000 arrests so far.

More than 200 people have been injured since the student mobilization began, “whether in accidents … or due to injuries caused by troublemakers,” said Education Minister Édouard Geffray.

WATCH | Hundreds of schools remain closed: Up to 500 schools in France to remain closed amid student protests | Duration closed caption 3:40 Hundreds of French high schools began a second week of closures on Monday as protests over dilapidated schools and classrooms, overcrowding and teacher shortages spread across the country.

Police have also severely injured some people, including a youth who was blinded in one eye after being hit by a flash-ball. France has suspended the use of stun grenades after 15-year-old boy's hand was mutilated in northern France.

Amnesty International condemned “the disproportionate use of force against secondary school protests," calling for police to de-escalate. At least 18 internal police investigations are underway into alleged police violence.

Why has the response been so aggressive?

The Interior Ministry is applying a policy of “absolute firmness” to break up blockades and prevent the destruction of public property. Twenty-four schools had been burned or ransacked on Sunday, according to the education minister.

French police forces have often been criticized by human rights groups and the UN for their use of excessive force, and the response to the student protests has sparked intense controversy, not least among parents.

WATCH | Teen loses hand in protests: Teenager loses hand in violent France school protests | Duration closed caption 2:02 A 15-year-old boy lost a hand during student protests across France calling for better school conditions. More than 5,000 young people have been arrested during the unrest, and dozens of schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education minister.

Critics blame the prime minister and interior minister for inciting the police by insisting the movement was a problem of social order rather than trying to address students’ demands.

Why is the government worried about these protests?

Even though most of the protesters are under 18 — the minimum voting age in France — the government still sees the continued uprising as a threat to public order, particularly now that parents, teachers and activists of all kinds have joined in solidarity.

Indeed, the government is concerned about a potential “coalition of anger,” in which frustration with a decade under Macron reaches a boiling point. Historically in France, youth movements have often served as a catalyst for wider social movements and upheaval.

World.title: Hudson & Rex welcomes actor John Reardon back
World.content:
Article content

A: I didn’t. It was really quite beautiful. It meant a lot to me — how much the show means to them — and it felt important for me to come back when I had the opportunity to help tell more stories. But I was truly touched at all the messages that people sent me. I would just love to say thank you. It meant the world to me.
