World.title: Peru Launches Military-Police Crime Command
World.content:
Security: Peru

Key Facts —Who. Keiko Fujimori, Peru’s conservative president since 28 July 2026, with the Armed Forces and the National Police. —What. A unified command of 1,350 troops and police, called the Combined Forces for the Fight Against Organised Crime. —Where. Announced at Army headquarters in San Borja, a district of Lima, where a control and operations centre will run. —When. Wednesday 7 October 2026, after a meeting of the National Security and Defense Council. —Status. Announced. We found no start date for field operations in the reports we reviewed. —As of. 7 October 2026, 23:44 GMT.

Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori announced a joint command of 1,350 soldiers and police officers to fight organised crime on Wednesday 7 October 2026. The force will run from a new control centre at Army headquarters in Lima, and Fujimori called it “a total offensive” against criminals.

What We Know

Fujimori presented the Combined Forces at the Plaza Cáceres of the Army headquarters in San Borja. The ceremony followed a session of the National Security and Defense Council, according to RPP and Nacional TV Perú.

The force has 1,350 members: 500 from the Army, 250 from the Air Force, 200 from the Navy, 80 from the Joint Special Forces and 320 police officers from specialised units. RPP attributes these figures to a statement from the Interior Ministry.

A large control and operations centre at Army headquarters will direct all actions, RPP and Infobae report. The plan also creates an elite group of police and soldiers for search-and-capture operations.

The Palace of Justice in Lima. File photo.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Lima (Peru) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Plan Includes

Fujimori said the government will remove foreigners who “came to break the law” from the country in record time. Infobae adds that the plan covers accelerated deportation of foreign nationals convicted of crimes.

The government also plans to take control of prisons and to isolate inmates who keep directing crimes from inside. A special commission will coordinate the financial intelligence unit, the intelligence directorate and private telecoms companies, according to RPP.

“The time has come to go forward in a total offensive,” Fujimori said, in our translation of her Spanish words. She said the armed forces must act within the Constitution and the law, citing Article 44, which makes the state responsible for protecting the population.

The Crime Problem Behind the Decision

Extortion is the crime Peruvians complain about most. The public prosecutor’s crime observatory reports that extortion cases have grown 33.8% since 2022, against 3.1% for all crimes it tracks, according to Infobae.

Official figures show 26,585 extortion complaints in 2025, up from 22,361 in 2024. Homicide rates have also climbed, from 8.6 per 100,000 people in 2021 to a provisional 10.7 in 2025, according to the national statistics institute INEI.

Police figures for early 2026 show fewer complaints than a year earlier, but prosecutors’ records and opinion surveys point the other way. A March 2026 report by the BCP-Credicorp crime observatory, using Ipsos data, found that a quarter of adults had been victims of extortion or knew a victim in the previous three months.

The gap between sources is part of the story. Peruvians say they feel less safe even where police counts fall, which is the pressure the new command answers.

Why This Comes Now

Fujimori took office on 28 July after campaigning on security, and crime has stayed at the top of Peruvian politics since. Her government is also asking Congress for decree powers on citizen security and the El Niño weather pattern.

The Chamber of Deputies voted on 6 October to give her 90 days of decree powers, with 66 votes in favour and 24 abstentions, according to Andina. The Senate must still approve or change the text before she can sign it.

What Is Not Known

The reports we reviewed give no date for the first operations. They also do not say how the new force will share command with existing police units, or how long it will stay together.

No budget for the command has been published. It is also unclear how the plan to remove foreigners will be applied, and which legal steps will govern those cases.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

Peru is one of the world’s largest producers of cocaine, according to the United Nations drug agency, so its security policy matters to US drug enforcement. Extortion and organised crime also affect mining, transport and retail firms that sell to US customers.

Visitors should expect a stronger military and police presence in some areas as the command starts work. Travelers should follow the US State Department’s advisory for Peru and local alerts, and should not read the announcement as a change in the current risk level.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Peru’s new unified command?

It is a joint force of 1,350 soldiers and police officers, announced by President Keiko Fujimori on 7 October 2026. It will run from a control centre at Army headquarters in San Borja, Lima.

Who is in the force?

The force has 500 Army, 250 Air Force and 200 Navy members, 80 from the Joint Special Forces and 320 police officers. RPP attributes the figures to the Interior Ministry.

What will the command do?

It will hunt criminals through an elite group, take control of prisons and isolate inmates who direct crimes. It also covers faster removal of foreigners convicted of crimes, according to Infobae.

Why does this matter to US readers?

Peru is one of the world’s largest cocaine producers, according to the United Nations drug agency. Organised crime also affects firms and travelers with US links.

World.title: Milei Calls Lula a Thief Ahead of Brazil Vote
World.content:
Politics: Argentina

Runoff · Sunday, 25 October Flávio Bolsonaro vs Lula: what happens next First-round results, how the runoff works, the key dates and who backs whom, in one guide. Read the runoff guide →

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro 83.8% · Lula 15.5% (US$175 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 83% · Lula 17% As of 7 October, 7:40 pm ET (00:40 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Key Facts —Who. Javier Milei, Argentina’s conservative president, and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s left-wing president, who is seeking re-election. —What. Milei posted the words “LULA LADRÓN” (Lula thief) over a photo of Lula on Instagram, according to Argentine media. —Where. On Instagram, from Buenos Aires, aimed at the Brazilian presidential runoff. —When. Wednesday 7 October 2026, 18 days before the runoff on Sunday 25 October 2026. —Prediction markets. Polymarket prices a Flávio Bolsonaro win at about 84% and a Lula win at 15.5%. Kalshi, regulated in the US by the CFTC, shows 83–84% and 16–17% (7 October 2026, 7:41 p.m. ET). These are bets, not polls. —As of. 7 October 2026, 23:44 GMT.

Argentina’s President Javier Milei called Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a “thief” in an Instagram post on Wednesday 7 October 2026. The post lands 18 days before Brazil’s presidential runoff on 25 October, where Lula faces Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

What We Know

Milei shared a graphic from the Cato Institute, a US libertarian think tank, with the words “LULA LADRÓN” in capitals over a photograph of Lula. Argentine outlets including El Tribuno, Cadena 3 and La Capital report that he repeated it in his Instagram stories.

The graphic carries a quote attributed to Ian Vásquez, the institute’s vice president for international studies. In our translation from the Spanish text, it says that what made people reject Lula and his party is, to a large extent, corruption.

On Monday 5 October, at a cabinet meeting, Milei called the first-round result “a great triumph” and accused Lula of running a “plan platita” at the end of the campaign. The phrase means a handout plan, a late spending push aimed at winning votes.

On Saturday 25 July Milei travelled to São Paulo and shared a stage with Flávio Bolsonaro at the Pacaembu stadium, at the PL party convention that made his candidacy official. Brazil called its ambassador in Buenos Aires home for consultations the next day, after Milei’s remarks there, according to Brazilian media.

Puerto Madero, Buenos Aires. File photo.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Brazil Elections 2026 Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Where the Brazilian Race Stands

Brazil’s electoral court, the TSE, counted 47.03% of valid votes for Flávio Bolsonaro and 45.16% for Lula in the first round on Sunday 4 October. Neither passed 50%, so the two meet again on Sunday 25 October.

The gap was about 2.2 million votes out of about 119.3 million valid votes. Some Argentine outlets quote slightly different percentages, so we use the TSE figures.

Abstention was 21.08%, which means about 33.5 million registered voters stayed home. With the race this tight, those voters are a pool both campaigns will chase.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a global prediction market, traders price a Flávio Bolsonaro win at about 84% and a Lula win at 15.5%, with about US$175 million traded. On Kalshi, which is regulated in the United States by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), the prices are 83–84% and 16–17% (read on 7 October 2026, 7:41 p.m. ET). These prices are real-money bets, not polls, and they can move within minutes of news like this post. A price of about 84% means traders see roughly five chances in six, not a certainty. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Why Argentina and Brazil Matter to Each Other

Argentina and Brazil are partners in Mercosur, the South American trade bloc, and Brazil is Argentina’s largest trading partner. A long feud between the two presidents therefore carries costs beyond the headlines.

The two governments have clashed before. We reported in July that Brazil recalled its ambassador and in August that Milei repeated the word “thief”.

What Is Not Known

It is not clear whether Brazil’s government will respond formally this time. We found no official Brazilian reaction to the post in the reports we reviewed.

Polls published after the first round are not yet in our data. It is also unknown whether a foreign leader’s post moves any Brazilian voters.

Milei has appeared with Bolsonaro’s campaign in public since July, and we do not know whether he will say more before the vote. Argentina’s government has not published a statement on the post in the reports we reviewed.

What to Watch Next

Two dates frame the next three weeks. Argentina’s statistics agency INDEC is due to publish September inflation on Tuesday 13 October, with the central bank’s market survey expecting about 1.9% for the month, against 1.7% in August.

Brazil votes on Sunday 25 October, with polling stations closing at 17:00 Brasília time (20:00 GMT). The TSE publishes the count on the night, and we will update our market prices after the result.

What It Means for US Readers and Investors

Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy, and the 25 October result will shape the direction of its markets, its currency and its trade policy. Investors who hold Brazilian shares or US-listed Brazilian companies are watching the margin as much as the winner.

Milei’s post also shows how far the race has become a regional contest between the right and the left. A US think tank’s graphic was the vehicle for the post, which ties the Brazilian vote to the American debate over Latin America’s political direction.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Milei say about Lula?

Milei posted the words “LULA LADRÓN” (Lula thief) over a photo of Lula on Instagram on Wednesday 7 October 2026. The graphic came from the US Cato Institute, according to Argentine media.

When is Brazil’s presidential runoff?

The runoff is on Sunday 25 October 2026 between Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula. Whoever wins a majority of valid votes becomes president.

Who is ahead in Brazil?

In the first round on 4 October the TSE counted 47.03% for Bolsonaro and 45.16% for Lula. Prediction markets, which are bets rather than polls, price a Bolsonaro win at about 84%.

Why does this matter to US readers?

Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy, so the runoff affects its markets and currency. Investors in Brazilian shares and US-listed Brazilian companies follow the race closely.

World.title: Caputo Takes Argentina’s IMF Case to Bangkok
World.content:
Economy: Argentina

Key Facts —Who. Argentina’s Economy Minister Luis Caputo, with Central Bank President Santiago Bausili and Vice Minister José Luis Daza. —What. Talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to unlock about US$900 million tied to the third review of Argentina’s loan programme. —Where. Bangkok, Thailand, at the IMF and World Bank Group annual meetings. —When. Monday 12 to Sunday 18 October 2026. —Status. No staff-level agreement announced as of 7 October. The IMF Executive Board has not scheduled a vote that we could find. —As of. 7 October 2026, 23:42 GMT.

Argentina’s Economy Minister Luis Caputo will fly to Bangkok on 12 October for the IMF and World Bank annual meetings. His aim is to unlock about US$900 million that depends on the third review of the country’s IMF programme.

What We Know

Economy Minister Luis Caputo will travel to Bangkok, Thailand, from 12 to 18 October 2026, according to Argentine press reports. He goes for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group, which the IMF says run on the same dates.

The delegation includes Vice Minister José Luis Daza and Central Bank President Santiago Bausili, with central bank Vice President Vladimir Werning also reported. Their aim is to unlock about US$900 million tied to the third review of Argentina’s loan programme.

The IMF said on 1 October that a technical mission led by Joyce Wong had visited Buenos Aires from 21 to 29 September. It added that talks continue toward a staff-level agreement, with tax revenues and fiscal targets among the topics.

A staff-level agreement is the first step. Argentine press reports that it is followed by Fund approvals and a vote by the Executive Board, and we found no announcement of a staff-level agreement as of 7 October.

The Economy Ministry in Buenos Aires, where Caputo works. File photo. Photo: Horacio Cambeiro, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Luis Caputo (Argentina) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Numbers the Fund Is Checking

The programme sets a primary surplus target of 1.4% of GDP for 2026. A primary surplus is the budget balance before interest payments.

The Economy Ministry reported that the accumulated primary surplus through August was about 1.1% of GDP, up from about 0.9% at the end of July. The 1.4% target is for the full year, and Política Argentina reports that the government is on course to finish slightly below it.

INDEC, the national statistics agency, reported that consumer prices rose 1.7% in August, down from 2.1% in July, after a peak of 3.4% in March. Annual inflation was 33.5%, down from 33.8% in July.

The IMF has pointed to lower inflation, higher reserves and a move from a fiscal deficit to a surplus. Its spokesperson, Julie Kozack, made those points at the 1 October briefing.

The Executive Board completed the second review on 21 May 2026, after a staff-level agreement in April, and that step opened about US$1 billion. We have covered how the third review tests a target that was already lowered once, and we explain how the IMF programme works.

What to Watch in Bangkok and Buenos Aires

Argentina’s statistics agency, INDEC, is due to publish September inflation on Tuesday 13 October at 16:00 Buenos Aires time (19:00 GMT). Forecasts in the EODHD calendar point to monthly inflation of 2.0%, up from 1.7% in August, and annual inflation near 34%, compared with 33.5% in August.

The meetings’ plenary session is on 16 October, and the IMF’s policy committee, the IMFC, holds its press briefing on 17 October, according to the IMF schedule. Those days give Caputo a stage to meet Fund officials and other finance ministers.

Argentina observes a national holiday on Monday 12 October, the day the Bangkok meetings open. The holiday is the Day of Respect for Cultural Diversity.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the IMF will reach a staff-level agreement before or during the Bangkok meetings. Argentine press reports that a waiver, which is permission to pass a review despite missing a target, is an option if a target is missed.

We found no date for an Executive Board vote on the third review. The timing of the US$900 million therefore remains open.

What It Means for US Readers and Investors

The United States is the IMF’s largest shareholder, so Fund decisions on Argentina matter in Washington as well as in Buenos Aires. A completed review would add to the central bank’s reserves and support confidence among holders of Argentine bonds.

A delay would keep attention on the reserves and on the 1.4% fiscal target. The Bangkok talks and the 13 October inflation figure are the next two signals.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Caputo going to Bangkok?

He will attend the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group, which run from 12 to 18 October 2026. His aim is to move forward the third review of Argentina’s IMF programme.

What is the US$900 million?

It is a payment tied to the third review of Argentina’s IMF programme, according to Argentine press reports. The IMF has not yet approved it.

What is a staff-level agreement?

It is an understanding between IMF staff and a government on a review, and it comes before the Executive Board votes. The IMF said on 1 October that talks toward one were continuing.

When is Argentina’s September inflation due?

INDEC is due to publish it on Tuesday 13 October 2026 at 16:00 Buenos Aires time. The EODHD calendar forecasts monthly inflation of 2.0%.

World.title: Chile Passes Rules on Police Use of Force
World.content:
Politics: Chile

Key Facts —Who. Chile’s Congress. The Senate voted 29 to 15 with one abstention, and the Chamber of Deputies approved the same report earlier that day. —What. A law that sets when Carabineros, the Investigations Police (PDI) and the Armed Forces may use force, in graduated steps up to lethal force. —Where. Chile. The final vote took place in the Senate on Wednesday afternoon. —When. Wednesday 7 October 2026. —Status. Ready for promulgation by the president. The Socialist Party entered a constitutional reservation, a formal objection to parts of the text. —As of. 7 October 2026, 23:43 GMT.

Chile’s Senate approved new rules on the use of force by police and soldiers on Wednesday 7 October 2026, by 29 votes to 15 with one abstention. The bill, which sets when officers may use force and when they are protected from blame, now goes to the president to become law.

What We Know

The Senate approved the report of a joint committee of both chambers, which settled differences between the two houses over the bill. The vote on Wednesday was 29 in favour, 15 against and one abstention, according to Meganoticias and El Dínamo.

The Chamber of Deputies had approved the same report hours earlier, with 111 votes in favour, according to La Tercera. With the Senate vote, the bill leaves Congress and goes to the president to be promulgated, the formal step that makes it law.

The rules cover Carabineros (the uniformed national police), the Investigations Police (PDI) and the Armed Forces. The joint committee left out Gendarmería, the prison guards, according to the Senate.

The text sets graduated levels of force, from a visible deterrent presence and verbal persuasion through less-lethal tools and physical control to, in the last resort, lethal weapons. Opposition critics said it does not name proportionality as a principle, according to Radio UChile.

Carabineros officers on a street in central Santiago. File photo. Photo: Carlos Figueroa Rojas, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Chile congress Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

When Lethal Force Is Allowed

Potentially lethal force is allowed only when earlier steps prove insufficient. The law lists the grounds, according to El Dínamo: fulfilling a duty, lawful self-defence, obeying a court order, detaining someone who resists, preventing an escape and protecting critical infrastructure.

The joint committee also approved the use of shotguns with riot-control ammunition, according to the Senate’s own news service. The aim is to prevent a serious and imminent danger to life or physical integrity, and the rule also covers infrastructure and military facilities.

Officers who follow the rules are covered by the criminal exemption for fulfilling a duty, which exists in the Penal Code, the Senate reports. Deputy Luis Pardo of the National Renewal party said officers who use force in line with their duty will be presumed innocent, according to Meganoticias.

Why It Matters to the Government

Pardo said the law gives security personnel legal certainty. Deputy Mauro González tied the vote to a separate bill, called Naín-Retamal 2.0, which would widen legitimate-defence protections for off-duty officers, according to Meganoticias.

The bill dates from 2023, before Kast took office, and now belongs to the government’s agenda against organised crime and terrorism, according to CIPER. This vote follows another security change we reported, when Kast doubled the police arrest window to 24 hours.

What the Opposition Says

The Socialist Party entered a constitutional reservation, a formal objection to parts of the text, and the Communist Party announced one as well, according to CIPER. La Tercera also reported the Socialist reservation.

Communist Senator Claudia Pascual said the final text prioritises discretion and immunity for the security forces, according to La Tercera. Opposition lawmakers criticised the bill for widening the cases in which lethal force is allowed, according to CIPER.

What Is Not Known

The date on which President José Antonio Kast will promulgate the law has not been announced. It is also unclear whether the constitutional reservations will lead to a formal challenge before the Constitutional Court.

The rules have no track record, and it is too early to say how courts will read them. The coverage we reviewed does not explain how police and soldiers will be trained on the new rules.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

For visitors, the law governs how police and soldiers respond to violence or disorder, not routine checks on tourists. Travellers should still follow local advice and the US State Department’s travel advisory for Chile.

Chile is the world’s largest copper producer, so a settled security framework is part of the investment picture. How the infrastructure clause is applied is the point to watch, and we also reported on US Ambassador Brandon Judd’s remarks on Chilean protesters and US travel.

More: Chile news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Chile’s Senate approve?

The Senate approved rules that set when Carabineros, the Investigations Police and the Armed Forces may use force. The vote on 7 October 2026 was 29 in favour, 15 against and one abstention.

When may officers use lethal force under the law?

Potentially lethal force is allowed only when earlier steps prove insufficient. The grounds include fulfilling a duty, lawful self-defence, a court order, stopping an escape and protecting critical infrastructure.

Who opposes the rules?

The Socialist Party entered a constitutional reservation, and the Communist Party announced one too. Opposition lawmakers say the text widens the cases in which lethal force is allowed.

When does the law take effect?

The bill has cleared Congress and awaits promulgation by the president. The date has not been announced.

World.title: Ceará’s US Exports Fall 78% in September
World.content:
Economy: Brazil

Key Facts —Who. Ceará, a state in Brazil’s northeast whose capital is Fortaleza and which is home to the Port of Pecém. —What. Exports to the United States fell 77.9% in September 2026 to US$42.94 million, from US$194.5 million in August. —Total. All Ceará exports were US$112.72 million, down 67% from August and 29.16% from September 2025. —Tariff. A 25% US surcharge on certain Brazilian goods took effect on 22 July 2026. —Caution. The published figures do not say which products drove September’s fall, so the tariff cannot be treated as the only cause. —When. Brazil’s trade ministry data, reported by O Povo on Wednesday 7 October 2026. —As of. 7 October 2026, 23:50 GMT

Ceará’s exports to the United States fell 77.9% in September to US$42.94 million, from US$194.5 million in August. O Povo reported the figures on Wednesday 7 October 2026 from trade ministry data, and a new 25% US surcharge on some Brazilian goods took effect on 22 July.

What We Know

Ceará sold US$112.72 million abroad in September, 67% less than the US$341.62 million of August and 29.16% less than the US$159.11 million of September 2025. Exports to the United States made up US$42.94 million of that total.

The United States took 57% of Ceará’s exports in August and 38.09% in September. The Netherlands moved into second place with US$8.28 million, or 7.35% of the total.

Imports reached US$279.8 million in September, which left a trade deficit of US$167.1 million. Through September, Ceará’s exports total about US$1.7 billion, up 4.6% from a year earlier, according to O Povo.

Praia de Iracema in Fortaleza, the capital of Ceará, with a ship on the horizon. File photo. Photo: Mayra Pavanello Munerato, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Ceará (Brazil) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Sharp Swing From August

August had been the opposite story. Exports to the United States reached US$194.5 million, 20.4% above July and 243.1% above June, the last full month before the surcharge.

Ceará’s total exports of US$341.62 million in August were the highest monthly figure of the year and 124.5% above August 2025, according to GCMais, citing the state industry federation FIEC. September then gave back most of that gain.

FIEC data reported by GCMais attribute the August jump mainly to iron and steel. For September, neither the O Povo report nor the figures it cites say which products drove the fall.

The Tariff Behind the Headline

On 22 July 2026, a 25% surcharge under Section 301 of US trade law took effect on certain Brazilian goods, according to Brazil’s trade ministry. A second Section 301 measure adds 12.5% on part of Brazil’s exports, so some products face a combined 37.5%.

The ministry estimates that the new measures reach 23.1% of Brazilian exports to the United States, based on 2024 trade data. Another 24.2% is covered by separate Section 232 tariffs.

Shipments already in transit before 22 July could enter the United States until 29 July without the surcharge. Brazil’s exports to the United States fell 13% in the first half of 2026, from US$20 billion to US$17.4 billion, the ministry says.

Why the Picture Is Not Simple

Cast iron, iron and steel made up 63.8% of Ceará’s exports in August, according to GCMais. Steel falls under Section 232, and reports say pig iron is exempt from the new surcharge, so the surcharge alone may not explain the monthly swing.

Monthly export figures can also move sharply with the timing of large ship loadings. That is a general feature of commodity trade, not a finding from this data set.

What Is Not Known

The ministry data used by O Povo do not name the products behind September’s drop, and we have not seen a breakdown from Ceará’s own authorities. It is also unclear whether buyers delayed orders or whether shipments moved to other months.

Whether October will recover or fall further is unknown. The next monthly figures will show whether September was a one-month shock or the start of a lower level.

What It Means for US Readers and Investors

For US importers, Ceará is one source among many for Brazilian goods. Its shipments to the United States are one measure of how the new surcharge is affecting trade.

For investors, the figures give a state-level signal of the tariff’s reach, set against a 13% fall in Brazil’s exports to the United States in the first half. For related reading, see our reports on Brazil’s corn exports and Brazilian industrial production.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Ceará’s exports to the US fall in September?

Ceará’s exports to the United States fell 77.9% to US$42.94 million, from US$194.5 million in August. Total state exports were US$112.72 million, down 67% on the month.

What is the US surcharge on Brazilian goods?

A 25% surcharge under Section 301 of US trade law took effect on certain Brazilian goods on 22 July 2026. A second measure adds 12.5% on part of Brazil’s exports, so some goods face 37.5% together.

Is the tariff the only reason for the drop?

The published figures do not say which products drove September’s fall, so the tariff cannot be named as the only cause. August was an unusually strong month, which makes the September comparison steeper.

Which countries bought more from Ceará?

The Netherlands moved into second place among buyers in September with US$8.28 million, or 7.35% of exports. The United States share of exports fell from 57% in August to 38.09%.

World.title: Brazil Clears American Airlines’ 8% Azul Stake
World.content:
Business: Brazil

Key Facts —Who. American Airlines (Nasdaq: AAL) and Azul, a Brazilian airline that left US Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in February 2026. —What. Brazil’s antitrust tribunal, CADE, voted unanimously on 7 October 2026 to approve American’s purchase of about 8% of Azul for US$100 million. —How. American will exercise two series of Azul subscription warrants, known as AZUL11 and AZUL19. —Condition. The approval depends on a concentration control agreement that CADE can enforce. Its terms were not yet public. —Dispute. Abra Group, which controls rival Gol, had challenged the deal. The tribunal approved it over that objection. —US link. American is a US-listed carrier, and United Airlines committed the same US$100 million to Azul earlier in 2026. —As of. 7 October 2026, 23:50 GMT

Brazil’s antitrust tribunal has approved American Airlines’ purchase of about 8% of Azul, the Brazilian carrier with which it is setting up commercial agreements. The unanimous vote on Wednesday 7 October 2026 puts a second US airline on Azul’s shareholder list, next to United Airlines.

What We Know

Azul told investors on Wednesday that American will invest US$100 million by exercising two series of subscription warrants. Those are Series 1 (AZUL11) and Series 4 (AZUL19).

Azul says the exercise will leave American with about 8% of its total and voting capital. According to Correio Braziliense, the stake comes with one of the seven seats on Azul’s board and one of five seats on a second governance body.

CADE’s technical staff had cleared the deal earlier, and Abra appealed that decision. The tribunal then voted unanimously to approve it.

An Embraer E195-E2 jet, a type that Azul flies. File photo.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on American Airlines (Brazil) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Background: Azul’s Restructuring

Azul left Chapter 11, the US bankruptcy process, in late February 2026, just under nine months after it filed. Its emergence brought US$850 million in new equity, including US$100 million from United.

American’s US$100 million was a separate investment that still needed the Brazilian ruling. With it, the two US carriers’ commitments add up to US$200 million.

What Azul does. Azul S.A., together with its subsidiaries, provides air transportation services in Brazil and internationally. It is also involved in the cargo or mail; passenger charter; development of frequent-flyer programs; intellectual property owner; travel packages; funding: aircraft financing; and provision of maintenance and hangarage services for aircraft, engines, parts and pieces, aircraft acquisition,…

The Conditions CADE Attached

Approval depends on a Concentration Control Agreement, known in Portuguese as an ACC. It turns safeguards that were private into duties that CADE can enforce directly.

According to Correio Braziliense, the terms identify sensitive matters such as pricing and strategy in advance. American’s representative must receive no information on them or step out of the deliberation.

Azul must also report any contract change that widens American’s influence. CADE must be told of future American purchases of stakes in airlines on Brazil-US routes.

Rapporteur Camila Cabral Pires Alves said American’s entry adds what she called a potentially relevant institutional channel of information and influence. That is our translation of her Portuguese wording.

Abra’s Objection

Abra argued that the stakes of American and United would give two US carriers influence inside Azul’s governance forums. It said this weakens their incentive to compete on routes between Brazil and the United States.

Abra said the three airlines together hold more than half of the traffic on key Brazil-US routes. The tribunal approved the deal over that objection.

What Comes Next

Azul expects CADE to publish the decision and the agreement in the coming days. It then plans to put its commercial agreements with American into effect, which CADE also approved.

Reports describe those agreements as covering codeshare flights, links between loyalty programmes and access to airport lounges. Neither airline has said how fares or schedules will change.

What Is Not Known

The text of the control agreement is not yet public, so the exact limits on American’s board seat are unconfirmed. We have also not seen a date for exercising the warrants or issuing the shares.

It is unclear whether CADE’s published decision will add conditions beyond those described in the reports. The full agreement will show how strict the safeguards are.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

For travellers on American’s flights to Brazil, closer ties with Azul could mean easier connections to Azul’s domestic network once the commercial agreements start. That depends on details the airlines have not yet announced.

For investors, the ruling removes a regulatory risk from American’s US$100 million commitment and from Azul’s funding plan. The exercise of the warrants should show up in Azul’s share count after it takes place.

Our earlier report covered CADE staff’s unconditional clearance of the stake in July. For more Brazil business news, see our Brazil industrial production report.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Brazil’s antitrust tribunal decide?

CADE voted unanimously on 7 October 2026 to approve American Airlines’ purchase of about 8% of Azul. The approval depends on a concentration control agreement that CADE can enforce.

How much is American Airlines investing in Azul?

American will invest US$100 million by exercising Azul subscription warrants of Series 1 (AZUL11) and Series 4 (AZUL19). Azul says this gives American about 8% of its total and voting capital.

Why did Abra Group object?

Abra, which controls Gol, argued that American and United together would gain influence inside Azul’s governance. It said this could weaken competition on Brazil-US routes, but the tribunal approved the deal over that objection.

What happens next?

Azul expects CADE to publish the decision and the agreement in the coming days. It then plans to start its commercial agreements with American, which CADE also approved.
