World.title: Rebranded Jaguar unveils its first electric sportscar: The Type 01EV
World.content:
Luxury car manufacturer Jaguar unveiled its first new model since its controversial rebrand two years ago at a flashy New York launch party attended by actress and new company ambassador Florence Pugh, in a bid to win over younger, richer and mostly American audience.

 

The luxury four-door GT Type01EV is Jaguar’s first foray in the electric vehicle (EV) market. Its ultra-modern, brutalist, sharp-edged design is a massive shift from its previously quintessential British elegance.

The radical design is an attempt by Jaguar’s hierarchy to shake off its previously antiquated albeit storied legacy that started as being a car for racing enthusiasts to one for the posh elite. They now have a newer, younger and richer demographic in their crosshairs.

Jaguar says the new model is the first production from its new Jaguar Electric Architecture (JEA), a dedicated platform for the next generation of Jaguar modes, as the company embraces its original motto “Copy Nothing” to create a vehicle they feel is unique.

It’s also gigantic.

Coming in at 5.2 metres long and 2 metres wide, it is longer than most SUVs and too long for most European carparks.

That makes it something of an awkward fit for Europe, where narrow roads are already struggling with the weight and size of today's monstrous vehicles. It would be far more at home on America's vast, endless highways.

But that has not stopped SUV numbers from exploding on EU roads in recent years.

The Type01EV is very low to the ground for its size, standing at only 1.4 metres tall, making it a particularly sleek looking vehicle.

It weighs in at a huge 2700 kilograms, significantly heavier than its competitors such as the Porsche Taycan Turbo GT (2,200kg) and a little more than the Mercedes-Benz EQS (2,585 kg) which shares a similar length.

The Type 01EV’s motor and battery are extraordinary too. Not only are they powerful, clocking in 1015 horsepower and taking it from 0 to 62 mph in 2.2 seconds, it boasts an impressive 478-mile (769km) range, way above most of its rivals, with only the Porsche Taycan marginally more powerful.

The battery also charges at 350kw, allowing it to charge 200 miles (321km) of range in just 13 minutes and go from 10% to 80% charge in just 22 minutes, making it even more appealing to drivers wishing to make the switch to an electric vehicle.

But it won’t be for everyone.

Base models will start at around €140,000 to €150,000 in Europe, with bespoke specifications and customisations taking it up beyond the €200,000 mark.

Jaguar’s rebranded new car does retain a sense of Britishness though, with the Type01EV designed, engineered and built in the UK, according to their website.

Orders are scheduled to open in early 2027, with the first delivers in Europe expected in the second half of 2027.

Jaguar is a British and global car icon known for models such as the Jaguar E-Type driven by Frank Sinatra, Steve McQueen and described by Enzo Ferrari as “the most beautiful car ever made”.

Before its rebrand in 2024, the company was facing a severe, multi-year identity and financial crisis caused by a failing business strategy that relied on an aging core audience and failed to win over younger consumers.

Jaguar was making cars that were not common enough to compete with BMW and Mercedes nor exclusive or “cool” enough to compete with Porsche or Bentley.

The car company took the plunge with a radical rebrand in 2024, releasing an advert that featured no car at all. Instead, models in brightly coloured clothing spouted slogans such as “live vivid”, “delete ordinary” and “be the jag you are”.

The campaign was criticised by many including political figures such as Donald Trump and Nigel Farage for “going woke,” with Elon Musk asking on social media platform X, “Do you sell cars?”

Jaguar defended the ad campaign, telling Sky News at the time that the company wanted “to be bold and disruptive".

The new model’s launch comes as parent company Jaguar Land Rover recovers from a cyberattack that forced the company to halt production last year. One month later, the company announced it would cut 4,000 jobs as part of a major cost-cutting drive.

Today’s unveiling is the culmination of a years-long strategy to reposition the car manufacturer.

World.title: Milan looks East: Chinese fashion takes centre stage for traditional craftwork
World.content:
There's been a lingering sense of a tide turning since Chinese brand ZHONGFANG.LIJIN unveiled its Brocade Reborn collection for spring/summer 2027 at Milan Fashion Week.

 

Its starting point was “Jin Mai” (锦脉), the living veins of brocade. The term refers to the warp and weft of the fabric, but also to the continuity of a tradition that evolves with each new generation.

A fashon industry veteran for more than 20-years, He Rong, founder and creative director of ZHONGFANG.LIJIN, is the beating heart of the collection. As a textile engineer, his practice centres on silk and intricately woven brocades, exploring how these traditional textiles can find a place in contemporary design.

Look 014 @ZOFHANG LIJIN

In Brocade Reborn, nature takes centre stage. Mulberry leaves, silkworms curled inside their cocoons and butterflies emerge as flowing lines, tactile textures and sculptural silhouettes. Brocade is transformed through pleats, intricate motifs and layered details, bringing a centuries-old craft into a distinctly contemporary wardrobe.

Look 004 @ZOFHANG LIJIN

The colour story is equally rooted in Chinese culture. Tianshui Bi evokes the tones of water and sky, Taoyao the delicate pink of peach blossom, Mihe a warm honey hue, Yuebai the soft white of moonlight, and Dailan a deep indigo. Together, the palette draws on Eastern aesthetics and the philosophy of the five elements, Wu Xing.

Look 028 @ZOFHANG LIJIN

The Milan presentation was He Rong’s first in the city, organised with the support of Haining China Home Textile City, one of China’s major textile industry hubs. More than a showcase of craftsmanship, it placed traditional Chinese textile techniques within the international fashion conversation, showing how heritage can be reworked for a contemporary runway.

From brocade to the everyday wardrobe

That dialogue between heritage and contemporary fashion continued with the second Chinese label at this year’s Milan Fashion Week. CHEN.1988 presented its “Insieme con Amore” spring/summer 2027 collection last month at Castello Sforzesco, marking a decade of the brand’s creative journey and its evolving approach to everyday dressing.

A model presents the latest collection @CHEN.1988

While ZHONGFANG.LIJIN starts with the story woven into the fabric itself, CHEN.1988 looks to the way clothes are worn today. The collection experiments with asymmetrical cuts, fluid draping, pleats, suede, corduroy and checks. Fitted silhouettes are balanced by looser, more relaxed shapes, while a restrained palette of black, grey, beige and burgundy is enlivened with flashes of green and navy.

A model presents the latest collection @CHEN.1988

Menswear and unisex pieces also take centre stage. The boundaries between womenswear and menswear are increasingly fluid, with the collection focusing less on fixed categories and more on creating clothes that adapt to the person wearing them.

A model presents the latest collection @CHEN.1988

This idea is at the heart of “Daily Attitude”, the phrase CHEN.1988 uses to define its approach to fashion. Rather than saving clothes for special occasions, the collection brings fashion into the rhythm of everyday life, turning versatile pieces into a canvas for personal style and self-expression.

CHEN.1988 designers Chen Long and Fu Zhichen. @CHEN.1988

CHEN.1988 was founded in 2016 by designers Chen Long and Fu Zhichen, both affiliated with the Jiangxi Institute of Fashion Technology. In 2025, Chen Long received the 29th China Fashion Designer“Golden Top Award”, one of the country’s most prestigious honours for fashion designers. The Milan show marked another step in the brand’s efforts to establish itself on the Italian fashion scene.

Chinese fashion seeks its own language

The two collections approach Chinese fashion from very different directions. One draws on the richness of traditional brocade and silk, while the other starts with the rhythms of the modern wardrobe. Yet both share the same ambition: to move Chinese fashion forward without turning away from its roots, while refusing to let heritage define its entire identity.

Look 027 @ZOFHANG LIJIN

Milan has become a stage for Chinese designers to show more than traditional craftsmanship.Their collections demonstrate how heritage techniques can be reworked, reshaped and woven into contemporary fashion while remaining connected to their origins.

World.title: Russia dismisses transparency calls amid reports of second Siberia plague case
World.content:
Russia dismissed calls for transparency over the death of a laboratory technician from plague in Siberia on Wednesday, as reports emerged of a second case of infection.

 

Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, said it saw "no epidemic risk" following the death of a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, identified as Darya Shipilova, who died last week in the town of Shelekhov near Irkutsk.

The agency said Shipilova had been "vaccinated and had immunity to the dangerous infections she was working with," and that nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no dangerous pathogens.

More than 90% of those who had contact with her had completed medical monitoring, it said.

The Kremlin dismissed reports of a second suspected plague case in Siberia, telling journalists that most media reporting on the situation was "false".

"The media are reporting a great deal right now, and the overwhelming majority of what the media are reporting around this situation is false information," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, urging citizens to rely solely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements.

Russian authorities have maintained since the start of the week that Shipilova died of pneumonia and that her cause of death remains "undetermined".

International concern persists

US President Donald Trump had a call with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin scheduled for Wednesday to address the plague incident, and his administration sent Moscow a demarche requesting additional information.

"We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government. We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," a US State Department spokesperson said on Wednesday.

Peskov said he had no information that the Kremlin had received any US official complaint.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus on Wednesday called on Moscow to clarify the situation over media reports of a second staff member with pneumonia of unclear origin.

"Timely, complete and transparent information-sharing in line with the International Health Regulations is critical," Tedros said.

The WHO said the day before that the possible case posed a "very low" risk beyond Russia's borders, citing the country's reduced contact with the rest of the world due to its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine and resulting sanctions.

It noted that the institute studied "dangerous pathogens" and that plague occurs naturally among wild animals in the Irkutsk region.

People walk past the building of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Irkutsk, Russia, on Wednesday 7 October 2026 AP Photo//Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Pneumonic plague, the most dangerous form of the disease, affects the lungs and can spread person to person through airborne droplets, with an incubation period as short as 24 hours.

It can be fatal without appropriate care, but the chances of recovery are high if identified and treated promptly. Symptoms include shortness of breath, coughing and blood-streaked sputum.

The more common bubonic plague is caused by the bite of an infected flea and can produce purulent ulcers.

If verified, the Siberia case would be Russia's first confirmed plague infection since 2016.

World.title: Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after botched execution
World.content:
Pike's lawyers have said she was very aware of Tennessee's failed execution effort. A judge has ordered state officials to preserve all evidence from the botched execution.

A US judge told the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed attempt to execute Christa Pike, whom lawyers say is "angry and confused" after waking up in hospital nearly a week after the ordeal.

Pike, who was sentenced to death for torturing and killing classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, survived despite being given two lethal doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug.

What do we know about Christa Pike's current state?

One of her attorneys spoke about the 50-year-old's state after the failed execution.

"She is angry and confused about everything right now," Randy Spivey said during a news conference, adding Pike is "very aware" of what was done to her.

"She cannot move either of her arms, both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what, if any, function she will regain in her arms," Spivey said, adding that "there's a long road ahead" for her recovery.

Pike is the only person known to have survived after receiving lethal injection drugs, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Luke Ihnen, another lawyer for Pike, said that "medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request."

Her lawyers continue to demand that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee commute Pike's sentence to life in prison and never reattempt her execution. The Republican governor had denied a clemency appeal two days before the failed execution.

Demonstrations were held against Christa Pike's execution Image: George Walker IV/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Pike's recovery period unclear

Experts say it is possible that the failed execution was due to a problem with the IV line that caused the injection to pool in her tissue rather than enter her bloodstream.

"Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown," her attorneys wrote in their court filing.

Pike's arms were burned and blistered due to the injection, according to her legal team, who are demanding that the prison authority holds all information from the attempted execution, including needles and execution logs.

It is not yet clear how Pike's recovery might unfold and whether she will be subjected to another execution attempt.

World.title: As US midterm elections loom, Trump's campaign tactics are becoming increasingly unusual, and expensive
World.content:
Despite not being on the ballot, Trump is campaigning hard ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. His tactics and promises have mostly been at the expense of US taypayers. Experts say some might violate federal law.

It's neither a joke nor fake news but a real report from earlier this week: Donald Trump has backed down. On Monday, the US president announced that a series of s aired in September promoting him and his administration would no longer be funded with taxpayer money.

"The radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our great USA, and paying for them with USA money," Trump wrote on his platform Truth Social.

He went on to claim that funding partisan ads with public money was a "rather standard thing to do," before adding that future ads would be paid with money raised from donations.

The ads themselves have caused some controversy in the United States. They ran in September between popular shows such as Saturday Night Live and football games, marked with the line: "paid for by the US government" — that is, paid with tax dollars.

The commercials showed scenes such as when US troops captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year but they mostly consisted of images and videos of Trump himself, along with combative messages that he would "expel the warmongers" or "throw off the sick political class," and ensure that the US did not become a communist state.

Why Europe's far right is turning away from Trump To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Public funds for personal praise

Political opponents and a series of NGOs responded to the campaign with sharp criticism. Not only does US law prohibit the use of taypayer funds for political s, but the ads also appeared shortly before the midterms — elections held near the midpoint of a president's four-year term.

On Tuesday, the US broadcasting network CBS reported that, according to contracting records, the US Department of Homeland Security had paid an agency $20 million (€17.9 million) for a "national media campaign."

The "rather standard" practice that Trump referred to actually applies to public service announcements, but this is not what the campaign ads are, argued the US non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

"Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising," the organization wrote in a public complaint to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ."Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump's recent campaign ads."

Independent experts have also voiced concerns. Patrick Malone, a professor in the department of Public Administration and Policy at American University in Washington DC, said the timing of the videos was problematic.

"You're not supposed to use taxpayer dollars to pay for anything that's campaign-related," he told DW. "Technically, [Trump] is not campaigning. He's not saying 'Vote for me!' The thing that's created the challenge here is the timing. Weeks before the midterms, this is a real big issue."

US Iran attack launched without US Congress, UN approval To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Will the Republicans keep their majority after midterms?

Voters do not choose presidents in the midterm elections but members of Congres, which comprises the Senate and the House of Representatives and is the legislative branch of the federal government. On November 3, those eligible to vote will cast their ballots for all the seats in the House of Representatives, and roughly a third of the seats in the Senate. Some states will also be choosing governors.

Republicans have not been faring well in recent polls, which may be why Trump has been trying to promote his party's achievements. The Republicans currently hold a majority in both houses, with 53 of 100 seats in the Senate, and 219 of 435 seats in the House of Representatives. This has enabled Trump to pass a large number of his proposals fairly easily.

But a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday indicates that this could soon change. "Voters age 50 or older preferred Trump's party over the Democratic Party by just 2 percentage points — 44% to 42% — compared to an 8-point Republican advantage in December," it found. This age bracket "is particularly important for midterm elections, when older Americans historically have made up large shares of the electorate."

Meanwhile, among voters under the age of 50, "Democrats led by 18 points," the survey showed.

The poll also found that opinions on Trump himself were low, with "32% of Americans giving a thumbs up to Trump's presidency." This level of approval, the study highlighted, was unchanged from an earlier poll "that saw the leader's rating at the lowest of his political career."

Republicans shy away from Trump's support

This could also be one of the reasons why Republican candidates do not seem so keen on making public appearances with the president, usually a highlight of a campaign trail.

Many US citizens associate Trump with high living costs, or the war with Iran, which has dragged on for over half a year now.

One Republican operative told the news website Politico on condition of anonymity that if the the president were to visit a battleground state — where Democratic and Republican support is fairly equal among voters — to campaign for his party, they suspected their "candidates would come down with COVID" to avoid having to attend.

In September, a number of Republicans skipped Trump's big party convention — typically reserved for presidential, not midterm elections — even though the event could have offered them a platform for their campaign.

Susan Collins from Maine and Dan Sullivan from Alaska, are just two examples of Republican senators whose seats are on the line and who did not attend. Neither did candidates for the House of Representatives from the swing states Arizona, Iowa and Michigan.

Trump offers Americans $5,000 for midterm victory To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump promises $5,000 payout if Republicans win

Those who skipped the event missed the president repeating an unusual campaign message: To encourage more people to vote, Trump urged supporters to "pretend" he was on the ballot.

And if that wasn't enough, he also promised each US citizen eligible to vote a $5,000 payout if Republicans maintained their majority in both houses of Congress.

Keeping that pledge could cost the federal government over $1.2 trillion, but observers doubt it would ever come to that.

"He has no money to do that with. It would have to be authorized and appropriated by Congress," Mallone explained. "I think the likelihood is very slim," he added. "It's one of those things like 'Mexico is going to pay for the wall.'"

Whether Trump's commercials or promised payouts will be enough to rally majority Republican support remains to be seen.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Evicted Spanish pensioner who sparked housing protests has died, Madrid tenant union says
World.content:
Maricarmen ⁠Abascal, the octogenarian woman whose eviction set off housing protests across Spain, has died, a tenants' union in Madrid has said. Unions are now calling for a nationwide general strike on November 11.

Maricarmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman at the center of the nationwide protests in Spain due to her eviction from her Madrid home, has died, the local tenants' union said.

"We are sorry to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding that Abascal's cause marked "a turning point in the history of this country."

Who is Abascal and how did she spark Spain's protests?

Abascal was evicted from the home where she lived her whole life on a stretcher after the company owning the apartment drastically increased the rent.

She had been hospitalized after the eviction took place due to exhaustion as an agreement with her home's owners was reached.

The Madrid Tenants' Union said the solution came "too late," labeling the ordeal "totally avoidable" and "torturous" for the 87-year-old.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez sent his condolences to Abascal's family after learning of her death.

"I send hugs to all of those who mourn this loss as if it was their own," Sanchez posted on his X account.

Voicing his sadness over Abascal's death, Spanish Minister for Territorial Policy Angel Victor Torres said she symbolized the plight of many people struggling with the country's housing crisis.

Spain's unions call for general strike

Spain's trade unions called on Wednesday for a nationwide general strike on November 11 over housing issues.

The UGT and CCOO unions urged the population to "mobilize for better salaries, for decent housing and for price controls in the face of inflation that undermines our purchasing power."

The strike "is the response to the insatiable real estate greed that speculates with one of the public's main rights, making access to a decent home practically impossible,", they said in a statement.

Housing crisis triggers snap election in Spain To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The nationwide protests triggered by Abascal's eviction and lawmakers' rejection of housing reforms intended to help tenants led Sanchez to call for early elections on November 29.

Sanchez, of the Socialist Party, is looking for a shift in the public narrative after his government's handling of the migrant crisis in Ceuta, as well as alleged corruption among his party's ranks.

World.title: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey: Could the Mecca defense pact become a game changer in the war against the Houthis in Yemen?
World.content:
Pakistan and Turkey have agreed to provide "practical measures" to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. Could a new alliance reshape the war against the Houthis in Yemen?

The latest iteration of Saudi Arabia's defense deal with Turkey and Pakistan, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, is taking shape amid the country's escalating conflict with Yemen's Houthi militia.

According to the trilateral defense commitment , which was signed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on August 7, 2026, an armed attack on any one of the three states involved should be regarded as an attack on them all.

Yet, despite ongoing Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Saudi attacks on Houthi militants in Yemen, neither Pakistan nor Turkey had joined Saudi Arabia's combat operations since the deal was signed, arguing that the command and operational structures were still being developed.

But since Monday, the situation has changed after an emergency meeting between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey's defense and foreign ministers and senior military chiefs in the Saudi capital Riyadh. According to a joint statement, Turkey and Pakistan decided to implement the collective defense commitments in practical terms immediately. This means providing military forces and capabilities and ensuring their rapid deployment in Saudi Arabia. The appointment of a retired Pakistani lieutenant general, Nauman Mahmood, as the alliance's first secretary-general was also announced. He will serve a three-year term.



"Ankara and Islamabad undoubtedly will seek to strengthen the Saudi kingdom's posture vis-a-vis the Houthi threat and demonstrate that the Mecca agreement can pass its first real test and show up as a game-changing alliance," Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East security at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, told DW.

"However, what the activation of the Mecca pact means operationally, including the specific capabilities deployed and the scope of their missions, has not been made public," she said, adding that this was "not unusual for such a military operation amid myriad sensitivities."

According to the 2026 Global Firepower military strength ranking, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey between them have about 1.4 million active personnel, some 3,400 military aircraft, 6,000 tanks and more than 340 naval assets.

On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia intercepted another ballistic missile north of Riyadh. Earlier this week, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces had launched a large-scale offensive, to recapture territory along the Red Sea coast around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the city of Mokha. Saudi Arabia launched airstrikes to support the offensive.

The ministers of the three signatory countries to the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement met in Riyadh on Oct. 5, 2026 Image: Mustafa Hatipoglu/Anadolu/picture alliance

Turkey considers a solution through dialogue

The scope of a potential Turkish military deployment remains unclear. Turkey is a NATO member, which means that any military involvement on its part could carry broader implications for the entire military alliance.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan noted after the meeting in Riyadh on Monday that there were not only military options on the table. "We also discussed what could be done to resolve the problem peacefully and through dialogue,"

Turkey's involvement in the Mecca defense deal has been criticized by opposition parties in the country. Under Turkey's constitution, international agreements generally require approval by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey but this has not yet been granted.

"How can the so-called Mecca agreement on joint defense be valid and implemented without having been submitted to the Turkish parliament for approval?" Namik Tan, an Istanbul lawmaker from the social democratic Yeni Parti and a former Turkish ambassador to Israel and the United States, asked in a statement.

Yani Bagcioglu, a retired Turkish admiral, also warned that "the risk of Turkish forces and commercial vessels linked to Turkey becoming targets of Houthi attacks should not be overlooked."

Pakistan's tightrope walk amid the Iran war

The third signatory, Pakistan, is walking its own particular tightrope. On Monday, Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif told Pakistani television channel Geo News that Pakistan and Turkey were playing a "supportive role," with their forces involved in "reconnaissance and other things," while Saudi forces were engaged in combat.



"Pakistan's contribution to the defense of Saudi Arabia is nothing new," Imtiaz Gul, an independent Pakistani security analyst, told DW. "The arrangement has existed for six decades," he said, adding that "defense against the Houthis nevertheless represents a different kind of challenge because the group is considered an Iranian extension and by implication, Iran would consider this an attack on its regional interests."

A direct engagement in Yemen at Saudi Arabia's side would, therefore, risk not only ending Pakistan's apparent neutral status as a mediator in the US-Iran war, but also strain relations with Tehran, he said. He pointed out that Saudi Arabia was a close ally of the US, while the Houthis are backed by Iran.

Houthi attacks on infrastructure, the East-West oil pipeline and the Saudi capital Riyadh have put pressure on Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to react Image: European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-3/REUTERS

Hisham Al-Omeisy, a Yemeni conflict analyst in Washington, told DW that "for years, a cornerstone of the Houthi narrative and rallying cry has been a fight against perceived external enemies." Accordingly, he added, foreign boots on the ground in Yemen would "not only backfire, it would solidify the Houthi local coalitions and fuel their recruitment drives."

World.title: Russia: WHO not able to 'fully' assess plague situation
World.content:
The UN health agency said Russia should be more transparent about the case of the plague as reports of a second case of the disease emerged. Russia played down any concerns, saying the population faces no risk.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said it could not fully assess the situation of the suspected plague death of a laboratory employee in Russia.

"We don't yet have the full picture of this event and we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov played down the reports as "false information," insisting only Russian authorities' official statements should be relied on.

What has Trump said about the suspected plague situation?

Peskov also said he had no information regarding a planned call between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation, despite Trump announcing such a call was scheduled.

Trump said the death of the technician did not appear to be linked to a biological weapon.

"We're going to find out soon, but we don't think so," Trump told reporters, adding that Russia claimed the incident was under control.

The US did make a formal request for more information on the matter from Russia, the AFP news agency reported.

Second suspected case reported

This comes after a 28-year-old female technician employed at a plague research institute in the Irkutsk region of Siberia died of the disease, possibly contracting it from a broken test tube.

According to the WHO head, Russia should clarify reports of a "second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause" at the institute.

While the United States, the European Union and the WHO have all called on Moscow to be transparent about the case, Russian authorities insist the population in the region is safe.

WHO head Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for more transparency from Russia Image: World Health Organization/AP Photo/picture alliance

"There are no epidemic risks for the population," the country's health agency said, adding its investigations had resulted in "no emergencies" and emphasizing the plague research institute's compliance.

"More than 90% of contacts have completed medical observation," the agency added. "The results of almost 5,000 laboratory tests did not reveal any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms."

In response to the reports, Mongolia said it implemented "health surveillance and monitoring measures" at the border between the two countries.

Pneumonic plague is a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs which can pass from person to person through the air, for example, via coughing.

World.title: Gerhard Schröder visits latest Russian employer, Hyperglobus
World.content:
Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schröder visited a Moscow supermarket in his new role on the supervisory board. Schröder is no stranger to retirement stipends in Russia — or the scandal that accompanies them.

Gerhard Schröder visited one of the Moscow branches of the new Hyperglobus supermarket chain on Wednesday, a few days after being named a member of its supervisory board.

Russian TV footage showed employees at the branch greeting the former German chancellor and his current wife, So-yeon Schröder-Kim, with sustained applause.

Schröder has current or recent links to a series of Russian businesses and to President Vladimir Putin, issues that have become increasingly contentious in Germany in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Schröder was German chancellor when Vladimir Putin first became Russian president; the pair have remained close since he left office, despite all that followed Image: Alexei Druzhinin/dpa/picture alliance

What is Hyperglobus' link to Germany?

The new Russian supermarket chain Hyperglobus was spun off from Germany's Globus Holding last year.

Last week, Hyperglobus announced that Schröder had been appointed to the supervisory board. The supermarket confirmed that the former chancellor and Social Democrat had visited a branch on the western outskirts of Moscow on Wednesday.

"I'm very pleased to be here, to see this wonderful hypermarket, to see the results of your work and to meet you, my wonderful colleagues," RBC television in Russia quoted Schröder as saying.

Schröder and his current wife, So-yeon Schröder-Kim, were greeted with sustained applause, Russian TV reported Image: RBC/Handout/REUTERS

Schröder also reportedly called last week for the continuation of remaining trade ties between Russia and countries like Germany amid the sanctions imposed since the start of the war in Ukraine.

"It is exactly in these crisis times that these ties are especially important: they allow us to hear each other and look for ways forward," newspaper RBK reported him as saying last Friday.

What's the deal with Schröder, Putin, Russia and Ukraine?

Schröder's close ties to Putin came under scrutiny even while he was still in office, notably in 2004 when Schröder responded to a question from a reporter by saying that, yes, he believed Putin was a "flawless democrat" or lupenreiner Demokrat.

Even 22 years ago, this assertion strained credulity in many eyes — not least among opposition groups or in war-torn Chechnya.

On leaving politics, Schröder kept close ties to the Kremlin and took up a series of senior roles, perhaps most famously on the board of the Rosneft energy giant and before that on the board of the Nord Stream gas pipeline project that was majority owned by Gazprom.

Putin has often said Schröder could negotiate a peace deal with Ukraine. Schröder, in turn, has declared himself willing. Image: Vladimir Rodionov/Ria Novosti/Kremlin Pool/dpa/picture alliance

In 2014, not long after the annexation of Crimea and as a Russian-backed civil war brewed in Ukraine, Schröder was Nord Stream's guest of honor in St. Petersburg, where he celebrated his 70th birthday in lavish style.

Four years later, after an election many in the West decried as bordering on a sham, Schröder took a prominent place at the 2018 swearing-in ceremony for Putin's fourth presidential term at the Kremlin (pictured above).

Now-deceased Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny once said Schröder was Putin's "errand boy."

In 2024, Schröder was stripped of a state-funded office and staff — typically provided to former chancellors — on the basis that he was no longer fulfilling any obligations tied to his previous role in government.

His party, the center-left Social Democrats, tried on several occasions to eject him as a member. Each attempt failed to clear the high legal bars required, and he remains a member, having joined in 1963.

Putin has often suggested him as a possible peace mediator between Russia, Ukraine and Europe — with Schröder also expressing a willingness to take on the role — even though the reality is he would likely be entirely unacceptable as a mediator to all parties other than Russia, and particularly to Ukraine.

World.title: German politicians warn of antisemitism on October 7 anniversary
World.content:
High-ranking German politicians marked the anniversary of the terrorist attacks that took place in Israel on October 7, 2023.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke about doing more to fight antisemitism within Germany, while also pressing for a two-state solution between Israelis and Palestinians.

"We are witnessing rising antisemitism in Germany — antisemitism that far too often goes unchallenged," Merz said, adding that his government "will do everything" to combat it.

"Jewish people must be able to live without fear throughout Germany," Merz said in a statement, also emphasizing Germany's support for Israel. "Our Israeli friends can count on our commitment to ensuring that such a crime never happens again."

'Political action' needed

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said antisemitism in Germany "flared up in an intolerable manner since October 7."

"Germany must continue to stand up against antisemitism and for Israel’s security, for the dignity and self-determination of the Palestinians, and for the prospect of peaceful coexistence in the Middle East," he said in a statement.

Federal Parliamentary Speaker Julia Klöckner commemorated the day by emphasizing that more needs to be done to combat antisemitism through "political action."

"Antisemitism should not be allowed to have a place on our streets or our political debates," she said.

Germany Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Israel in December 2025 Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

Germany stands with Israel

Some 1,200 people were killed in the attack, carried out by Palestinian militant group Hamas and its affiliates, while 251 people were kidnapped to Gaza, in the deadliest attack on Jews since the end of the Holocaust.

More than 74,000 people have been killed in the Gaza Strip in Israel's war following the attack, with some countries and human rights groups saying Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians.

Demonstrations were held across Germany for victims of both the Hamas attacks and the Israeli war that followed.

In Berlin, a crowd of around 1,700 people, many waving Israeli flags, gathered at Bebelplatz, according to police estimates. Israeli Ambassador Ron Prosor and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt also attended. Bebelplatz was the site of Nazi book burnings following the party's seizure of power in 1933.

Dobrindt called antisemitism a "poison" that threatened to infect parts of society, adding, "We must clearly and consistently stand against it every day."

Germany has supported Israel throughout the war, although Merz did halt of delivery of some military equipment to Israel following growing legal concerns over the war in Gaza, including arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.

Although Germany is a party to the treaty that created the ICC, Merz vowed not to arrest Netanyahu should he travel to Germany.

World.title: Transgressive, edgy DIY: What the 90s meant for British art
World.content:
The 1990s are remembered for Britpop and provocative fashion, but beyond the nostalgia, it was a decade of cultural experimentation and social change. Tate Britain's new exhibition looks past the familiar icons.

The 1990s in Britain are often remembered through a haze of nostalgia consisting of rave culture, Britpop and provocative art and fashion by the likes of Tracey Emin and Alexander McQueen.

Undeniably, the decade was a time of major change in British society — the long reign of Margaret Thatcher had come to an end and the West entered a period of relative post-Cold War stability.

Meanwhile, British cultural icons like Oasis, the Spice Girls and Vivienne Westwood garnered international fame.

But Tate Britain's new exhibition "The 90s: Art and Fashion," which opens on October 8 and runs through February 14, 2027, urges viewers to look beyond the familiar names and images.

Even though now prominent artists such as Damien Hirst and Juergen Teller are among the show's 70 contributors, the exhibition also aims to highlight the creative input of those in communities which were left out of the mainstream discourse.

After all, says chief curator Edward Enninful in the exhibition's program, "the energy of the 90s was not concentrated in a single movement, but distributed across communities, disciplines and geographies that have not always been equally represented."

Fashion editor and style icon Edward Enninful curated the exhibition Image: Adama Jalloh

An inclusive perspective

For Enninful, the exhibition is personal: The Ghanaian-born British fashion editor, stylist and creative director became the youngest-ever fashion director of i-D Magazine in the 90s at age 18, helping shape the diverse and experimental London fashion scene of the 1990s. He later became editor-in-chief of British Vogue in 2017.



Enninful writes that he and his co-curators aimed to present a body of work which "reflects a broader landscape of practices and voices that shaped the period, many of which operated beyond the structures of visibility at the time." The exhibition pays special attention to artists of color and women whose work was not necessarily showcased as prominently at the time.

Black masculinity became "a site of cultural negotiation" in Britain in the 90s, writes co-curator Helen Little in the program text: "Figures such as Chris Ofili, Steve McQueen, Keith Piper, Koto Bolofo and Ozwald Boateng reimagined the Black masculine, challenging the racist specter of Black men, who had been defined as part of a masculinity crisis linked to post-industrial decline and excluded from the narrative of 'Cool Britannia.'"

Just like "Swinging London" in the 1960s, "Cool Britannia" became a widespread phrase to refer to the 1990s as an era during which British youth culture, pop music, art and political optimism boomed.

British-Ghanaian/Dominican photographer Eileen Perrier featured women of color who were rarely celebrated at the time Image: Eileen Perrier/DACS

DIY meets Dr. Martens

The 90s also offered artists plenty of chances to create without waiting for support from traditional gatekeepers. Britain entered the decade in recession, but that economic uncertainty also left artists free to do what they wished.

Empty buildings and industrial spaces were turned into informal venues. A 23-year-old Damien Hirst orchestrated "Freeze," a self-organized student exhibition in 1988 in a disused London warehouse. It became a landmark early art exhibition for the generation of artists known as the "Young British Artists" or YBA.

Artists Sarah Lucas and Tracey Emin opened The Shop, a temporary art gallery and social space in 1992, as a place where exhibitions could develop outside established galleries. Lucas and Emin also paved the way for women artists thanks to their deeply personal works and their edgy expressions of female liberation.



While the Spice Girls helped make feminism accessible to a younger generation of Brits in the 90s by popularizing the "girl power" slogan and shaping "identity through agency power and resistance," as Tate curator Helen Little argues, Emin and Lucas meanwhile "presented a new visual language of clothing as art to tackle societal taboos around female sexuality, vulnerability and desire" — from t-shirts with provocative slogans to a grunge look of scuffed Dr. Martens boots with razor blades. Their work "held a mirror up to gender, behavior and identity," Little writes.

Sarah Lucas broke away from feminine ideals in raw works such as this 1997 photo titled 'Chicken Knickers' Image: Sarah Lucas/Sadie Coles HQ

Fashion and haute couture in the spotlight

At the same time, the British fashion industry came into the international spotlight.

In a feminine sensuality counter to the gender stereotypes dismissed by Emin and Lucas, waif-like Kate Moss came to represent the feminine ideal of the 1990s. Dubbed "heroin-chic," the style was an antithesis to the glamorous, athletic physiques of the supermodels who preceded her. Corinne Day's photographs of the model led to the raw aesthetic to be labelled "grunge" after the anguished style of rock music hailing from Seattle and led by Nirvana.

The trend has undergone significant cultural reexamination since then: "Along with the look also came criticism that the strung-out look of drug or alcohol addiction was glamorized while encouraging serious eating disorders in a generation of young women," points out Alex Farquharson, director of the Tate Gallery in his foreword to the exhibition.

The new Tate Britain exhibition includes photos of 90s icon Kate Moss Image: Juergen Teller

The 1990s were also an exciting era for Britain in haute couture, as legendary designers John Galliano led Dior, while Alexander McQueen started directing Givenchy at the age of 27.

McQueen's runway presentations were more akin to performance art than commercial fashion shows — and they often included historical critiques. Among them was the famous finale of his Fall/Winter 1998 collection at a London warehouse, during which the model stood in a circle of flames. Titled "Joan," the show was a reference to the killing of Joan of Arc.



McQueen designed several other runway shows that reflected on British history, with topics of conquest and punishment repeatedly coming to the forefront. His 1995 presentation "Highland Rape" referenced the history of Scotland's subjugation, with the designer describing it as "England's rape of Scotland."

McQueen's fashion shows were more like performance art and included historical critiques of Britain Image: Guy Marineau/Vogue/Condé Nast

As co-curator Jessica Vaughan points out in her exhibition text: "Art, fashion and photography were not simply transgressive reactions … but reflected a genuine public unease with Britain's global identity and its past."



In a world that can now feel increasingly mediated by screens, algorithms and established platforms, the artwork of the 90s offers a reminder of the value of physical spaces and fresh DIY creativity of the last smartphone-free decade.

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

World.title: Muere Maricarmen, la mujer que encendió la lucha contra los desahucios en España
World.content:
El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

La mujer de 87 años ha fallecido este miércoles en el Hospital Gregorio Marañón de Madrid, según ha confirmado el Sindicato de Inquilinas en un comunicado

Maricarmen Abascal, la mujer que encendió la lucha contra los desahucios en España, ha fallecido este miércoles en el Hospital Gregorio Marañón a los 87 años, según ha confirmado el Sindicato de Inquilinas en un comunicado. El 23 de septiembre fue desahuciada de su casa de Retiro, en la que vivió durante siete décadas. Seis años antes, una empresa compró su piso por un precio irrisorio para la zona precisamente porque ella vivía en él. Con una pensión de 1.400 euros, la mujer nunca dejó de pagar el alquiler, de renta antigua, y las facturas: unos 500 euros al mes en total. En 2020 los propietarios le dijeron que debía dejar el apartamento, porque el contrato ya había sido subrogado dos veces, primero a su madre ―que no constaba como inquilina, por una ley franquista― y luego a ella. Y desde entonces la intentaron desalojar cuatro veces y no aceptaron ninguna de las propuestas que recibieron para o bien pagar la diferencia del alquiler (le pedían 1.600 euros) o comprar el apartamento.

En ese comunicado, firmado también por su familia y su abogada, recuerdan que permanecía hospitalizada desde el desahucio. “Si bien se consiguió un acuerdo histórico que le habría permitido volver a su vivienda, esta solución ha llegado demasiado tarde”, lamentan. Los firmantes consideran que lo ocurrido tras su desalojo ―manifestaciones multitudinarias, acampadas en las plazas, adelanto electoral y convocatoria de una huelga general― supone “un antes y un después en la historia de este país”, pero advierten de que “el coste para llegar hasta aquí ha sido demasiado alto”. Y se despiden con la petición que ella les repetía: “Luchad, seguid luchando por lo que es vuestro”.

Pablo Monge Maricarmen posa en su vivienda de la calle Alcalde Sainz de Baranda, el 22 de octubre de 2025. SAMUEL SÁNCHEZ Maricarmen, en octubre de 2025 en la celebración de la paralización de su tercer intento de desahucio. SAMUEL SÁNCHEZ Maricarmen, tras la paralización de su tercer intento de desahucio en 2025. SAMUEL SÁNCHEZ Maricarmen participa en la protesta contra su desahucio cerca de su casa el 2 de junio. JUAN BARBOSA Pasacalles convocado por el Sindicato de Inquilinas para denunciar su desahucio, el 2 de junio. JUAN BARBOSA La mujer de 87 años, en su piso del barrio de Ibiza (Madrid), antes de ser desahuciada, el 21 septiembre.
