The ECtHR found Georgia’s 2021 extradition of Aslan Sumbaev, who faced serious criminal charges in Russia, lawful only after Russia provided official diplomatic assurances that it would prevent torture and ensure proper detention conditions.

“Please also specify what individual guarantees and subsequent monitoring mechanisms were applied in relation to the extraditions that have already taken place,” the Social Justice Center wrote.

World.title: Georgia without an opposition? How ruling party moved to ban its opponents through constitutional lawsuit
World.content:
The ruling party Georgian Dream has asked Georgia’s Constitutional Court to ban five opposition parties. Four of them crossed the five per cent threshold in the 2024 parliamentary elections. According to official figures from the Central Election Commission, election stability risks, a total of 784,820 voters — 37.79% of those who took part in the election — voted for the four parties.

What legal grounds does the government cite for seeking to ban the five parties? What does the term “collective United National Movement” mean? How has the list of parties facing a ban changed, and under what conditions does European law allow such a ban? JAMnews examined the Georgian Dream lawsuit, relevant legislation and European practice to answer these questions.

Georgian Dream registered its latest lawsuit with the Constitutional Court on 24 September 2026, under case No. 1979.

The list of parties facing a ban includes Unity — National Movement, Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia — Lelo, Gakharia for Georgia and Federalists.

As of 5 October 2026, the court has not yet published a decision on whether it will accept the lawsuit for consideration on the merits, and it has not yet set a hearing date.

The First Chamber is hearing the case, with Vasil Roinishvili serving as the reporting judge. Under the law, the court must issue its final decision within nine months of the filing — no later than 24 June 2027.

If the court upholds the lawsuit, all opposition forces that crossed the electoral threshold in the last parliamentary elections could disappear from the country’s political system.

Under current legislation, the authorities can also ask the court to ban another political organisation that acts as a “successor” to an already banned party.

An election campaign promise

Bidzina Ivanishvili at a Georgian Dream rally, April 2024.

The idea of banning opposition parties did not emerge spontaneously within Georgian Dream. Its founder and honorary chairman, Bidzina Ivanishvili, publicly stated even before the 2024 parliamentary elections that, after the vote, the government would deliver a “strict political and legal verdict” to the “collective National Movement”.

In other words, the idea of banning the opposition did not emerge after the election. It formed part of the election campaign itself.

“After the election, we will have the opportunity to deliver a strict political and legal verdict to the collective National Movement.”

Ivanishvili also explained why, in his view, this did not happen in 2012. He said the government did not yet have sufficient resources at the time:

“Over these years, we have accumulated enough resources to begin fully strengthening our sovereignty…”

A statement made almost six months before the election gradually turned into a concrete political plan. In August 2024, Georgian Dream openly announced that it needed a constitutional majority in the election to declare the “collective National Movement” illegal. The European Commission included the plan in its report that year.

Then EU High Representative Josep Borrell, speaking in the European Parliament, described the promise to ban opposition parties as one of the worrying developments during Georgia’s election campaign.

Two years later, that campaign promise has turned into a concrete lawsuit filed with the Constitutional Court.

Three lawsuits, three lists — how the number of parties facing a ban grew

The lawsuit changed three times over the course of one year.

The Constitutional Court registered the first lawsuit on 31 October 2025, under case No. 1912. Eighty-eight members of parliament signed it. They sought to ban three political forces:

Unity — National Movement

Coalition for Change

Strong Georgia — Lelo

Later, on 21 April 2026, 89 MPs filed a second lawsuit, No. 1958. They added a fourth party, Federalists, to the list.

The list of parties facing a ban grew again in September 2026.

On 24 September, the Constitutional Court registered lawsuit No. 1979, signed by 88 MPs. This time, the authorities are seeking to ban five parties, including former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia’s party, For Georgia.

The law gives the Constitutional Court a maximum of nine months to rule on such a case. Each new lawsuit has therefore sparked debate over whether that period starts again from the beginning.

The authors of the lawsuit hope the Constitutional Court will complete the process by January 2027, by which time all five parties would have been banned.

Opposition representatives, meanwhile, argue that Georgian Dream is actually prolonging the process by adding new parties.

On what grounds can a party be banned?

Georgia’s Constitution sets out specific grounds for banning a political party.

It prohibits parties whose goals include overthrowing or forcibly changing the constitutional order, undermining the country’s independence or violating its territorial integrity. The authorities can also ban parties that promote war or violence or incite national, ethnic, regional, religious or social hatred.

Only the Constitutional Court can ban a political party.

The Georgian Dream lawsuit relies on these constitutional grounds and argues that the listed parties’ activities target the state.

A significant part of the argument draws on the findings of a temporary parliamentary investigative commission, known as the Tsulukiani Commission.

One of the lawsuit’s key arguments concerns the opposition parties’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the 2024 election, parliament and the government.

The plaintiffs also link the opposition parties’ actions to “sabotage”, calls for Western sanctions against the Georgian authorities and attempts to “punish” the country.

The lawsuit, for example, treats the opposition’s refusal to recognise the election results and its view that Georgian Dream is an illegitimate government as “sabotage”.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also cited the legitimacy of the government when explaining why the authorities added Gakharia’s party to the list.

He said that although the party, unlike its “fellow opposition parties”, agreed to take part in parliamentary work, it still does not recognise the constitutional order or the legitimacy of the government:

“It is true that they entered parliament, but to this day they do not recognise the constitutional order or the legitimacy of the government. Under these circumstances, the spirit of this political party’s activities is no different from that of the other relevant political parties,” he said.

Why these parties?

The lawsuit explicitly cites the parties’ political influence as a reason for seeking their ban. It also mentions other opposition parties, such as the Republican Party, which does not appear on the list, and says:

“At present, they do not have significant influence on politics or a realistic prospect of crossing the electoral threshold. Accordingly, at this stage, there is no apparent need to ban them.”

A brief overview of the five parties facing a ban: Политические силы, объединенные “Грузинской мечтой” в единый “черный список”, имеют разное происхождение, историю и идеологию. Некоторые из них действительно произошли из политической семьи «Единого национального движения». Некоторые пытались занять независимое пространство именно между ЕНД и «Грузинской мечтой». Политическое же ядро партии Гиорги Гахария и вовсе вышло из самой «Грузинской мечты». «Единство — Национальное движение» «Единое национальное движение» экс-президента Михеила Саакашвили — самая старая партия в этой пятерке и единственная, имеющая опыт пребывания у власти: в течение 9 лет она являлась правящей партией Грузии. На выборах 2024 года ЕНД официально получила 211 216 голосов — 10,17%. Уже долгие годы партия переживает кризис лидерства и на данный момент находится в режиме переходного управления. В августе 2026 года был создан временный управляющий совет, руководителем которого стал Иракли Павленишвили. Избрание постоянного председателя партии должно состояться позже. Главным лицом, принимающим решения в партии, по-прежнему остается Михеил Саакашвили, который уже пять лет находится в тюрьме. ЕНД позиционирует себя как резко проевропейская и евроатлантическая политическая сила. Её историческое ядро — это политическое наследие правительства Саакашвили. Именно правление ЕНД в 2004-2012 годах является главной мишенью большей части иска «Грузинской мечты» и обвинений комиссии Цулукиани. Coalition for Change Coalition for Change was created ahead of the 2024 elections and brought together several different political forces. The coalition included Nika Melia and Nika Gvaramia’s Akhali party, Zurab Japaridze’s Girchi — More Freedom and Elene Khoshtaria’s Droa. Akhali is a pro-European centre-right liberal party. Girchi — More Freedom has a more distinctly right-libertarian economic platform, while Droa has a liberal and activist profile. In the 2024 election, the coalition received the largest number of official votes among the opposition forces — 229,161, or 11.03%. Most of its leaders had previously been associated with the UNM. The coalition brings together parties that broke away from the UNM or emerged independently at different times. Strong Georgia — Lelo The core of Strong Georgia is the Lelo party, which Mamuka Khazaradze and Badri Japaridze founded in 2019. Both entered politics after careers in business. A broader coalition formed around Lelo in 2024. It included Ana Dolidze’s For People, Aleko Elisashvili’s Citizens and Levan Tsutskiridze’s Freedom Square. The coalition sought to present itself as an independent alternative to both Georgian Dream and the former ruling UNM. The party has a pro-European, centrist-liberal profile. Economic development, institutional reform and Western integration have remained central themes in Lelo’s programmes. In 2024, Strong Georgia officially received 182,922 votes, or 8.81%. Gakharia for Georgia Giorgi Gakharia’s party stands out from the other four parties in the group because of its origins. Gakharia was not a member of the government under Mikheil Saakashvili. Instead, he served as economy minister, interior minister and eventually prime minister under Georgian Dream. He resigned as prime minister in February 2021 and founded his own For Georgia party in May. The party initially sought to present itself as an alternative to both Georgian Dream and the UNM. It received 7.79% in the 2021 municipal elections and 161,521 votes, or 7.78%, in the 2024 parliamentary election. Gakharia’s case shows how broadly Georgian Dream applies the concept of the “collective National Movement”: today, the category also includes a political force led by one of Georgian Dream’s former leaders. Federalists Federalists are the newest party among the five. Giga Bokeria, Tamar Chergoleishvili and their allies founded the party in August 2024 after leaving European Georgia. Giga Bokeria chairs the party, while Tamar Chergoleishvili heads its Tbilisi organisation. The party identifies individual freedom, human rights, European development, free competition, decentralisation and strong democratic institutions as its core principles. Politically, it is a pro-European and liberal force with a more right-wing economic platform. Federalists did not take part in the 2024 parliamentary election. Bokeria and Chergoleishvili’s group has a long-standing political conflict with Mikheil Saakashvili and today’s UNM.

At the same time, the lawsuit notes that the question of whether these parties are unconstitutional could arise in the future if they gain significant influence over the political process.

Initially, the “Federalists” also fell into the category of parties with “no realistic prospect of crossing the electoral threshold”. However, in March 2026, they joined the “Opposition Alliance”, a nine-party coalition. In April, Georgian Dream also called for the Federalists to be banned.

Thus, according to the lawsuit, a party’s political influence is one of the factors that the plaintiffs themselves take into account when seeking to ban it.

Представители оппозиционного альянса, март 2026 года

How all opponents of the government became the “collective National Movement”

The “collective National Movement” is neither a party nor a legally recognised political organisation. It is a political term coined by Georgian Dream that it has used for years to group various opposition forces into a single political camp, thereby portraying its opponents as a common “enemy”.

Over the years, the boundaries of this category have gradually expanded. It has come to include not only the National Movement itself (UNM, the former ruling party) and parties that broke away from it, but also forces that positioned themselves as alternatives to both the UNM and Georgian Dream. These include Mamuka Khazaradze’s Lelo and Giorgi Gakharia’s party, even though Gakharia himself previously served as prime minister for Georgian Dream.

The term then expanded further. Irakli Kobakhidze included not only opposition parties but also non-governmental organisations and media outlets as part of the “collective National Movement”:

“They are all in the same pot… All the radical opposition parties, all these radical NGOs, their radical media,” Kobakhidze said.

According to Georgian Dream’s current narrative, the political differences between these forces are not significant. The ruling party portrays them as different parts of a single network controlled from abroad. This logic brings together parties with different histories, leaders and political platforms under the “collective National Movement”.

The rhetoric has gradually acquired a specific political goal. In 2024, Kobakhidze compared removing the “collective National Movement” from the political system with banning the National Socialists in post-war Germany.

A year later, he said: “This crisis within the collective ‘National Movement’ must deepen, and it will deepen, ultimately leading to the complete destruction of the collective ‘National Movement’. Only then will Georgia develop a healthy democratic system.”

What does the attempt to ban the parties mean? Views

Representatives of the opposition parties themselves see the Georgian Dream lawsuit not as a separate legal dispute but as part of a broader process of restricting political competition.

Their main argument is that the government is using the courts to remove from the political arena forces that remain its electoral competitors.

Giorgi Sioridze, a representative of the Strong Georgia — Lelo alliance, points to the fact that the list of parties facing a ban has changed several times. He says that each new lawsuit restarts the nine-month period for considering the case.

He believes this allows the government both to retain the option of banning the parties and to delay a final decision.

Giga Lemondzhava, a representative of Coalition for Change, sees the party ban as a new stage in what he describes as authoritarian politics. However, he says political struggle cannot be ended simply by cancelling a party’s legal registration.

The National Movement takes a similar position. One of its leaders, Levan Khabeishvili, called on the opposition in a letter sent from prison not to focus entirely on the parties’ legal status: “Don’t get hung up on the issue of banning parties! They have banned the country!”

His message is that accepting the legal framework created by Georgian Dream would make the opposition dependent on an agenda set by the government. Political resistance, he argues, should not depend on a party’s registration.

The case of Giorgi Gakharia’s party is particularly notable. For Georgia took part in the 2024 election, later entered parliament and does not support violent struggle against the government. Given all this, the party’s MP Giorgi Sharashidze questions how the main constitutional grounds cited in the lawsuit apply to them:

“Unconstitutionality, calls for violence, calls to overthrow the government… What does any of that have to do with us? … We even entered parliament.”

Giorgi Gakharia, meanwhile, sees his party’s addition to the “blacklist” as part of a broader process. In his view, the authorities are trying to leave no functioning critical opposition within institutional politics:

“Regardless of whether they ban us or not, we will not back down in the struggle to restore Georgia’s democracy and protect its European and Euro-Atlantic path.”

The Federalists’ case exposes another contradiction. The party did not take part in the 2024 parliamentary election. Its leaders previously belonged to former President Mikheil Saakashvili’s political team, but they have been in sharp conflict with both Saakashvili himself and the UNM, the party he founded, for many years. Despite this, the authorities also regard them as part of the “collective National Movement”.

Party leader Tamar Chergoleishvili says banning a political competitor is unacceptable to her regardless of her attitude towards that competitor:

“Of course, we see all the other parties as competitors, but we want to defeat our competitors on a level playing field, through fair competition, not as a result of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s bans.”

Georgian Dream explains the process very differently.

According to the authorities, the issue is not about eliminating political competitors but protecting the democratic system. Georgian Dream MP Levan Machavariani argues that opposition parties that appear different on the surface are actually parts of the same political network. He says dividing them into “radical”, “semi-radical” and relatively “constructive” forces is artificial and serves as a way for a common political centre to assign them different tasks.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze follows the same logic. He says the government promised voters to “neutralise foreign agents” and is now fulfilling that promise:

“We made a promise to voters that we would neutralise foreign agents in our country, and we are genuinely fulfilling that promise.”

Kobakhidze also uses this argument to explain the ban:

“It is very important that the state make a decision on this issue — a decision that serves the national interest.”

When can democracy ban a political party?

Europe has precedents for banning political parties, but authorities treat such bans as an extreme measure, usually in very different circumstances from those in Georgia. Banning five parties at once would be unprecedented.

Under the standards of the Venice Commission, authorities may justify dissolving a party if it uses violence or advocates overthrowing the democratic constitutional order. A peaceful call to change the political system or constitution does not, in itself, justify a ban.

European practice focuses not on how radical a party’s position is, but on whether its goals and actions pose a real threat to the democratic order and whether sufficient evidence supports that conclusion.

European case law also sets a high threshold. Spain banned Batasuna after authorities established its links to the ETA terrorist organisation. In Turkey, in the Refah Partisi case, the court considered evidence that the party sought to establish a theocratic system and had made statements linked to the use of force.

In Germany, meanwhile, authorities ultimately did not ban the NPD in 2017, even though the Constitutional Court found that the party’s goals were incompatible with the democratic order. However, the court concluded that the party lacked the real ability to achieve those goals.

What Europe says about Georgia’s case

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has taken a particularly strong position on Georgia.

Even before the 2024 election, a PACE monitoring delegation said Georgian Dream’s calls to ban the opposition threatened political pluralism.

In 2025, PACE described the planned ban as targeting “virtually the entire functioning democratic opposition” and said such a move would effectively create a one-party system in Georgia.

In June 2026, the Assembly made its position even clearer.

Resolution No. 2664 says the initiative to ban “virtually all democratic opposition parties” is unacceptable. It says implementing the initiative would effectively create a one-party dictatorship in Georgia, which would be incompatible with membership in the Council of Europe. The Assembly called on the authorities to withdraw the lawsuit filed with the Constitutional Court.

The European Commission’s 2025 report also describes “serious democratic backsliding” in Georgia and says legislative and institutional changes threaten political pluralism. The report also notes that the ruling party has effectively consolidated control over the legislative and executive branches of government.

What happens if the parties are banned?

Banning the five parties could have consequences far beyond cancelling their names and legal registrations. The issue is what kind of political competition will remain in Georgia ahead of the next parliamentary election in 2028.

If the Constitutional Court upholds Georgian Dream’s lawsuit, all opposition forces that crossed the five per cent threshold in 2024 could disappear from the political arena. According to official Central Election Commission figures, nearly 800,000 people voted for them in total — about a quarter of all voters.

The current legislation also allows the authorities to extend restrictions to people linked to the banned parties. The court can prohibit them from establishing or joining other parties, standing as candidates in elections or holding political office. Authorities may also terminate the mandates of sitting elected MPs.

A new party name would not automatically provide a way around the ban. The law already includes the concept of a “successor party”. If a new political force substantially repeats the goals, activities or membership of a banned party, the court can ban it as well.

Under the Georgian Dream scenario, all of this could effectively leave the country without political parties or politicians representing the current opposition.

The process is not taking place in isolation. In recent years, the government has also adopted several laws that have sharply tightened the legal environment for foreign funding, grants and the activities of NGOs and media outlets.

Meanwhile, anti-government protests continue in Georgia, and the political confrontation between the authorities and their opponents remains highly tense.

The 2028 election is key to understanding the political significance of these developments. If the court upholds the lawsuit and the current restrictions remain in force, Georgia could enter the next parliamentary election with all four opposition forces that crossed the threshold in 2024 legally dissolved. The mechanism for quickly banning possible successor parties would already be in place.

Ban on opposition parties in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan’s corruption whistleblowers: protection on paper and in practice
World.content:
Azerbaijan drafts anti-corruption bill

Azerbaijan has drafted a separate bill aimed at encouraging and protecting people who report corruption. The bill was submitted to the Milli Majlis on 5 October and is due to be discussed by a parliamentary committee on 6 October.

The initiative comes amid continuing complaints that police officers demand money from citizens, while journalists investigating corruption are sentenced to lengthy prison terms. Existing legislation already provides protections for people who report corruption. The key question, therefore, is from whom – and how – the state intends to protect citizens after they report such cases.

Protection provided by law

Article 11-2 of the Law on Combating Corruption prohibits disclosing the identity of a person who reports corruption without their consent, as well as threatening them or their relatives. It also prohibits dismissing an employee because they have filed a complaint, transferring them to another position, making unlawful deductions from their salary or obstructing their career progression.

If an employee provides evidence that retaliatory measures have been taken against them, the burden of disproving the allegation falls on the employer. The law also prohibits assigning a complaint for review to the person against whom it was made or to anyone with an interest in the outcome of the investigation.

Information registered through an internal reporting procedure must be examined within 20 working days, after which the person who submitted it must be informed of the outcome. If a complaint concerns the head of an organisation, the person may approach a higher-ranking official or a specialised anti-corruption body. The obligation to investigate reports and inform complainants of the outcome therefore existed before the new bill was introduced.

However, a 2025 report by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) points to significant gaps in the implementation of these safeguards. Azerbaijan has no specialised body, unit or official dedicated exclusively to protecting people who report corruption. The authorities were also unable to provide examples of the provision placing the burden on employers to disprove evidence of retaliation being applied in 2023-2024.

The report also notes that public disclosure through the media and social networks is not recognised as a protected channel for reporting corruption. This gap is particularly significant for people who report wrongdoing to journalists rather than to state bodies.

Alleged $300 bribe demand and claim of violence

On 28 August, Gündəlik Naxçıvan reported that a young driver had been detained. According to the outlet, police officers said the driver was under the influence of alcohol. He denied this and said he was willing to undergo a medical examination at a hospital.

Instead of being given a medical examination, he was allegedly asked to pay 500 manats (about $300):

“They told me: either you pay the money now, or they will take both you and the car away.”

According to the outlet, after the driver refused to pay, additional traffic police officers arrived at the scene. Five or six officers allegedly used force against him. Witnesses said the driver suffered a broken arm and ribs as a result.

The complaint therefore concerns not only an alleged demand for a bribe, but also claims that force was used instead of allowing the driver to undergo a medical examination and challenge the allegation against him.

Threats of drug possession and other criminal charges

On 10 September, Gündəlik Naxçıvan published another complaint from residents of Ordubad. People who had returned from Russia said they were taken from their homes and brought to a police station, where they were tested for drugs in a toilet without a doctor present.

One complainant, who asked to remain anonymous, said his test was negative but that he was nevertheless asked to pay 10,000 manats (about $5,882). He said that after being threatened with arrest and torture, he paid 5,000 manats (about $2,941).

Similar allegations have been made in the past. In a Toplum TV report published on 17 December 2025, Shiraz Guliyev, who had returned from Turkey, said he was asked to pay 300 manats (about $176.50) near the Sadarak customs checkpoint on the grounds that he had allegedly dropped a cigarette butt. Guliyev said he told officers that he did not smoke, but was threatened with arrest on charges of resisting police if he refused to pay.

In June 2025, blogger Mehman Huseynov alleged that officers from Baku’s Khatai district police station No 37 beat five teenagers and released them after receiving money from their parents.

Lawyer Khalid Bagirov told Meydan TV that the problem was not the absence of mechanisms for holding officers accountable, but that those mechanisms were not being effectively applied.

What do the official figures show?

The Main Anti-Corruption Directorate under the Prosecutor General’s Office said it reviewed 5,655 complaints in the first half of 2026. A total of 54 criminal cases involving 102 people were sent to court. Of the calls received through the “161” hotline, 4,062 were registered as reports of corruption-related offences.

The figures show that investigations are being carried out. However, the number of cases sent to court does not indicate how effectively people who report corruption are subsequently protected from pressure or retaliation.

This distinction is particularly important in cases involving complaints against the police. A person who complains about an officer with the power to detain them, take them to a police station and formally record offences is seeking more than the return of money. They also need guarantees that those powers will not be used against them in retaliation. Receiving a complaint and protecting the complainant are two separate tasks.

According to an OECD report assessing the situation in 2023-2024, Azerbaijan has made no significant overall progress in combating corruption since 2022. The system for declaring the assets and interests of public officials was not operational, while gaps also remained in declaration forms and procedures for their electronic submission and verification.

In Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, Azerbaijan scored 30 out of 100 and ranked 130th out of 182 countries. Despite an eight-point increase compared with the previous year, the score remains low in terms of perceived levels of public-sector corruption.

Arrests of journalists investigating corruption

The authorities’ pledge to protect those who report corruption also contrasts with the situation surrounding the Abzas Media case. On 20 June 2025, seven defendants in the case were sentenced to prison terms ranging from seven years and six months to nine years. They included journalists Ulvi Hasanli, Sevinj Vagifgizi and Hafiz Babali, who had investigated corruption.

The defendants rejected the charges against them. Reporters Without Borders described the sentences as the result of a politically motivated trial aimed at silencing those who expose corruption and injustice.

Against this backdrop, several questions arise: Is a person who reports an alleged demand for a bribe protected from retaliation? Is the alleged offence independently investigated, and are the findings made public? And can a journalist who exposes corruption continue their work without facing the threat of imprisonment?

World.title: Sovereignty, territorial integrity and non-interference in the internal affairs of States are principles of the UN Charter - Shahriyar Hajiyev
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. Azerbaijan reaffirmed its commitment to the promotion and protection of human rights, highlighting the humanitarian consequences of the former conflict, including landmines and missing persons, First Secretary of the Permanent Mission of Azerbaijan to the United Nations Shahriyar Hajiyev said at the Third Committee of the eighty-first session of the United Nations General Assembly under agenda item 70: Promotion and protection of human rights.

"Upholding the inherent dignity and equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family is of the utmost importance today, as our world faces serious challenges arising from escalating conflicts, deepening inequalities and the impacts of climate change.

Securing human rights and freedoms is the highest-priority objective, as determined by the Constitution of Azerbaijan, and continuous legal and institutional reforms are being undertaken to maintain steady progress in the promotion and protection of human rights.

Azerbaijan attaches particular importance to cooperation with United Nations human rights mechanisms, in particular the Universal Periodic Review, the treaty bodies and the special procedures mandate holders, by regularly submitting national reports on the implementation of international human rights instruments and maintaining dialogue with monitoring mechanisms.

Restoring the human rights of Azerbaijanis displaced as a result of the former conflict has always been a priority area for the state. Azerbaijan’s systematic rehabilitation and reconstruction measures under the Great Return Programme have already enabled 96,000 persons to return to and live in the territories liberated from occupation.

These efforts are seriously hampered by the extensive presence of mines, killing and seriously injuring more than 400 individuals, which requires genuine cooperation in rendering them harmless. At the same time, the issue of over 4,000 persons registered as missing is another remaining humanitarian problem.

Since the end of the conflict, 32 mass graves containing the remains of 253 individuals have been discovered. These graves provide further evidence of the wilful killing of civilians and other persons protected under international humanitarian law.

Providing all necessary information on burial sites, opening of archives and collection of witness statements are among the measures to be implemented for realisation of the right to know for the missing persons’ families. Azerbaijan will continue to mobilize all its resources to shed light on the fate of persons whose whereabouts remain unknown.

Accountability is undeniable and must be an inevitable consequence of the offences committed. Azerbaijan has taken decisive steps to investigate and prosecute serious offences committed against its civilians and other protected persons during the conflict, in full accordance with its national legislation and international obligations.

Concerning the report (A/81/211) submitted to the Third Committee by the Working Group on the rights of peasants and other people working in rural areas, Azerbaijan emphasizes that mandate holders must be guided by the aims and principles of the Charter of the United Nations. Furthermore, it is incumbent upon special procedures to exercise their functions in strict accordance with their mandates, and the information they present should be reliable, cross-checked and drawn from relevant and credible sources, in accordance with Human Rights Council resolution 5/2, entitled “Code of Conduct for Special Procedures Mandate-Holders,” of 18 June 2007. Unfortunately, the above-mentioned report does not meet these requirements.

Sovereign equality, respect for territorial integrity and non-interference in the internal affairs of States are fundamental principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations. We oppose growing trends of politicisation of human rights and double standards, or interference in States’ internal affairs under the pretext of human rights on various international platforms.

In this regard, we stress that certain issues brought to the attention of the Committee, including those related to China, must be approached with that understanding and in full conformity with the mentioned principles," Shahriyar Hajiyev said.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 8, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020 in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation.

Trend presents the chronicle of the twelvth day of the Second Karabakh war:

- the ministry of defense of Azerbaijan reported that the Armenian armed forces have been shelling the villages of Goranboy, Terter, and Aghdam regions since the early morning hours. There were killed and wounded. As a result of rocket attacks by the Armenian army in Ganja, several civilian objects, one car and residential buildings were damaged.

- a person who posed as a captured Azerbaijani on social media turned out to be an Armenian

- the ministry of defense of Azerbaijan has published video footage of armored vehicles taken as a trophy, which, while fleeing, were thrown in Horadiz by the Armenian military. Later, the defense ministry published another video footage of war trophies captured from the Armenian Armed Forces.

- Armenian armed forces fire at Azerbaijan’s Barda from 'Tochka-U' high-precision tactical missile system. Another rocket fired by the Armenian Armed Forces at Barda hit a restaurant and a school, injuring seven people. Armenia’s Grad missile launcher which attacked Azerbaijan’s Barda and Tartar destroyed.

- Azerbaijan's Ministry of Defense has published anothervideo footage of the destruction of enemy armored vehicles

World.title: Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan hold another round of consular consultations (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. The foreign ministries of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan held another round of consular consultations in Baku on October 7.

The Azerbaijani delegation was led by Emil Safarov, Head of the Consular Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan, while the Uzbek delegation was headed by Abduvakhit Tursunov, Deputy Head of the Consular and Legal Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Uzbekistan.

Representatives of Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Science and Education, State Migration Service, State Border Service, as well as the Embassy of Uzbekistan in the country also participated in the consultations.

The consultations focused on the current state and prospects of consular cooperation between the two countries.

The meeting also stressed the importance of advancing relations between the two countries in the fields of migration, justice, internal affairs, education, social affairs, as well as strengthening legal framework aimed at ensuring rights and protection of both countries’ citizens.

Following the consultations, the protocol of the meeting was signed.

World.title: Mental health capacity restored in November after fire, government says
World.content:
Tasmania's health minister says most of the North West Regional Hospital's (NWRH) mental health capacity will be restored in November, after a woman allegedly set fire to the region's only public inpatient mental health facility.

The 19-bed Spencer Clinic at the NWRH has been closed since the fire damaged part of the building last month, prompting concerns about mental health services in the region.

Health Minister Bridget Archer said 10 rooms within the clinic will be brought back into service next month, with repair work underway to deliver a four-bed high care unit and a six-bed acute inpatient unit.

Woman charged over fire in hospital mental health clinic A 28-year-old woman is charged with arson after a fire at the North West Regional Hospital in Burnie on Saturday night.

Ms Archer said an additional five beds will be made available on the hospital campus in the coming weeks, and the Health Department will continue to rent three beds at the neighbouring North West Private Hospital.

Mental Health Lived Experience Tasmania chief executive Tash Smyth praised the Health Department and frontline workers for their work to continue to deliver mental health care for people in the north-west.

The Health and Community Services Union (HACSU) has also welcomed the measures but said there are still issues to work through, including the flow-on effects from losing beds from the private system.

Fire and smoke damage to the mental health unit at the North-West Regional Hospital in September. (Tasmanian government)

Advocate urges rethink on care model

Going forward, Ms Smyth said the closure of the Spencer Clinic had provided an opportunity to reconsider how mental health care is provided in the region.

"Spencer Clinic was a very traditional acute inpatient model. There are better ways of doing things," she said.

" Yes, it's a shock. You think … we've lost 19 beds. But did we need those 19 beds, or do we need a different type of service to address the needs of the community? "

Ms Smyth said the interim arrangements will include sub-acute beds separate to high dependency beds, which weren't previously available at the Spencer Clinic.

"There will always be people in the community that do need a hospital setting … but is there a different way that we can do this? And sometimes it takes a crisis to get us to start thinking creatively about a more contemporary model of care," she said.

HACSU state secretary Robbie Moore says there is an opportunity to improve mental health services in the north-west. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

HACSU state secretary Robbie Moore said the response to the fire had been positive, but the system still had capacity issues.

"We are welcoming that they do have some interim arrangements that will mean there will be hospital beds available for people on the north-west," he said.

"What they're not dealing with is that by taking the private beds out of being available on the north-west, those patients are likely to then end up in the public system.

" And we don't have the capacity to deal with that. "

A TFS officer inspects fire and smoke damage to the mental health unit. (Tasmanian government)

Wait continues for new unit

A new 22-bed mental health unit to replace the ageing Spencer Clinic has been in the pipeline for several years.

The $40 million dollar facility was first promised by the Liberal government during the 2021 election campaign.

'Not enough' mental health beds in Tasmania after arson attack, union warns A health care union says there will be major issues moving forward following the loss of 19 beds for mental health patients in deliberately-lit hospital fire.

At the time, then-premier Peter Gutwein said the project would be finished in 2025.

More than five years later, construction still hasn't started.

The government last week announced the building contractor for the project.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health said the contractor is due to start work on site as soon as next week.

"Construction is expected to be complete in the first half of 2028, and we will continue to work with the contractor to expedite works where possible," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Breaking: Snowtown serial killer James Vlassakis walks out of Adelaide Pre-release Centre
World.content:
Snowtown murderer James Spyridon Vlassakis has been filmed leaving the Adelaide Pre-release Centre after having his parole confirmed almost a month ago.

The decision to release the so-called "bodies in the barrels" killer, following the completion of his non-parole period, was upheld in September after the South Australian government attempted to block it.

The 46-year-old moved from a South Australian prison to the pre-release centre in Adelaide's northern suburbs last month.

The Adelaide Pre-release Centre is located alongside Yatala Labour Prison in the northern suburbs, and allows prisoners to "transition from custody to the community".

Vlassakis will live at the centre for up to 12 months while the Parole Board monitors his progress and decides what conditions he will need to comply with once he is released into the community.

James Vlassakis was sentenced to life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 26 years. (Supplied)

He was the youngest of the four perpetrators involved in the Snowtown serial killings between 1992 and 1999.

Vlassakis was handed a life sentence with a non-parole period of 26 years for his involvement in the murders of Fred Brooks, Gary O'Dwyer, David Johnson and his half-brother Troy Youde.

World.title: Friends pray for burned Melbourne schoolboy after botched alleged arson
World.content:
A schoolboy fighting for life after setting himself alight in a botched alleged arson attack received his orders via WhatsApp, the ABC can reveal.

Vision shows two other people leaving the 13-year-old boy for dead after two vehicles were set alight on Woolwich Way in Taylors Hill, in Melbourne's north-west, on Monday morning.

The 13-year-old boy was rushed to hospital in a critical condition after being engulfed in flames in Taylors Hill. (Supplied)

The boy remains in a critical condition with severe burns to his upper and lower body.

The ABC can reveal the trio was tasked with targeting the address by middlemen who had communicated with one another using aliases on WhatsApp in the lead-up to the incident.

After allegedly setting the two cars on fire, the trio had attempted to flee the scene in an allegedly stolen car, but crashed it seconds later.

The two others then ran away, leaving the 13-year-old on fire behind.

Close friends of the boy, who attends a secondary school in Melbourne's northern suburbs, told the ABC they were praying he survived.

One friend, who cannot be named because they are underage, said: "He is a great guy. I felt alive with him."

Another friend told the ABC: "He is more than just a friend to us. He is someone who brought so much laughter and happiness to everyone around him.

"We have so many memories together that I'll always hold close to my heart and it would really be sad if we lose him.

" No one deserves that. He was a funny person with so much love for everyone around him. "

Two cars were destroyed in the firebombing and the Woolwich Way home was damaged. (ABC News)

"He was always making people laugh, even when nobody was expecting it," another close friend said.

"He was caring, loyal and always there for his mates.

"We're really worried about him. We're just hoping and praying that he pulls through."

It is understood phone data will be central to the police investigation into the arson, which is among a string of similar incidents across Melbourne over consecutive nights.

Multiple vehicles were torched in Springvale, Reservoir and Oakleigh East overnight.

Yesterday, homes in Balwyn North and Maidstone were damaged by fire, following arsons in Keilor and the Taylors Hill fire involving the 13-year-old.

Loading...

The incident is not the first of its kind to leave Victorians with life-threatening or deadly burns.

Last month, a man in his 20s sustained what police described as "life-altering" burns while trying to torch a Melton tobacconist.

Another 52-year-old man spent almost six months in hospital before succumbing to his injuries after attacking a dessert bar in Chapel St.

Innocent woman Katie Tangey, 27, was killed when arsonists mistakenly targeted her brother's Truganina townhouse, where she had been house-sitting at the start of 2025.

World.title: US expected to charge former Venezuelan president with more crimes
World.content:
Former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores are expected to face new criminal charges in the United States over allegations that Americans detained in Venezuela were tortured, according to US officials.

Mr Maduro, who led Venezuela for 13 years, and Ms Flores, were captured in a US military operation from their home in Caracas In January, and brought to New York to face drug trafficking charges.

Mr Maduro, 63, and Ms Flores, 69, have pleaded not guilty and their trial is expected to begin in June.

Nicolás Maduro was captured by US officials in January. (Truth Social/Donald Trump)

According to CNN, which has cited people familiar with the investigation, the new torture charges relate to the alleged wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens in Venezuela during Mr Maduro's rule.

The report said prosecutors were also considering charging several other people for their alleged role in torturing Americans.

CNN said charges could be announced as soon as Thursday, local time.

A spokesperson for the Manhattan US Attorney's office, which brought the charges, declined to comment.

Lawyers for Mr Maduro and Ms Flores did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Escalating tensions with US before capture

Mr Maduro's tenure as president was marked by tensions with the United States.

Washington accused his government of detaining Americans as leverage to extract concessions, such as relief from financial sanctions.

Americans whom the US classified as wrongfully detained during Maduro's tenure included five oil executives arrested on graft charges.

Nicolás Maduro during a rally against an escalation of US actions before his capture. (Reuters: Leonardo Fernandez Viloria)

They were freed in 2022 in exchange for two of Ms Flores's nephews who had been convicted in the US of drug trafficking.

Since Mr Maduro's capture, Venezuela has been led by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has increased cooperation with the Trump administration.

Mr Maduro and his wife have been detained in a federal jail in Brooklyn, New York.

Ms Flores is due to appear in Manhattan federal court on Thursday, local time, where her lawyers are expected to request she be released from jail before the trial due to health reasons.

Prosecutors oppose her release.

Reuters/AFP

World.title: Man jailed for luring 4yo girl away from front yard and raping her
World.content:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of sexual abuse.

A man who raped a four-year-old girl in a Darwin town camp after luring her away with watermelon while she played in a front yard last year has been jailed for at least seven years.

If you or anyone you know needs help: Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467

Nathaniel Farrell, 34, pleaded guilty in the Northern Territory Supreme Court to one count of rape following the June 14 attack and was sentenced to 10 years in prison with a seven-year non-parole period last week.

The court heard the girl was playing in the yard with a three-year-old boy when Farrell lured her into a house where he removed her nappy and violently digitally raped her before tying the nappy back in place.

The girl's mother quickly noticed her missing and called police before finding her walking back towards her house in tears, repeating "the big man, the big man".

After realising the child was bleeding under her nappy, the girl's mother again called police who found Farrell's DNA on her body.

A non-publication order prohibiting Farrell's name from being released to the public has been lifted. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

In sentencing, Chief Justice Michael Grant said while it was Farrell's first sexual offence, he had a long history of violence against women and breaches of court orders, including parole and domestic violence orders.

"The offender has a history of offending against women and presents a continuing danger to the community, and particularly female members of that community," he said.

" The offender's prospects of rehabilitation must be considered as all but extinguished, at least for so long as he continues abusing drugs and alcohol. "

A stable upbringing

Chief Justice Grant said although Farrell had grown up in a disadvantaged remote community and started drinking and abusing volatile substances as a teenager, "his upbringing was quite stable and not blighted by domestic violence or alcohol abuse".

He said like "many teenagers", Farrell had experimented with drugs as a youth and moved on to cannabis and methamphetamine as an adult, but under the circumstances his addiction was not a mitigating factor.

"Although it may be accepted in a general sense that the offender grew up in the circumstances of social and economic disadvantage which blight Aboriginal communities in the Northern Territory, and that has some mitigating effect, that consideration cannot lead to the imposition of a sentence that is disproportionate to the gravity of the offending," he said.

Chief Justice Michael Grant described the offending against the "very young and vulnerable" child as "brazen". (Supplied: NT Supreme Court)

" In assessing the extent of that mitigating effect, I am unable to conclude that the offender has been subjected to disadvantage of any great degree and extent, or that there is any direct nexus between those circumstances and the offending conduct. "

Chief Justice Grant said Farrell's offending involved "the egregious sexual abuse of an infant causing injury" and was "towards the upper end of the range in terms of objective seriousness".

"The child was very young and vulnerable, the offending conduct was brazen," he said.

"There was a degree of what the Crown has described as 'rudimentary planning' in luring the victim to a secluded location with the promise of watermelon."

Suppression order lifted

Chief Justice Grant also lifted a suppression order banning the publication of Farrell's name and declined a request from his lawyer the he be marked "at risk" due to a "fear of being hurt in the prison as a result of this offending being made public".

"That is not a sufficient ground on which to be marked at risk under the relevant practice direction but I will make sure my associate tells the sheriff what your concern is," he said.

"That is ultimately a matter for the correctional authorities, he does not seem to be suffering under any sort of duress at the moment."

Farrell will be eligible for parole in 2032.

World.title: More problems emerging along WA's high-profile 'electric highway'
World.content:
Travellers say Western Australia's high-profile "electric highway" is failing to keep pace with demand, and risks deterring road trips to remote parts of the state.

Launched in 2025 to significant fanfare, WA's electric vehicle charging network comprises 110 charging points between Mundrabilla, on the Nullarbor Plain in the state's remote south-east, through to Kununurra in the East Kimberley.

But the network has been plagued by reports of broken chargers and malfunctioning equipment, triggering increased "range anxiety" from drivers navigating remote parts of the state.

With EVs outselling petrol and diesel cars in Australia for the first time in August, Australia's North West tourism chief executive officer Bill Tatchell said EV infrastructure was becoming more crucial.

"The distances here are enormous, so confidence in the availability and reliability of charging is probably even more important in the North West than it is in metropolitan areas," he said.

"The state's EV Network has made a significant difference by creating a charging spine through the region, but over time we will need to keep building on that."

Drivers and tourism officials say a lack of available charging infrastructure could deter people from "bucket list" road trips to WA's Pilbara. (ABC News: Chris Lewis)

Perth woman Catherin Robinson is a new EV owner who undertook a 1,500 kilometre drive north to Karratha to visit family, after owning her car for only two weeks.

Ms Robinson described her journey as "sink or swim".

"Range anxiety was very, very real," she said.

"There needs to be more availability, closer together, not so sparse, and chargers that work."

Catherin Robinson (left) and sister Cynthia Horrobin at the EV charging station in Eneabba. (Supplied: Catherin Robinson)

Ms Robinson believed the lack of chargers meant travellers could not properly explore the region.

"We had to go from A to B and even though we wanted to … it wasn't worth the time charging to go off," she said.

"It could never have been a spur-of-the-moment decision to go and explore a bit more."

Bill Tatchell said improvements and access to the region's chargers would be critical as EV use grew.

"Road trips are fundamental to tourism in the North West," he said.

" As more Australians move into electric vehicles we need to make sure owning an EV doesn't become a reason not to travel north. "

Wary heading to the country

Michael Kerr, another EV owner from Perth, made the 2,700km round trip to Karijini National Park this year and said he would be unlikely to make the trip again.

Mr Kerr said he had to plan the multi-day journey around broken chargers and waiting hours to power up at slow chargers added to the stress of the trip.

"You have to keep an eye on what's working," he said.

"You have to be careful about judging the distances you travel between charges."

At one stop, Mr Kerr barely made it to the charger, rolling in with only 20km of range left on the EV's battery.

Michael Kerr says he enjoyed exploring Karijini National Park, but the drive north in an EV had some challenges. (Supplied: Michael Kerr)

Having travelled to Karijini on previous trips in a petrol vehicle, Mr Kerr described the charging network as "pathetic" and has written to the state government about his concerns.

"It's an EV charging line … once you get off the main [North West Coastal] highway, it's bad, really bad," he said.

" We won't be doing that trip again anytime soon, now we're pretty wary about heading off to the country. "

Fail grade for network

In its 2026 State of the EVs Report released last month, the Electric Vehicle Council rated the WA government three out of 10 across 26 metrics.

The report found the WA government was underperforming, despite its strong financial position, with weak supports for charging infrastructure and passenger and freight vehicles.

Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the state government had provided the backbone of EV charging infrastructure.

Road traffic accounts for a significant number of visitors to the Pilbara each tourist season. (ABC News: Chris Lewis)

But she did not respond when asked whether the government would consider expanding the network.

"We've connected more than 7,000 kilometres of Western Australia across 110 charging points," Ms Sanderson said.

"We've also supported WA organisations and businesses to install chargers at destinations across the state through three rounds of Charge Up grants."

'Tombstones in car parks'

EV expert Kai Li Lim said there was often a "bigger and better" mentality when it came to chargers, but slower, cheaper options in strategic locations could be more affordable.

"If you're going to stay at national parks, for example, and you may be parking your car for two to four hours at a time, you don't need to have the big fat DC chargers charging your car," he said.

Kai Li Lim says maintenance needs to be a consideration when installing chargers. (ABC News: Jess Davis)

Dr Lim said maintenance must be factored in when new chargers were commissioned, whether publicly or privately owned.

"We are starting to see this whole notion of chargers … almost like tombstones in the car parks," he said.

"Nobody wants to take ownership of the chargers anymore.

"A charger breaks down in the Pilbara and you have technicians over east, when do we send the technician over to the Pilbara to fix the chargers?"

EV owner Michael Kerr says nothing is "straightforward" or "easy" when planning remote trips in his new car. (Supplied: Michael Kerr)

Dr Lim said there was also a bigger industrial decarbonisation picture to consider when weighing up the value of remote charging networks.

"It's important to make sure that the infrastructure that we build across the country, and not just in WA, is also supporting freight electrification."

World.title: How Vika and Linda made leap from backing singers to hall of famers
World.content:
Australian Tongan siblings Vika and Linda Bull are among our nation's most celebrated and dynamic vocal duos.

Beyond their sublime harmonies, however, the singing sisters are very different people whose music tastes were "polar opposites" growing up.

"I'm a little bit country, and Vika's a little bit rock'n'roll," Linda says on Take 5 with Zan Rowe.

" We're 17 months apart, but our attitude to life, at times, has been radically different. "

Watch every episode of Take 5 with Zan Rowe right here Catch interviews with Shania Twain, David Byrne, Darren Hayes, Jacinda Ardern and more.

Older sister Vika admits to being the wilder of the two growing up. But she was also a natural leader and trailblazer.

"I have the guts to do that," she says. "But business? It's this one.

"Linda's very careful. Considers everything. Sometimes too much, and it drives me crazy.

"She's seen me just bumble through and make a wreck of things."

Linda adds: "I did watch that and go, 'I don't think mum would survive two of us like that.'"

The pair's differences are their strength, Linda reasons.

"Our voices, personalities [and] tastes are different. But we cover a lot of ground because we work as a team."

Across four decades as successful recording artists, the OAM recipients and recent ARIA Hall of Famers have stuck to the same motto:

" Sisters first, singers second. "

Finding their voice

The first person to notice how Vika and Linda's dissimilarities complemented each other was their mother.

"She recognised Vika had a higher voice, and I naturally had a lower one. She would coach us with holding the note, how to sing in tune," Linda says.

"Teach us different parts people were singing on the radio. We'd just go around the house practising."

Raised in the conservative suburb of Doncaster in 1970s Melbourne, "we stood out," says Linda.

Their mixed heritage and cultural practices set them apart at primary school. But they delighted in attending Tongan church each Sunday and the visceral experience of the choir.

"It's frightening and exhilarating; just the best thing you'll ever hear," gushes Vika.

A young Vika and Linda Bull pose with their mother and father. (Supplied: Vika and Linda Bull)

Mama Bull was less than happy when Vika, who had left school early to pursue singing, convinced her little sister, a few years into a university degree, to do the same.

"That was a bad day in the Bull household," Vika smirks.

"Mum goes, 'Not you too!' It's your fault, you taught us!" Linda jokes.

"That was our pact with mum: we'll stick together. 'Don't get the tattoos. Don't take drugs.' And so we didn't."

"Well, you didn't!" Vika counters.

For Take 5, Vika & Linda selected songs by other famous vocal families, including Neil and Tim Finn and The Staple Singers. (ABC TV: Giulia Giannini McGauran)

In the late 1980s, Vika and Linda gained wider attention with The Black Sorrows, their intimate harmonies and soulful power the secret sauce on tunes like Chained To The Wheel and Never Let Me Go.

"I didn't know what a gift Joe [Camilerri, band leader] was giving me at that time. It was a great band to be in [and] Joe just said, 'Go for it.'"

Double J — a place for music lovers Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

During this era, Vika and Linda moonlighted as celebrated singers-for-hire on albums from Hunters and Collectors, John Farnham, Deborah Conway and more.

"You don't want to overshadow the singer," explains Vika. "You're kind of like the icing on the cake. You're there to support and lift."

By 1994, they departed The Black Sorrows to step out on their own.

"I remember the day. It was hard to leave that band. Being in the Sorrows, we would've remained backing singers. We just thought, 'We want to start telling stories as well.'"

Linda adds: "In our own way. We'd been interpreters of [other people's] music, but we felt if we don't try … we're wasting our time."

Going solo together

When the Bull sisters were ready to leap, side by side, some Australian music royalty was ready to help give them a push.

Featuring on Archie Roach's 1990 classic Charcoal Lane introduced Vika and Linda to Paul Kelly.

"He said we should sit down and write songs; 'Give it a crack!'" remembers Linda.

"He was the first person to say that, even though we hadn't written one song."

Kelly devoted a "year of Thursday afternoon writing sessions" to the duo, coaxing them with yarns and musical sketches.

"He'd be so patient, just trying to draw us out of our shells. He realised the key to Vika and I would be conversation. 'That's a good story; that's a good idea to write a song.'"

Hear extended episodes of Take 5 right here Dive even deeper into the music that has inspired your favourite artists on the Take 5 podcast.

Vika confesses the Gravy Man made her especially shy.

"I was always incredibly intimidated at those sessions. Too worried about [saying] something stupid. 'He's going to think it's corny!'

"I'd hold back a lot. 'I'll go make a cup of tea.' I wish I was more bold … I could've used the time better."

Vika & Linda were long-term members of Paul Kelly's live entourage and sang on several of his albums. (Stephen Booth)

Regardless, Kelly got results, kicking off a lifelong friendship and collaboration with Vika and Linda, including the early single We've Started A Fire.

"As soon as he busted out that, and it was a reggae feel, I'm like 'Ooh, this is for us!'" recalls Linda.

The track featured on the duo's 1994 self-titled album, a platinum-selling release co-produced by Kelly and featuring breakout hit When Will You Fall For Me, written with Hunters & Collectors frontman Mark Seymour.

"[Kelly] had a lot of faith in Vika and I. Watching him in action really taught us a lot."

Loading Instagram content

No bull

The aging combination of experience and wisdom means those butterflies have long been quelled. And Vika and Linda are more confident than ever.

Their career-spanning memoir, No Bull, inspired Where Do You Come From? the duo's ninth album and among their best, including a title track exploring experiences of childhood racism.

"When you're older females and been doing it for a long time, you have a duty to be honest," says Linda.

"You hear women say it a lot at our age: I don't give a shit anymore.

"Shake off all this stuff that's happened and just be me. For Vika and I, we've done it together and at the same time."

Vika adds: "It certainly gave me confidence. Linda has always had it, but I've been a bit shy to show my words or sing them.

"Most of my life I haven't felt calm. I've [felt] reckless, wild, just want to punch everyone in my way.

"But I'm just not like that anymore. I'm at peace, I'm happy to just let things happen; if they do and if they don't, I don't care."

World.title: Seafood shop owners fear being forced to close due to gillnet ban
World.content:
Business owners in north Queensland are concerned about the economic flow-on effect of the looming Great Barrier Reef gillnet ban.

Some commercial fishers fear they will have to leave the industry and seafood shops may be left with no other option than to close.

Peter and Heather Bradford are worried about the future of their business. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

In Ayr, Heather and Peter Bradford serve locally caught seafood to about 150 families a week and say their business will not survive without gillnet fishers on the water.

"Next year we'll have to probably close the shop," Mr Bradford said.

"Cut out the netting, there's 80 per cent of our business, so we've got no other option but to close."

Gillnet ban looming

Gillnets are used to catch certain species of fish, including barramundi, by their gills.

In 2023 the Queensland and federal governments made the decision to phase out the use of gillnets in the Great Barrier Reef fishing zone by June 30 2027.

The governments provided financial assistance to licensed fishers at the time of the decision and established the temporary NX licence, which allowed fishers to use gillnets under strict on-board camera monitoring.

The state government has been working with fishers to find an alternative fishing method in the last three years, such as trapping and line fishing.

Barramundi is largely caught using gillnets. (ABC News: Brooke Tindall)

But as the expiry of the NX licences approach, no solutions have been rolled out to fishers.

South of Townsville, Alva Beach commercial fisher Neil Green said the other options trialled had not been successful so far.

"The intent was to have alternative gear running by 2027. That's been a failure," he said.

Neil Green is one of 25 NX licensed fishers in Queensland. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Mr Green said without change he would probably be forced to retire, but he was worried about more than his own future.

"It's not about me — it's about the next generation of fishers that are coming on that we're talking about," he said.

Push to buy more time

Mr Green is among several fishermen in the industry pushing for a three-year extension to the ban, which has the support of Shadow Minister for Northern Australia Susan McDonald.

"It will allow [the fishers] to demonstrate that gillnet fishing is incredibly targeted on the species that the fishermen are taking," she said.

Susan McDonald supports the seafood industry's call for a three-year extension on NX licences. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Senator McDonald said the 2027 deadline would increase reliability on imports.

"If we allow more seafood to be imported from offshore, we are handing over seafood production to countries that don't have the same high standards that Australia does," she said.

Back in Ayr, Ms Bradford said importing seafood had not worked for her and her husband's business in the past.

"We couldn't compete with [the major supermarkets] price-wise, so it's not going to be viable for us at all," she said.

Ms Bradford said other small seafood businesses were in the same boat.

"Fish and chip shops will be gone, especially all up along the north coast," she said.

Threatened species at risk

Not everyone agrees that putting off the eventual gillnet ban is a viable option.

Australian Marine Conservation Society (AMCS) Great Barrier Reef fisheries campaign manager Simon Miller said a three-year extension of the NX licences would come at a cost to wildlife.

"The current gillnet fishery, the NX fishery, is still catching thousands of threatened species each year," he said.

"We do urge the Queensland and Australian governments to fully deliver their commitment to phase out gillnet fishing from the reef by June 30 next year."

The AMCS is against extending temporary licences but Mr Miller says there is support for finding alternative fishing gear.

"We need to be looking to the future for genuinely sustainable ways to catch these fish and put them on Queenslanders' plates, but without this impact on threatened species," he said.

The gillnet ban has caused uproar in the commercial fishing industry. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Queensland Primary Industries Minister Tony Perrrett said he was aware of the calls to extend the NX licences.

"We look for solutions, that's why that trial work is important as it continues to make certain that there is alternate gear into the future," he said.

As for onshore businesses, he said the department was not at the stage of discussions for compensation for impacted businesses.

"There's still NX fishing licences in place, as was agreed to by the previous government, but it's something that we continue to watch and monitor," he said.

A federal Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water spokesperson said the Queensland government was responsible for the management, regulation and enforcement of fisheries.

The spokesperson said changes to regulations for the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park were made to support commitments by the Queensland government.

"This includes the removal of gillnets in the Marine Park from 1 July 2027… The Australian Government does not support delaying these reforms coming into effect," the spokesperson said.

World.title: International student cuts risk ‘very significant hole’, universities warn
World.content:
NationalUniversity International student cuts risk ‘very significant hole’, universities warn Jackson Graham and Christopher Harris October 8, 2026 — 11:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australia’s higher education sector was already grappling with a decline in foreign students before the Coalition revealed its plans this week to slash commencements by 55,000 each year, a pledge that experts say risks “creating a very significant hole” in university budgets. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor’s announcement on Tuesday came as the number of international student visa approvals plunged under Labor, with one in four applicants now being rejected. Australian Catholic University vice chancellor Zlatko Skrbis fears debates surrounding international students have become over heated. James Brickwood The increase in visa rejections has come ahead of recent policy announcements from the government to curb overall migration by cutting net migration, including by targeting visa hopping and reducing visas for family members of students. The Coalition’s pledge includes a reduction to the share of international students in higher education to below 25 per cent, abolishing the temporary graduate visa that allows students who have finished their studies to live and work in Australia temporarily, and cutting international student commencements to 240,000 per year – down from the government’s planning level for next year of 295,000 students.



Australian Catholic University vice-chancellor Zlatko Skrbis, who studied in Victoria as an international student in the 1990s, said the accumulation announcements affecting international students were already being weighed into student decisions. Related Article Exclusive

Immigration Taylor to slash migration by two-thirds in bid to rival One Nation “I think it’s fair to say that across the whole sector, we are noticing a shift in the market,” Skrbis said. “It’s anxiety about the safety of their investment in international education opportunities. These are not insignificant decisions that people are making to come to Australia and study.” Universities Australia chief executive Luke Sheehy said curbing international students would be “extraordinarily challenging” for universities. “Universities are already under significant financial pressure. Public funding has not kept pace with the cost of teaching, research and infrastructure, and international education has helped fill that gap,” he said. “For some universities, these policies risk creating a very significant hole in their budgets. We cannot yet put a definitive sector-wide dollar figure on the impact, and the effect would not be uniform across institutions.”



He said successive governments encouraged the growth of international education while universities increasingly relied on that revenue to fill gaps in public funding. “Universities did not arrive at this funding model by accident,” Sheehy said. “If governments want fewer international students, they need to explain what will replace that funding and what the consequences will be.” The number of primary applicants for higher education visas approved by the federal government declined by 25 per cent over the past three years, falling from 261,317 visas in 2022-23 when Labor took office, to 195,607 visas in 2025-26. Over the same period, the rate of approvals fell from 87.5 per cent to 84 per cent, despite a reduction in applicants. In 2024, the University of Sydney modelled that a 30 per cent reduction in student visas – the equivalent of 63,500 fewer international students enrolled – the following year would cause universities overall to lose $1.1 billion in revenue.



Another perspective Letters The proposed migration cuts make zero economic sense The same year, researchers for the University of Melbourne and Monash University found that it would cost the state $5.9 billion if there were 30,000 fewer foreign students at Victoria’s universities. At Australian Catholic University, Skrbis warns that the political debate could harm Australia’s reputation among students abroad. “We shouldn’t be confusing legitimate concerns with political expediency. That’s where my concern lies. I’m hopeful that we can have a reasonable debate around the numbers,” he said. “I absolutely agree there are certain things that happen within the current system that need to be looked at. Visa hopping is absolutely a legitimate area of concern and focus.” The Group of Eight lobby group – whose members include the University of Melbourne and University of Sydney, UNSW Sydney and Monash University – opposes removing the temporary graduate visa, pointing out they include engineers, researchers and specialists.



Western Sydney University vice-chancellor George Williams said many students at the university went on to fill gaps in nursing and aged care. “Our international nursing students work in the region’s hospitals and health facilities, helping address a shortage of about 10,000 nurses in the fast-growing region,” he said. He pointed out that roughly a quarter of every dollar of revenue from international students is reinvested in supporting Australian students at the universities. “This support is vital to keep students from poorer backgrounds in study.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy.
