World.title: El Nino is Mother Nature’s way of telling us we’ve ruined coffee
World.content:
NationalCoffee Opinion El Nino is Mother Nature’s way of telling us we’ve ruined coffee Michelle Cazzulino Writer October 8, 2026 — 11:30am

October 8, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

First there was the cappuccino. Then there was the frappuccino. Then that gave way to the crappuccino – a chameleon-like, caramel-spiked, pumpkin-spiced, hyper-blended atrocity-in-a-keep-cup. OK, I made that last one up, but I’m sure someone in Sydney would happily order it and pay a small fortune for it. All that came before the World Meteorological Organisation predicted a strong El Nino event this summer, which is expected to play havoc with cocoa, coffee and vanilla crops in coffee-producing nations such as Brazil and Vietnam, where local growers are already struggling with higher temperatures and reduced rainfall. A matcha dreamee, velvet botany, mudcha, Vietnamese egg coffee and salted coffee. Dion Georgopoulos So Australian coffee drinkers can soon look forward to sampling the El Ninoccino, a nice warm cup of absolutely nothing that’s the inevitable result of export bans, energy price spikes and the rising cost of fertiliser and fuel, driven by conflict in the Middle East. For forlorn caffeine aficionados recently released from the bonds of credit card machine surcharge enslavement, the sudden emergence of the El Ninoccino is the latest blow to a coffee scene which, much like the solar system, keeps expanding at the edges for reasons no one can quite fathom. It’s fancy. It’s annoyingly complex. It requires money and choices and a Bruno Mars soundtrack.



It’s possible, of course, that the creation of the El Ninoccino is a negative feedback loop designed by the planet to maintain homeostasis. In short, when Mother Nature got jack of all the idiot amateur baristas polluting her Insta feed with their home-brewed double shot cookie dough skinny foam lattes, she forced them into extinction by making coffee beans a luxury item. Related Article Coffee 'Deconstructed coffee': It's for snobs, not hipsters, says Melbourne cafe behind beaker brew It’s time for a return to first principles. Since we can’t change the weather, let’s work on the variables we do have control over. It’s coffee, not a social history lesson or an earnest explanation about how five cents from every triple cortado sold by your inner-city local goes to supporting worker conditions on an obscure Bolivian plantation. Especially not when you’re expected to drink it alfresco, perched on a milk crate at 7am in winter. Acceptable cup sizes are small, medium or large. Not grande or venti, and certainly not regular, which, as everyone knows, is really just code for “this is a size small in sheep’s clothing and will be charged at the same price as a medium”. All the frippery – weird-flavoured cream, foam, anything fluffy that isn’t milk – is banned. And before everyone starts bleating about soy and almond and oat varietals, they can stay, OK? We’re giving them a greasy side-eye and no one’s really that happy about it, but they’re allowed because dietaries and dairy intolerances and … good grief, you made your point.



Ice, especially the bespoke crushed stuff from a specialised dispenser, is out. Again, it’s coffee. If you’re thirsty and need a pick-me-up and it has to be cold, have a Coke. Or a Powerade. Or a slice of yesterday’s coffee cake. Related Article Opinion

Food This nation’s coffee myth must be confronted. It’s overrated and at $6 a cup, overpriced James Panichi Journalist And lest we be accused of temperature bias, any customer who comes in bleating about “extra hot” qualifies for immediate expulsion from the premises. Coffee should only be served at one official temperature, and that’s a million bajillion degrees. If it’s not capable of reducing one’s tongue to molten lava five minutes after it hits the table, it’s time for a new machine or a faster waitress. This next one’s important, so lean in, would-be amateur barista social media influencers, because I’m talking directly into your annoying clip-on mics here. If a drink takes more than three ingredients and/or involves a specialist blender and/or requires a recipe to produce, it’s not coffee, it’s liquid tiramisu. All the supporting infrastructure – the swizzle sticks, the straws, the slotted spoons – are as incidental to proceedings as that video you posted yesterday about the Shein top you thought you hated but you now think is so cute and are allegedly obsessed with. Speaking of things people think they want but don’t actually need, the list of prohibited coffee toppings includes (but is certainly not limited to) hundreds and thousands, weirdly oversized chocolate bits and anything that requires drizzling.



That brings us to the biggest sticking point of all: having freed ourselves from the shackles of unnecessary paraphernalia, how much does our defanged cup of coffee cost? Who knows, but here is one guiding principle: if a second mortgage is in order before the bill can be settled, it’s too expensive. If all else fails, there’s always instant coffee. Or an El Ninoccino. Michelle Cazzulino is a Sydney writer. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: The Spare Room by Helen Garner is now an opera. Does it work?
World.content:
Key points OPERA: The Spare Room by Helen Garner has its world premiere

THEATRE: Eliza at Southbank Theatre is a psychological thriller

THEATRE: Eric Jiang’s Rhomboid has its Melbourne premiere at fortyfivedownstairs

JAZZ: Julian Banks Quartet perform at Cross Street Music Hall

THEATRE: Koreaboo at Malthouse draws from lived experience

OPERA

The Spare Room ★★★★

Playhouse, until October 10 If you’re familiar with Helen Garner’s 2008 book, The Spare Room, you might think: how on earth could this be made into an opera? The Spare Room by Helen Garner has been adapted into an opera. Jeff Busby A semi-autobiographical meditation on what it is to care for someone who is dying, to put your own beliefs aside and support them indiscriminately, the book is visceral about the awfulness of cancer. The pain, the sweat, the pissing the bed. Levity is long gone. Composer Jane Hammond and her longtime collaborator, librettist Therèsa Borg, however, saw The Spare Room as ripe for the operatic picking.



With Garner’s blessing, a gestational process of almost five years ensued, finally resulting in Victorian Opera’s latest world premiere. It is a remarkable achievement, and it would be remiss not to mention: the author, composer, librettist, director, conductor, the two star performers and CEO of the company are all women. Natalie Jones and Antoinette Halloran star in The Spare Room. Jeff Busby In contemporary chamber style, Hammond has scored for 13 players, who here manage tiny moments of introspection and huge emotional outbursts. Bach is mentioned often in Garner’s text, and Hammond deftly weaves in some of the Three-Part Inventions, creating a gloriously layered amalgamation of styles and colours. Some of the magic is lost, however, in the amplification of voices and certain instruments, particularly percussion, which threw out the balance at times. Mic-ing opera singers means that, for the most part, there is no vocal light and shade, and we are left longing for some pianissimo.



As Helen, Natalie Jones is grounded and direct, with steely vocals that, suitably, border on shrill when the situation calls for it. Opposite Jones is Antoinette Halloran, perfectly cast as the woo-woo Nicola. Halloran still has such electric presence and the most magnificent stage face, and Nicola’s more expansive music suits Halloran’s lyric voice. Related Article Performing arts Helen Garner on the worst three weeks of her life The work itself gets better as the night progresses, and when the drama matches the book in its level of intensity. The confrontation between Helen and Nicola is extraordinary. Your enjoyment of this opera might depend on how wedded you are to Garner. There are moments of comedy, perhaps required for a two-hour stage adaptation, but do not align with the original text. There is a sense of belonging in seeing one’s own experience on stage. Cancer has touched almost everyone, and amid a very Melbourne staging, where there are comments about the weather, people riding bikes, this very masthead used as a prop – it’s validating to see women’s anxieties and naturalistic experiences presented in this heightened art form.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies



THEATRE

Eliza ★★★★★

Southbank Theatre, The Sumner until October 31 Prognoses of AI’s impact upon humanity has reached fever pitch, but in Tom Holloway’s play, we are catapulted into the past to grapple with the very same questions we’re seeking answers to 60 years later. Dan Spielman (left) and Manali Datar in Eliza. Pia Johnson Dr Joseph Weizenbaum (Dan Spielman) is a mercurial visiting professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, as intent on repressing the traumatic memories of his escape from Nazi Germany as he is on heralding the advent of digital computers. When his secretary, Becky (a bewitching Manali Datar) makes a seemingly inconsequential joke about the back-and-forth cadence of talk therapy, it opens the doors to the creation of the world’s first chatbot: Eliza.



The breathtaking scale of invention is mirrored in the expansiveness of Dale Ferguson’s vertiginous set. Rows upon rows of systematically aligned towers of working files and cascading sheets of glass lend an unexplainable depth and dimension to the stage, creating rabbit warrens for the characters to lose themselves in as their sense of reality and personhood begin to blur. The play traces the ethical quandaries inherent in AI back to its genesis. Weizenbaum is shown to be well-meaning, but his disavowal of personal disclosure, refusal to listen until it’s too late and his betrayal of Becky, in particular, is a recurring theme that can be extrapolated to AI’s routine, large-scale copyright thefts in the present day. Although set in the 1960s, Eliza raises philosophical and ethical concerns about the role of AI in society. Pia Johnson The famed sycophancy of AI that is leading to current crises of consciousness is shown to have had very much the same effect when it was conceived in the 1960s, as people yearned to unburden themselves to what they perceived to be a neutral entity. Under Paige Rattray’s direction, the rapid-fire play unfurls at the brisk pace of a psychological thriller as a collective psychosis and breakdown of legibility takes hold of the characters in different ways, as they talk around one another without truly understanding each other.



This strange incomprehension finds its expression in the motif of starlings, which is, incidentally, the namesake of a company spying on Weizenbaum’s exploits. Related Article Arts Culture wars and a swing to the right: A new take on Gone With the Wind is coming Through spectacular audiovisual mastery and a stunning Hitchcockian reckoning, the forward march of progress is disturbingly realised in increasingly absurd and surreal ways as Weizenbaum figuratively and literally chokes on the irreversible weight of what he has set in motion. Spielman excels as the fulcrum, superbly marrying the constant whirring of a beautiful mind with an inexplicable childlike naivete. Datar’s transition from unknowing to seemingly all-knowing in a role that Holloway resurrected from the annals of history is chilling, and there isn’t a role that Hamish Michael can’t play, as he dovetails seamlessly between aggrieved research assistant, enthused journalist and lofty powers that be. The philosophical and ethical concerns that Eliza raises are by no means new to anyone engaged in the broader debate around AI, but in this undidactic, morally nuanced play, the inextricability of latent humanity and technological advancement is laid bare once more.

Reviewed by Sonia Nair



THEATRE

Rhomboid ★★★★

fortyfivedownstairs, until October 11 Heartfelt, funny and sexy. Eric Jiang’s Rhomboid beautifully captures the ambiguity of platonic and romantic love through the orbiting lives of Xavier (Ken Paolo) and Sebastian (Lawrence Hawkins). Chad Rosete, Lawrence Hawkins and Ken Paolo. George Jefford From high school through to the onset of their careers, Xavier and Sebastian have been trying to figure out what they mean to each other. As they get older, and other paramours enter their lives — the introduction of supporting actor Chad Rosete, who plays both Xavier’s casual hook-up Lachie and Sebastian’s serious partner Felix— their relationship becomes murky and untethered.



The chemistry between the cast is fantastic, and the dialogue is pithy and fast-paced, with pop culture references woven in. This doesn’t take away from the emotional depth of the story, as they delve into jealousy, queer identity and the unevenness that can exist in friendships and love. Sebastian candidly admits that he “loves being the only Asian in a white crew”, and that he feels threatened by other Asian queers who are “more successful, smarter or hotter” than him. Lawrence Hawkins and Ken Paolo as Sebastian and Xavier. George Jefford The set (by Amy Todd) is simple and flexible: a tower of blocks looms in the centre, assembled like Tetris. The actors move the blocks between scenes to transform into a club, a station, an art gallery, a mountain for hiking, or a wedding, with simple yet effective changes to lighting, blocking and sound. The shifting of time between scenes is seamless, as gentle instrumental piano plays and a moving scene is projected, as if peering out the windows of a car on a highway, onto the blocks.



Margot Morales’ direction shines through in these choices, setting up the story like it’s a New York City-set indie rom-com; even the lead photo for the show positions Sebastian and Xavier on a steel stairwell between two brick buildings. Related Article Arts Three titans of politics, sport and media had a meeting in the 1980s. A new play imagines what was said The space is used well. When Sebastian is drunk, dancing erratically on his own in the club in the corner, and Xavier spots him from across the room out of the corner of his eye while dancing with Lachie, you can feel the tension and awkwardness. In scenes depicting text message exchanges, the characters are positioned apart across the blocks, facing away from each other and speaking out loud. The only critique is that it is a little long; tightening the scripts and scene choices would make the already strong material even punchier. A scene between three characters overexplains the significance of the rhomboid and feels clunky; the show is at its best when it leans into innuendo and subtext. Nonetheless, it was refreshing to witness theatre that centres queer young people unapologetically, without the usual trappings of a coming-out story. At the end, we’re left with this lingering thought: love isn’t clear-cut like a square — it’s angular and leaning like a rhomboid, changing and shifting with the passage of time.

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar



JAZZ

Julian Banks Quartet ★★★★

Cross St Music Hall, October 2 Almost a decade after releasing his previous album, saxophonist Julian Banks has brought his latest album to life in a rush of inspiration and energy. The Julian Banks Quartet performed at Cross Street Music Hall on Friday, October 2. Leila Maulen Just four months after recording the new material, here it was: available on CD and launched on Friday night with an exuberant live performance at the Cross Street Music Hall. The convivial Brunswick venue was the perfect place to hear this music. The tunes Banks writes – like the rooms at Cross Street – are warm, inviting and innately appealing without trying to impress.



The new album, OxyMoron, celebrates Banks’ renewed passion for playing and performing his own music after navigating various life challenges in recent years, and is imbued with a positive spirit that a live setting amplified. This gig clearly meant a lot to the saxophonist, and every phrase that emerged from his tenor was filled with feeling. His marvellously rich tone magnified the soulful allure of his melodies and added muscular vigour to his solos. Saxophonist Julian Banks has released his first album in a decade. Leila Maulen His bandmates (guitarist Louis King, bassist James Gilligan and drummer Joe Talia) gathered beside rather than behind him, reflecting their role as equal contributors in this enterprise. King’s electric guitar could float in a fuzzy haze or bite into a distortion-laden solo; Gilligan’s semi-acoustic bass guitar was by turns sinuous and insistent; and Talia conjured up languid shuffles and headily propulsive grooves with effortless ease.



Captain Happy skipped nimbly between shifting time signatures, while the album’s title track saw the band veering into crunchy rock territory without losing the sense of warmth or approachability that characterises Banks’ music. Perhaps the night’s most affecting piece was Little Dove – a ballad dedicated to Banks’ young daughter, whose burgeoning love of music helped reignite Banks’ passion for his own, and who sat proudly in the front row at the launch.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas THEATRE

Koreaboo ★★★

Malthouse, until October 10 Inspired by playwright Michelle Lim Davidson’s own experiences and directed by Jessica Arthur, Koreaboo is a two-hander that surveys contentious issues of race, diaspora and belonging, with a light touch. Heather Jeong (left) and Michelle Lim Davidson in a scene from Koreaboo. Gianna Rizzo



Davidson herself plays Hannah, a young Australian who travels to Seoul in an attempt to reconnect with her estranged birth mother, Umma (Heather Jeong). It’s only their second meeting. We learn that although she was born in South Korea, Hannah was adopted as a baby and grew up in Newcastle, NSW. At the start, the two women fail and flail in communication. Hannah was expecting a summer-long stay – a long enough period, perhaps, for meaningful reconnection; Umma (mother in Korean), however, believed it was just going to be a short vacation. The two women in Koreaboo fail and flail in communication. Gianna Rizzo Umma’s behaviour toward her daughter thrums with wariness, as though one were greeting a stranger. Maybe, she suggests, Hannah should be visiting Seoul’s touristy spots instead. The entire performance is staged in a small convenience store run by Umma, lovingly decked out in all manner of brightly coloured snacks, and with harsh fluorescent lighting thanks to designer Mel Page. The two women move within the space as they interrogate, parry and deflect.



Davidson explores a raft of issues, including the question of identity. Hannah’s hyphenated background (Korean-Australian) means she’s part of both cultures and wholly of neither, and at first, Umma’s brusque criticism of Hannah’s language skills feels like a wholesale rejection of her daughter’s “Koreanness”. Seeking both maternal and cultural acceptance, Hannah feels crushed to receive neither. Related Article Performing arts Star of ABC hit The Newsreader mines real-life family drama for new project Their common language – and one that helps them move toward connection and bridge distance, it turns out – is K-pop. The title actually refers to someone who’s not of Korean heritage but who is obsessed with Korean pop culture. Koreaboo swerves to the unexpected and surreal when both performers begin to sing and dance. There is a talent show in the offing to prepare for, and a chance for Hannah to become more Korean. It’s all surface-level cultural appropriation, though, much in the same way that Umma learnt English by watching TV, becoming so familiar with the lives of the characters in Sex and the City that she can quote from them. After a shaky start, Jeong and Davidson become good sparring partners and friends as they navigate the tricky mother-daughter relationship anew after years apart. Umma’s backstory is revealed: the reasons behind Hannah’s adoption and how her yearnings for a singing career were quashed because of filial obedience to her own mother. Korean culture is not just skincare and pop music, but, like a lot of Asian countries, there’s an expectation to conform to parental demands.



Koreaboo packs in a lot during its 90-minute stage time – maybe too much, as there is a lot of jumping about trying to cover a lot of ground. The beginning set-up takes a while to develop and can be tightened, and the ending feels rushed. And although the singing and dance sequences are overextended and as distracting as they are humorous, the play’s value is drawn from highlighting the possible consequences of adopting a child, removing them from their motherland, and raising them in an entirely foreign environment. Even if they embrace the riches of a new life in their host country, there are always losses to be reckoned with.

Reviewed by Thuy On OPERA

The Turn of the Screw ★★★

Palais Theatre, until October 1 Operatic takes on the supernatural span the centuries, but no modern work is more revered and feared than Benjamin Britten’s The Turn of the Screw. The 1954 opera follows a governess who takes up residence at an English country house, only to find the spirits of two dead servants are haunting the children now in her care. From left: Rachelle Durkin, Genevieve Gray and Oliver Thadoe Naing in The Turn of the Screw. Jeff Busby



Finally, an opera where the muffled screams drifting in from Luna Park next door actually add to the drama, rather than detract! This is a piece that has potential to be The Shining-level unnerving. When staged up close and creepy, the eerie singing and sinister spectacle can captivate like a demonic spirit itself. Here, the huge set and vast stage dwarf the drama – in pivotal moments, the singers are far away from each other; we are far away from them. Detachment creates a disconnect that does not serve some excellent performances. Durkin, Michaela Cadwgan and Kanen Breen in The Turn of the Screw. Jeff Busby It is, after all, a chamber opera. Britten scored it for just 13 instruments. Perhaps no Australian conductor knows more about the English composer than Paul Kildea, and the reduced Orchestra Victoria was guided superbly by him. Rachelle Durkin (Governess) was more maternal than hysterical, with a self-assured, impressive vocal performance to match. Kanen Breen’s voice is sharp and cold and uses his lithe physicality to intensify Peter Quint’s menace, despite donning the most unflattering wig anyone’s ever been cursed to wear (it’s a confusing choice, when it’s clearly mentioned how handsome Quint is).



One exceptional discovery to come from this production is soprano Genevieve Gray (currently a university student), who sings the older child, Flora. Gray possesses a vocal evenness and an array of colour that belies her youth. Neither a spook nor a snore, though with moments of satisfaction, this production feels like a missed opportunity to bewitch more people with the mystery and magic of operatic storytelling.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies MUSIC

Lady Blackbird ★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, September 30 It’s been decades since Lady Blackbird – raised in an evangelical Christian household in New Mexico – abandoned her church-music roots, along with the religious doctrines that no longer defined her. Singer Lady Blackbird.



These days, the message underpinning her music is much more personal, but no less spiritually charged. The American singer (born Marley Munroe) has a voice to rival any gospel queen, but it’s now self-empowerment and self-acceptance she champions, rather than submission to an external force. In Melbourne on Wednesday, as part of her debut Australian tour, Lady Blackbird cut a striking figure as she arrived on stage: floor-sweeping black dress, elegant cane and signature platinum afro. Her three-piece band (guitarist Chris Seefried, bassist Jonathan Flaugher and Melbourne drummer Felix Bloxsom) stoked a gritty, distortion-flecked fire around the singer for Pink Floyd’s Mother, then retreated to the shadows for Blackbird, the haunting Nina Simone song that inspired the singer’s stage moniker. Related Article Melbourne live reviews This haunting play celebrates the solidarity and strangeness of found family On Collage, the amped-up fuzz of electric bass and guitar magnified the drama but almost submerged Blackbird’s glorious vocals. Then the mood softened – first with the addition of acoustic bass, then acoustic guitar. This was Blackbird in heartfelt confessional mode, her gorgeously grainy voice brimming with emotion on a clutch of originals: the soulfully swaying Lost and Looking, the jazz-tinted Five Feet Tall and the lilting, folky Man on a Boat. Seefried switched to piano for the wistful If I Told You before ushering in another cloud of psychedelia on a heady rendition of The Beatles’ Come Together. Blackbird’s musical world is unconstrained by genre, and her emotional commitment and authenticity allow her to make each song her own, whether it was written by her or others.



Imaginative arrangements and reharmonisations also allow the audience to hear old songs with fresh ears. In Blackbird’s hands, Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door became a hushed torch song, exquisitely understated. Her spellbinding encore – I Am What I Am – was equally unadorned, stripped of its Broadway sequins to become a quietly defiant affirmation of identity.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Charlton keen to see Satono Glow in clear air for Coolmore audition
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Charlton keen to see Satono Glow in clear air for Coolmore audition Craig Kerry October 8, 2026 — 11:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Tom Charlton has his fingers crossed for better luck with Coolmore Stud Stakes prospect Satono Glow when she races in Sydney for the first time on Saturday since a sickening watch in the Percy Sykes Stakes. Satono Glow has won three of her four starts, including an impressive last-start finish in the group 3 Cap D’Antibes Stakes (1100m) at Flemington on September 12, and steps out in the group 2 Roman Consul Stakes (1200m) on Saturday at Rosehill. Satono Glow winning the Cap D’antibes Stakes at Flemington on September 12. Getty Images The first-up victory attracted interest from an Everest slot-holder but Charlton, co-trainer John O’Shea and connections chose to keep the filly on track to the group 1 Coolmore (1200m) at Flemington on October 31. “There was a call about her, but we didn’t want to do that,” Charlton said.



“We were toying between the Danehill or this race, but ultimately we just preferred her preparation be in Sydney before a potential tilt at the Coolmore.” Satono Glow, a $NZ260,000 buy at the 2025 Karaka Sale, won on debut at Warwick Farm before a three-length demolition job in the group 3 Thoroughbred Breeders Stakes at Flemington. She then started a $5 hope in the group 2 Percy Sykes Stakes (1200m) at Randwick, where she looked set to unleash behind a wall of runners for most of the home straight before seeing clear air late to finish fourth. Zac Lloyd has the ride again on Saturday, after Jamie Melham was aboard for the Flemington wins. “Unfortunately, it didn’t go our way, but we are happy with her anyway,” Charlton said of the Percy Sykes. “Last start, it probably didn’t surprise us but the manner of her win, we thought it was a strong enough race on paper, but the way she won was impressive, and it was encouraging.”



Satono Glow was into gate nine of 12 with the scratchings of Hostwin King and Omolong on Thursday and was challenging for favouritism at $2.90 (TAB) with Bjorn Baker-trained Paradoxium ($2.60), which is coming off his own 1100m group 3 straight track win at Flemington, in the Poseidon Stakes. Charlton and O’Shea also have Peyton ($41) in the Roman Consul. The Zoustar colt won a Gosford maiden first-up on August 28 but was then scratched at the barriers at Warwick Farm. In his first preparation he had placings behind subsequent Golden Rose placegetters Under Focus and St Gotthard. Kerrin McEvoy has the ride from barrier seven. Charlton said the group 3 Red Anchor Stakes (1200m) at Flemington on October 24 could be a target after Saturday. “He unfortunately just missed a run the other day when he played up in the barriers, so he probably hasn’t had the ideal preparation going into this race, but it’s important he has a run before maybe stepping towards another stakes race later in the carnival,” Charlton said. “His form as a two-year-old was excellent, behind Next Episode, Under Focus and St Gotthard, so he’s going really well.”



The stable has King Pedro ($15) in the feature $2 million Hill Stakes (1900m) after initially nominating four. Mister Rizz and Starzintheireyes will instead run in race three, while Klondike was saved for the St Leger Stakes. King Pedro, also with McEvoy to ride, announced himself as a potential Melbourne Cup horse after winning the Stayers and Grafton Cup in the winter. However, the five-year-old import was now likely to have a short spring and be aimed at the Sydney Cup in the autumn after illness delayed his return. Kerrin Mcevoy and King Pedro win the Stayers Cup at Rosehill in June. Getty Images “It hasn’t been the ideal prep for him,” Charlton said. “He was meant to go towards the Metropolitan and the cups in Melbourne, but he just got sick at the wrong time and missed the boat.



“He’s just been a bit behind, but he resumes on Saturday and we’re very happy with him. “It’s short of his best and in a significantly harder grade than he’s been contesting, but I’m sure he can run a good race.” In the $1.5 million Alan Brown Stakes (1400m), Charlton is confident Linebacker can challenge if given a better set-up, after he returned with a one and half-length fourth in the Bill Ritchie Handicap last start. The group 1 winner, heading towards the Five Diamonds, was an equal $6.50 favourite from gate 10. “He was very good the other day,” Charlton said. Trainer Tom Charlton and jockey Zac Lloyd. Getty Images



“It was slowly run race. He definitely wasn’t suited. I believe he was the only horse to run home in sub-33 [seconds for the last 600m], so that was a good effort. He’s certainly not 100 per cent just yet, but he’s going well enough to run a really good race.” Former Tulloch Lodge mare Agarwood, $11 for the group 3 Nivison, is chasing a breakthrough victory after a solid but winless first campaign for the O’Shea-Charlton yard. “She’s been running really well and she’s physically come on again, so we are really hopeful she might be able to make this grade this preparation,” Charlton said. “It’s obviously a strong race on Saturday, but we’re trying to get her a breakthrough at stakes level and she’s been pretty close.”

World.title: NZ Rugby seeks High Court injunction to block PNG Chiefs name
World.content:
The simmering trademark dispute between New Zealand Rugby and Papua New Guinea's incoming NRL franchise has erupted into a legal battle after NZR filed a High Court injunction to stop the new club from using the Chiefs name.

In a statement released on Thursday, NZR said it is seeking both an interim and final injunction which stops the use of the names "PNG Chiefs", "Chiefs" or any other similar names in New Zealand.

The move represents a major escalation in the dispute and threatens to disrupt the PNG club's plans to formally unveil their inaugural jersey and branding in Port Moresby on October 21 - less than two weeks away.

The PNG team, which is set to join the NRL in 2028 as the competition's 19th franchise, is backed by a $600 million Australian government funding package. The Chiefs Super Rugby club have argued that allowing another professional sporting franchise to use the same name in the same trans-Tasman market risks undermining a brand it has spent three decades building.

NZR chief executive officer Steve Lancaster said for 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an "incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans".

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific. We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."

Lancaster added that since October 2025, when the expansion side's name was confirmed, NZR has shared its concerns with the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) and has sought to engage them to agree a positive outcome.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans. We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand," he said.

The Waikato side has used the Chiefs name since 1996 and holds registered trademarks covering its logo in New Zealand and internationally, including Australia.

The Super Rugby club's position appears to be backed by IP Australia, which has reportedly raised repeated concerns about the PNG's club's attempts to secure trademark protection for its name.

The ABC last week reported the NRL has received three adverse reports in response to the PNG club's trademark applications, with IP Australia declaring there is a "real and tangible danger" of brand confusion.

An adverse report from IP Australia is a formal notice identifying issues with a trademark application that need addressing before it can be accepted.

The choice of the Chiefs name has particular significance in PNG.

Prime Minister James Marape announced the name last year after a public process, saying the word reflected the country's history, with chiefs - both men and women - having played an important role in communities across the nation's many tribes.

Chiefs CEO Simon Graafhuis said the 'Chiefs' identity also carries significant cultural meaning and connection the Waikato and Bay of Plenty regions.

"We know it means a great deal to our players and coaches past and present, fans and supporters here and around the world," he said.

World.title: Indefinite ban on taking sea life from large parts of Auckland and Coromandel coastlines
World.content:
The government has indefinitely banned taking some sea life from large parts of the Auckland and Coromandel coastlines.

The ban followed a review of intertidal species in the two regions, prompted by community tensions over harvesting from rockpools.

Fisheries Minister Shane Jones earlier placed a two-year ban on harvesting from intertidal areas in the northern Hauraki Gulf.

On Thursday, he said harvesting for a large range of marine invertebrates would be banned on Auckland's east and west coasts, Waiheke Island, and Coromandel.

Certain species, including cockles, crabs, kina and pīpī, were excluded from the ban.

Jones said while he was reluctant to close coastlines, it was necessary to protect a broad range of species that were vulnerable to overharvesting.

"Fossicking in a rockpool is a Kiwi tradition. It's a pastime that's been enjoyed by generations of New Zealanders. However, it's being exploited by a selfish few who are taking far too much kaimoana. This behaviour is endangering these fragile ecosystems and putting at risk our beloved coastal areas."

Harvesting in the intertidal zone on beaches, rocky shores and rockpools, the area in and around where the tide comes in and goes out, would be heavily limited with exceptions in place for only certain species that could be taken sustainably, he said.

A 2m depth limit would be used to define the area, meaning areas that were accessible at low tide would be covered by the ban.

New daily limits would also apply outside of intertidal zones, he said.

The changes would be in place until revoked by the Oceans and Fisheries Minister, with continual monitoring and review to determine their impact and whether further measures were needed.

Jones said people needed to accept that the Auckland-Coromandel area was facing a steep decline in sea life.

"It has taken me a while personally, on a journey as the Minister. Given my background in the far north, I regard the ability to interact with the marine environment as a key birthright feature.

"How do we move forward and manage the Hauraki Gulf and enable the legacy interests of Kiwis like my good self who grew up fossicking, beachcombing, and tutū-ing around in the marine environment?"

He said he had faced "significant pressure" from Aucklanders and taken professional advice from the fisheries scientists.

"As the population expands, local residents have witnessed the reduction in the quality of their marine environment through excessive harvesting in rock pools in what we call the intertidal zone.

"I hope that these restrictions give you some confidence that we can, by working together, afford better protections and safeguards for those things that perhaps we've taken for granted as Kiwis.

"It is a significant step forward in an area that's been very highly politicised."

He said protections across the rest of the country were something to be considered.

"I've just come back from Taranaki and Mahara Okeroa, their Kaumātua, a former MP from Helen Clark's government. They are desperate to have their rāhui extended because they too are seeing egregious cases of organised groups going down there and ransacking the Reef Pāua.

World.title: Man found dead in Northland's Dargaville, homicide investigation launched
World.content:
A man has been found dead in a Dargaville house on Wednesday afternoon.

Police said they are launching a homicide investigation after being called to Hoeroa St at 2.40pm to find the man dead.

Detective Senior Sergeant Shane Pilmer, said an investigation is now in the early stages to determine the full circumstances around the death.

"A scene guard has been established and will remain in place while a scene examination is conducted.

"A post-mortem examination and formal identification of the victim will be carried out over the coming days."

Pilmer said people can expect to see more police presence in the area.

"We know this incident will be unsettling for the community.

"Police want to reassure residents that a dedicated team of investigators is working to establish exactly what happened and who is involved."

World.title: Who is right about Investment Boost? We're still not sure
World.content:
Audio player for " Can my landlord put a political billboard on my home? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1792519%2Fwho-is-right-about-investment-boost-we-re-still-not-sure

Can my landlord put a political billboard on my home? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 9m

When it comes to the savings that Labour can make by cancelling Investment Boost, who is right?

Labour said it will save $7.7 billion if it cancels the policy, which allow businesses to claim an immediate 20 percent tax deduction on the cost of qualifying new assets.

But Finance Minister Nicola Willis said the cost of Investment Boost is actually only $5.5 billion over the forecast period - leaving a gap of $2.2 billion.

But does it?

Even the experts say it is a bit confusing.

Dentons partner Bruce Bernacchi said he had not seen the modelling behind it, but Willis's explanation made sense.

"The way Investment Boost works is, let's say you buy an asset for $100, you get to write off 20 percent upfront and then you bring its cost down to $80 and then you depreciate that remaining $80 over the life of the asset.

"You're not getting an extra tax write-off, you're just accelerating it. I think what the government is saying is you get this extra 20 percent but then your tax depreciation in later years is reduced because you've already taken that 20 upfront.

So they're saying the $5.5 billion is the net cost over the forecast period. That to me intuitively makes sense. You've got this upfront 20 percent but then you have reduced deductions in alter years."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said it was hard to judge without seeing the parties' workings.

"The start date of repeal and what is clawed back matter a lot. National is quoting the cost of keeping the scheme while Labour is quoting the revenue from stopping it.

"The scheme's cost falls over time because assets already bought get smaller deductions later, and that claw-back continues after a repeal. So repeal should raise more than the scheme's ongoing net cost."

An economist who did not want to be quoted said he could not make head nor tail of the argument. He said one view of Investment Boost was that it had no permanent effect on the fiscal position at all because it was only a timing issue of when depreciation occurred.

Another tax expert said it was hard to say without seeing the calculations.

"I think Labour would need to provide some more concrete explanation here as it's difficult to unpick it ... They gave a fiscal cost but also had a counter $2.6b increase in tax revenue, from a combination of economic growth and lower depreciation in future years."

World.title: US designates prominent Fiji businessman for advancing 'China-based interests'
World.content:
The United States has designated a prominent Chinese businessman in Fiji for "significant corruption" on behalf of China-based actors.

Zhao Fugang, owner of the Yue Lai Hotel in Suva and the Overseas Chinese Service Center located within it, is alleged to be a senior member of a syndicate involved in drug smuggling, money laundering, and human trafficking, according to the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP).

In a statement on Wednesday (Thursday NZ time), the US State Department said Zhao actively pays bribes to Fijian citizens to "advance China-based government, business, and criminal interests".

"His actions constituted significant corruption and adversely affected US interests in Fiji," the statement read.

The designation renders Zhao and his immediate family ineligible for entry into the US.

An OCCRP investigation in 2024 revealed that the hotelier has been in the crosshairs of Australian and other Western intelligence agencies since mid-2023.

It said his business interests stretch from tourism to property development, and his personal relationships have extended as high as former Prime Minister Frank Bainimarama.

Zhao has stayed silent on those allegations.

He has established himself as a prominent figure in Fiji's social scene, often seen at Chinese cultural and celebratory events alongside key government figures - both during the Bainimarama era and under the current administration.

RNZ Pacific has reached out to Zhao via his hotel for comment. RNZ Pacific has also requested comments from the Chinese Embassy in Fiji and the Chinese Association of Fiji.

World.title: Pacific losses go far beyond money, climate champion tells regional symposium
World.content:
The Pacific political champion for loss and damage has told a Pacific symposium that the region losses from climate impacts go far beyond money.

Tonga's Hu'akavameiliku Siaosi Sovaleni said non-economic losses and damages from the climate crisis must be recognised in policy and finance.

He was speaking at the Pacific Symposium on Loss and Damage, which is part of the pre-COP31 meeting currently being held in Nadi. Pacific leaders and climate experts have gathered to discuss Pacific priorities head of the annual UN climate talks next month.

Hu'akavameiliku, who is a former Tonga prime minister, said Pacific losses go well beyond what can be measured, in money, culture, identity, heritage, biodiversity, health and community connections.

He said that traditional knowledge must be explicitly recognised in loss and damage policy and finance.

"These losses are largely undercounted," he told the symposium.

He shared the five key Pacific messages, which are:

Pacific losses go far beyond money, and non-economic losses and damages must be recognized in policy and finance.

Recognition is not enough. Finance must be accessible, adequate, predictable, grant-based, and reach the communities without adding to national debt.

Our losses, our solutions, indigenous and traditional knowledge and responses must be locally led.

A single methodology cannot capture all Pacific losses. Flexible and locally grounded methods are needed, consistent enough to build a credible shared regional evidence base through the Pacific Loss and Damage Outlook.

Ambitious climate action remains fundamental and keeping 1.5 degrees Celsius within reach is the best solution to prevent loss.

Hu'akavameiliku said what many do not see hardly receives any financial support, which affects the whole climate resilience cycle.

"What is not counted is rarely financed," he said. "That is why evidence is the foundation of our case for action and for finance."

Hu'akavameiliku pointed to the El Niño drought now affecting his own island nation, which last month triggered a fifth payout to Tonga from the Pacific Catastrophe Risk Insurance Company (PCRIC), as an example of a Pacific-owned system delivering early money for early action.

He stressed that insurance is not enough, as some impacts lie beyond what can be avoided, adapted to or insured.

The Fund responding to Loss and Damage received 176 funding requests from 119 countries amounted to US$2.8 billion.

That is more than 11 times what the Fund has available.

"Responding to loss and damage is not a charity," he said.

"The advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice, which our region fought for, confirmed that States have binding obligations on climate change and breaching them has legal consequences.

"This is a matter of climate justice."

Hu'akavameiliku requested donors and partners that Pacific countries rally around these five key messages as one regional voice.

Two people have been injured in a traffic incident in Auckland's Mt Albert

World.title: Arrest made following South Auckland kindergarten break-ins
World.content:
A man has been arrested after a string of break-ins at kindergartens and childcare centres in South Auckland.

Police said they've had six reports of break-ins across Papatoetoe and Ōtāhuhu over September and October. Electronics and cash were among the items stolen, they said.

Counties Manukau West area commander Inspector Dave Christoffersen said forensic results from two of the scenes help them identify a suspect.

"With a consistent pattern to the offending, investigators believed a single offender was responsible for the series of break-ins," he said.

Police were also able to track a stolen device from one of the centres to an address in Ōtāhuhu. Officers arrested a 22-year-old man at a house on Hutton Street. He has been charged with six counts of burglary.

World.title: Adelaide 36ers coach claims he was 'targeted' by refs in United loss
World.content:
Adelaide 36ers coach Trevor Gleeson says he was "targeted" by NBL referees in his side's 96-91 Ignite Cup loss to Melbourne United on Wednesday night.

Gleeson was left flabbergasted after being whistled for a technical foul by referee James Griguol during the second quarter of the 36ers' third straight defeat.

Griguol made the call from the opposite corner of the court at the Adelaide Entertainment Centre.

"I was talking to one referee [Andrew Goodman], because Whitey [36ers guard Isaac White] got a backhand right in the face," Gleeson said.

"The other referee on the other side of the floor gives me a technical foul, when I'm having a conversation with [Goodman].

"I think I was targeted for that today."

Gleeson was also frustrated by an incident in the third quarter.

With 7:17 left in the term, Gleeson requested to challenge an offensive foul against centre Nick Rakocevic, who scored while colliding with Melbourne's Fabijan Krslovic.

After a lengthy delay, Gleeson was told the decision would stand and the replay centre would not entertain his challenge.

"They already reviewed it [Rakocevic's foul] and you can't challenge a review," Gleeson said.

"No-one told me.

"I'll talk to [NBL head of referees] Scott Butler and say, 'Why?', and send him [video] clips again."

A 23-16 disparity in free-throw attempts, favouring Melbourne, also earned Gleeson's ire.

That was on the back of a similar 23-14 differential in foul shots favouring the New Zealand Breakers in the 36ers' blowout 88-72 home loss on Sunday.

"It's frustrating when the opposition team comes here and they shoot more free throws than us both times," Gleeson said.

"The guys deserve more than that.

"Coming back [to the NBL] after five years, I would have thought the referees would really go in front.

"I've got a good relationship with Scott [Butler], but it just seems that when the bright lights come on, something else happens."

The 36ers' loss leaves the club second last on the NBL ladder.

World.title: LIV Golf loses star over 'unacceptable' terms
World.content:
Former world number one Jon Rahm is quitting LIV Golf, robbing the breakaway circuit of one of its biggest stars while it fights to emerge from bankruptcy.

Rahm's attorney John Beck, speaking at a hearing in the US Bankruptcy Court of New Jersey, said the two-time major champion made his decision after looking over details of LIV Golf's planned next phase.

"Mr Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0, as ‌the parties have been referring to it, and has determined that those terms are unacceptable as to him, and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0," Beck told the court.

Other golfers asked a ‌US bankruptcy judge to help terminate their contracts and clarify their ability to negotiate with ⁠other tournament organisers and sponsors as their LIV contracts go unpaid.

LIV has ‌already agreed to terminate Sergio Garcia's contract after determining the ‌league would not honour its terms.

LIV Golf files for bankruptcy LIV Golf files for bankruptcy, flagging a restructure with a massive loan from the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia.

Attorneys for Bryson DeChambeau, Cameron Smith, An Byeong-hun, Marc Leishman, Cameron Tringale and Matthew Wolff asked the judge to allow those players out of their old contracts.

Ending those contracts would not preclude those players from agreeing to participate in LIV 2.0.

Rahm, one ‌of the most high-profile players to ‌join LIV Golf, has won three consecutive season-long individual titles since joining the circuit in late ‌2023.

When LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 protection in New Jersey last month, its filing ‌listed several star golfers as creditors ⁠still owed millions in unsecured claims.

Among them, Rahm had the largest claim among players at $US7.5 million ($10.8 million).

Earlier this week, LIV secured funding from BC Partners to help it emerge from restructuring and strengthen its financial footing ahead of the 2027 season.

The financing, ⁠up to $US300 million ($430 million), remains subject to bankruptcy court approval and customary conditions.

Reuters

World.title: Major Australian gambling companies face restrictions if NT bill passes
World.content:
Some of Australia's largest gambling companies would be forced to implement deposit caps for people aged 18 to 24 if a private member's bill passes the Northern Territory parliament.

Fifty online bookmakers are licensed in the NT, including Sportsbet, Ladbrokes and Bet365, and independent MLA Justine Davis's bill would see a string of new laws imposed upon them if passed, including the deposit caps.

The NT's gambling regulator is Australia's de facto watchdog for online bookmakers, due to the abundance of companies that choose to be licensed in the Territory because of its low taxes.

It means those companies and their national customers would be impacted by the proposed NT laws if they pass.

Justine Davis says the federal governments's recent gambling reforms do not go far enough. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Under the proposed changes, monthly deposits for punters aged 18 to 21 would be limited to $500, and to $1,000 for those aged 22 to 24.

Ms Davis's bill also seeks to place an outright ban on inducements, such as bonus bets and VIP schemes, after the Albanese government legislated inducement restrictions in recent federal reforms.

If the bill passes, it would also place a "positive duty" on NT-licensed bookmarkers, requiring them to take "all reasonable steps to prevent harm to customers".

The maximum disciplinary penalty that could be imposed on bookmakers by the NT regulator would also be increased from $194,000 to $10 million, or 10 per cent of annual revenue.

An NT body serves as the de facto regulator for Australia's online gambling industry, with 50 bookmakers licensed in the Territory. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

Ms Davis said the federal government's reforms did not go far enough and therefore the NT needed to act.

"So we now are in a real position where we can actually show some leadership in the Northern Territory and say, 'Here's some simple changes that we can make,'" she said.

" The changes are not going to stop gambling, but they are going to prevent harm being done to people, both here in the Territory and across Australia. "

A letter urging the NT government to support Ms Davis's bill has been signed by 33 advocacy organisations and leaders, including several federal MPs including independent Andrew Wilkie.

Andrew Wilkie says the proposed reforms would make the NT a "national leader" in gambling policy. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr Wilkie said Ms Davis's bill "attempted to do what the federal government has so far failed to do".

"It genuinely will go some considerable way to doing the federal government's job and it would put the Territory front and centre with reform that would trickle through the rest of the country," he said.

" It would make the Territory a national leader in this space. "

Bill aims to reform de facto regulator

A 2023 online gambling inquiry led by late Labor MP Peta Murphy recommended the federal government ban inducements without delay and implement comprehensive bans on gambling advertising within three years.

Peta Murphy was a leading figure in a parliamentary inquiry into online gambling before her death at the age of 50. (ABC News)

The Albanese government's reforms, passed in August this year, subsequently put an onus on bookmakers to stop sending inducements to customers who showed signs of problem gambling.

A national ban on advertising during sports broadcasts until 8:30pm, and throughout children's programs, was also included in the federal changes.

Labor and Coalition close in on deal on gambling reforms Labor and the Coalition agree to establish a single register that would allow Australians to opt out of wagering ads across online platforms, as part of a tentative deal to pass gambling reforms.

Ms Davis's bill seeks to ban s that are "likely to be available to children".

The 2023 inquiry also recommended a national gambling regulator be established, to take responsibility away from the Territory's regulator, the part-time NT Wagering Commission (NTWC).

In lieu of a national regulator, Ms Davis's bill would introduce more rigorous conflict-of-interest regulations for members of the NTWC, including the establishment of a public register of declared conflicts.

The building in Darwin where the NT Wagering Commission has its offices. (Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan)

It would also prohibit commission members from accepting gifts from bookmakers, after the regulator's chair previously admitted he had accepted corporate hospitality.

The NT government passed its own laws earlier this year which prohibit NTWC commissioners from owning race horses or holding betting accounts with NT-licensed bookmakers.

An annual tax cap for NT-licensed gambling companies was also doubled by the government, from $1.5 million to $3 million.

'How much misery are we going to allow?'

Gambler-in-recovery Shiva Panchalingam, 37, is another supporter of Ms Davis's bill.

In addiction from age 18 to 24, Mr Panchalingam said he gambled in casinos and with online bookmakers until time in a Sydney rehabilitation centre "saved" him.

Shiva Panchalingam previously lost his whole life savings to gambling addiction. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"I was going to put gambling before everything I loved — my family, my friends," Mr Panchalingam said.

"I was doing a degree that I really enjoyed — I had a pretty good life, and very quickly I was willing to sacrifice that all, hurt people I love.

" The hard part is, people don't understand what that's like. "

Mr Panchalingam said he had since relapsed multiple times, with online betting "always triggering it off" because it was "so easy to access".

During one relapse, after moving from Sydney to Darwin eight years ago, Mr Panchalingam said he lost his whole life savings at the time — $30,000 — in just two weeks, with no support network around him.

If you or anyone you know needs help: National Gambling Helpline on 1800 858 858

Lifeline on 13 11 14

Kids Helpline on 1800 551 800

MensLine Australia on 1300 789 978

Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467

Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636

Headspace on 1800 650 890

"People put on thousands of dollars in betting and there's no duty of care to see if they're actually able to do it," he said.

Mr Panchalingam has since set up a support group run by people in recovery, and said he was now able to build his life rather than feeling "like he is just surviving".

"One of the flip sides of going through what I did is I'm really grateful and appreciative of what I have," he said.

Shiva Panchalingam says multiple people in Darwin in the midst of gambling addiction have died by suicide in the past few years. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

But he said others had not been so fortunate, and urged NT politicians to vote for Ms Davis's bill.

"In two-and-a-half years, there's been multiple people in Darwin who have died by suicide as a result of the gambling," Mr Panchalingam said.

"How much misery are we going to allow?

" You're allowing an Australian and Territorian to be miserable, so that someone else can make a lot of money off them. "

Ms Davis is scheduled to introduce her bill in parliament next Wednesday.

NT Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby said the government would "consider all sensible proposals on their merits".

"But let me be clear: while we encourage all people to gamble responsibly, you can't legislate personal responsibility," she said.

Ms Davis said she had been told by Shadow Racing Minister Chansey Paech that Labor would support the bill, and backbencher Dheran Young said in a social media post that Labor was "proud to support" it.

However, Deputy Opposition Leader Ed Smelt said Labor wanted the bill to be referred to the NT Legislative Scrutiny Committee.

World.title: CA 'actively' looking at women's schedule as Aussie stars raise concerns
World.content:
Cricket Australia (CA) says it will attempt to bring the national women's side back into the peak of summer, after officials met with frustrated senior players.

Multiple players have raised concerns over the women's schedule in recent weeks, which includes four straight years of no home internationals or WBBL during school holidays.

Ellyse Perry and Beth Mooney have also highlighted fears it will stunt the growth of junior cricket.

Australia plays Bangladesh and New Zealand in three one-day internationals (ODIs) and T20s respectively over the next fortnight.

A home ODI series against New Zealand is scheduled for March.

Concerns over summer gap for women's cricket Concerns are growing about the lack of women's cricket in school-friendly slots over summer, amid warnings the schedule will hurt the game's growth among girls.

Among the concerns of players is a lack of consistency in their schedule to build up crowds, along with games on school nights that families largely will not attend.

The issue was raised at a function on Monday night in Brisbane to recognise the Australian team's T20 World Cup win.

"We're looking at that actively," CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said.

"[Head of cricket] James Allsopp led the conversation with the Australian women's team about this exact issue, so we're talking, we've got dialogue with them.

"We would love to see more cricket played in this window. We have to understand the global components … but we've got to get more cricket into our summer."

Greenberg's comments come after Mooney was particularly critical of the current schedule.

"We're in a bad time slot and it's a bad time of year for parents," Mooney said earlier this week.

"They're not dragging their kid out to watch a 7pm T20 on a Tuesday night or whatever it is.

"We're not getting crowds, it's not marketed well. There is no big-ticket item where people go, 'the Australian women's team play here at this time every year'.

"We want to be relatable athletes. And if we're not front and centre of the summer, it makes it pretty difficult when it's meant to be a summer sport."

AAP

World.title: Aussies hit back at ex-players in build-up to first South Africa Test
World.content:
Travis Head has accused former Australian players of levelling unfair criticism at the current Test squad, saying the game has changed significantly since they played.

Just a day after Matthew Hayden slammed selectors and accused them of promoting "the greatest pile of mediocrity" for calling up Nic Maddinson, Head took his own stand in South Africa.

Australia's vice-captain refused to name particular ex-players or comments, but took issue with commentary about the team's batting at a time when averages have dropped worldwide.

Stats show Test runs drying up Test batters are averaging less, scoring more quickly and getting out more often — and we have the charts to prove it.

Head noted the current side had been through a "sticky situation" with the group of past players, in a clear nod to Justin Langer's dramatic exit as coach in 2022.

"I think [we're] unfairly judged a fair bit from a group of past players … that put the bullet through a lot of players," he said ahead of the first Test against South Africa in Durban.

"But that's what they're paid to do. Some of them need a job, so they go after us, and that's totally fine.

"This group is strong enough to deal with those sort of things. That's how it is.

"It's unfortunate, sometimes, to have some of that feedback from a generation of players that we have huge respect for, but that's the caper."

The suggestion of a generational split between Australia's two best eras of the past 50 years has long bubbled away.

This was particularly the case following Langer's exit after his side's 2021/22 Ashes win, when he rejected a contract offer of only six months.

"They're [ex-players] a very proud bunch of guys," Head said.

"We went through a bit of a sticky situation a few years ago where they stood up and were pretty proud about one of their own (Langer).

"But in saying that …we play for the same cause. We have huge respect for it.

How Sandpapergate rocked Australian cricket In 2018, Sandpapergate rocked Australian cricket to its very core. Here's how a febrile atmosphere colluded with a team persistently testing the limits of acceptability to change the game.

"It's always a balancing act with … what they say and how you take it."

Test batting averages have dropped by close to 20 per cent from the end of the 2010s, while the Sheffield Shield has witnessed a similar downturn since the mid-2000s.

While critics have pointed to the drop in averages coinciding with the rise of T20 cricket, Head pointed to conditions as a major factor.

"It's pretty obvious to see what the wickets were like back then to now," Head said.

"We have huge respect for what's come before us, but it's a completely different game.

"Sometimes it's commented around unfairly on some of the wickets that teams have played on, whether that be Sheffield Shield or Test cricket.

"We've seen games go quicker than ever. We've got a lot of stats that suggest that the ball's doing a lot more."

AAP

The most famous race on the Supercars calendar is here, with thousands of fans flocking to Mount Panorama in regional New South Wales for the Bathurst 1000.

Fifty-four drivers across 27 cars will battle over the 1,000-kilometre endurance race in an event that always produces drama.

Here is what you need to know about this weekend's Bathurst 1000, including when the race begins and how you can follow the action.

When is the Bathurst 1000?

The Great Race will be held this Sunday, October 11, at Mount Panorama in Bathurst.

There will be four days of action culminating in the 1,000km race on Sunday.

Here is when each of the key sessions begins in your state or territory.

Brodie Kostecki hunting Bathurst pole record Supercars star Brodie Kostecki can surpass Australian motor racing legends Peter Brock and Allan Moffat with a Bathurst record this weekend, but will do it without the support of his engineer.

In Australia, you can watch the race on both free-to-air and pay television, as well as streaming platforms.

The Seven Network is the free-to-air broadcaster, and you can watch it on Channel 7 or via the online streaming platform 7plus.

Foxtel and its streaming platform Kayo will also be broadcasting the race. On Foxtel, the race will be shown on Fox Sports channel 506.

What weather is forecast for the Bathurst 1000?

Sunday is set to be sunny at Bathurst, but rain threatens to cause chaos at Mount Panorama on Saturday. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Rain affected last year's Bathurst 1000, leading to a wild and thrilling finale at Mount Panorama.

For now, the 2026 drivers can breathe a sigh of relief based on the current forecast.

Sunday at Mount Panorama is expected to be sunny, with a maximum temperature of 26 degrees Celsius.

Matt Payne and Garth Tander won an extraordinary edition of the Bathurst 1000 in 2025, despite crossing the line second.
