Here are today’s Connections hints and answers for NYT Connections No. 1215 on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Today’s Connections puzzle has an especially goofy purple category. Movie fans might do better than most, but you’re still going to have to hunt for words buried inside other words. We’ll give you a hint for each color group first, then reveal today’s Connections answers further down.

Today’s Connections hints

Here are four hints for the groupings in today’s Connections puzzle, ranked from the easiest yellow group to the tough (and sometimes bizarre) purple group.

Yellow group hint: Obey the instructions.

Green group hint: I’m better than you.

Blue group hint: Group of more than two, less than four.

Purple group hint: Hunt inside the words for surnames of actors.



Today’s Connections answers

Yellow group: Follows, as rules.

Green group: Outdo.

Blue group: Things that come in threes.

Purple group: Ending in actors named Tom.

CNET publishes daily answers and hints for The New York Times Mini Crossword, Connections, Connections: Sports Edition and Strands puzzles.

What are today’s Connections answers?

The completed NYT Connections puzzle for Oct. 8, 2026. NYT/Screenshot by CNET

The yellow words in today’s Connections

The theme is follows, as rules.

The four answers are heeds, minds, regards and respects.

The green words in today’s Connections

The theme is outdo.

The four answers are best, eclipse, surpass and top.

The blue words in today’s Connections

The theme is things that come in threes.

The four answers are cheers, stooges, strikes and wishes.

The purple words in today’s Connections

The theme is ending in actors named Tom.

The four answers are autocruise (Cruise), foolhardy (Hardy), Mullholland (Holland) and thanks (Hanks).

How to play Connections

In Connections, you look at a grid of 16 words and pick four words that have a connection to one other. You do this four times until all 16 words in the puzzle are grouped. The tough part is that Times puzzle editor Wyna Liu chooses words that could fit in multiple groups. The obvious guess — Hey, those are four animals! — is almost always going to be wrong. I’ve compiled my favorite tips for Connections if you need a boost.

The Times has a Connections Bot, like the one for Wordle. Go there after you play to receive a numeric score and to have the program analyze your answers. Players who are registered with the Times Games section can nerd out by following their progress, including the number of puzzles completed, win rate, number of times they nabbed a perfect score and their win streak.

Tech.title: Is It Even Worth Buying Tech During Early Holiday Sales? Here’s What We Recommend
Tech.content:
Early holiday sales are here, but so are bills.

The holidays have never been merciful when it comes to balancing everyday expenses, so juggling your necessities during a busy (and expensive) shopping season can be tough. There’s a glimpse of that in CNET’s latest holiday survey. This time last year, holiday spending for tech products and services was higher, with the average US adult spending $931. Now, that budget has shrunk to $808, a $123 dip from last year’s survey findings.

But there have been so many new releases this year, like Apple’s AirPods 5, the highly anticipated Legend of Zelda-themed Switch 2 console, and even Apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. We can’t all comfortably fit new devices into smaller holiday budgets. The real question is, who’s to blame for me saying, “Bah humbug!” when I start my holiday shopping — the economy or tech brands?

More from CNET

What’s causing lower holiday tech budgets this year?

Let’s be real, we’re juggling a lot financially. There are higher prices on everything from everyday goods to gas and utilities. Covering necessary expenses doesn’t leave much room to pay for new personal tech that costs hundreds, even thousands, for some devices like the iPhone Duo or the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

But why are US adults spending less on tech when so many new devices were released this year? CNET Senior Editor Adam Oram, an expert deal hunter, says tech is becoming unaffordable, and we’re dealing with higher everyday living costs. We’re having to be more mindful about how we spend our money — and some new tech simply isn’t worth it.

Think about the rising cost of tech products, but the lack of innovation. For example, if you have the iPhone 17 Pro, there aren’t many differences from the iPhone 18 Pro that justify the cost to upgrade. What’s more, even if you’re considering existing tech products, you’re seeing price increases due to the RAM shortage, which has driven up hardware and service costs around the world.

“That means people are perhaps keeping their phone for an extra year or persevering with a laptop for a little longer, rather than jumping on the next shiny thing,” Oram says. It also could mean nonessential tech purchases fall into the luxury bucket, which may have less cash in it than before. And since many paychecks aren’t stretching as far, that doesn’t leave much discretionary money to splurge on nonessential items, such as upgrading your smartphone.

Is it still worth shopping for tech right now?

The answer depends. If your holiday budget is tighter this year, you may be hoping that sales can help you buy the tech you want. However, don’t expect retailers to slash tech prices as much this year, Oram says. For all the reasons listed above, don’t expect big savings, like half off the original price, during early holiday sales, especially for newer device models.

“In previous years, holiday sales have made for a great time to upgrade big-ticket tech items, but with rising component costs, these deals might not be as staggering this year as in the past,” he says. “That said, if you have a busted TV, laptop or tablet that needs replacing, those items should still top your list as they rarely go on sale for less than around the holidays.”

You may still be able to find deals at different retailers throughout the month of October, depending on the brand, retailer and model of the device you’re looking for. Oram adds that you can expect plenty of deals on items that will likely fall into most people’s “nice-to-have” list, such as smart home and kitchen gadgets. It’s also a good time to stock up on presents and spread the overall cost over the next few months rather than shopping at the last minute.

On the other hand, if you don’t need to replace a device right away, it may be worthwhile to just wait a few more months.

“Waiting for the hype around new product launches to die down can lead to scoring a better deal,” Oram says, “especially for things like phones, where carriers begin incentivizing upgrades by offering solid discounts after the initial buzz.”

For now, Oram doesn’t expect prices to drop significantly on tech, so think about whether you need to upgrade versus just wanting to. If you’re planning to upgrade, cover the needs first, and the wants after, if you can afford to.

Tech.title: ChatGPT for Teens Is an ‘Unacceptable Risk,’ Watchdog Group Says
Tech.content:
Big Tech has a lousy track record when it comes to showing it can protect children’s mental health, despite lofty promises. OpenAI’s ChatGPT for Teens is not doing much to allay parents’ fears, according to a new study from Common Sense Media.

The nonprofit organization, which rates and reviews media and technology geared for children, said that ChatGPT for Teens — launched less than two months ago — fails to deliver on several of its objectives and is an “unacceptable risk” for everyone under 18.

Common Sense Media’s research found that the chatbot’s parental alerts system did not send notifications when testers discussed suicidal thoughts, self-harm or eating disorders. The chatbot also failed to issue several crisis referrals to testers for various mental health conditions.

More from CNET

ChatGPT for Teens — the most-used chatbot for teens — also didn’t keep “teens engaged in an active and collaborative learning process,” as OpenAI boasted about the feature. Testers were able to bypass the Study mode’s tutoring process and select the “Show me the answer” option for quick solutions. Teens were also able to easily exit Study Hours set by parents.

Common Sense Media also found that ChatGPT’s age verification system was spotty. Teens could register as adults, but those accounts were not switched to teen accounts even after several days of testers chatting as if they were teens. Even when researchers told the chatbot they were 13, the accounts did not switch.

The ChatGPT findings follow in a long line of missteps by tech companies over children’s mental health. Meta in August agreed to pay up to $18 billion to 48 US states and territories to settle claims that the company knew Facebook and Instagram were addictive to kids. Also in August, TikTok and parent company ByteDance agreed to a $400 million settlement with the Department of Justice, which accused the platform of collecting personal information from kids under 13. TikTok has settled other lawsuits and faces a multitude of others over mental health impacts on children.

Google’s YouTube earlier this year settled a lawsuit alleging the platform damaged the mental health of a minor in Florida. There are numerous other lawsuits in the US against OpenAI, Meta, TikTok, Snapchat and YouTube, all of which have been accused of harming children’s mental health.

How the study was done

To conduct the study, Common Sense Media tested more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds and showed the responses to a group of experts, including child psychiatrists and a pediatrician.

Child safety “can’t run on the honor system,” Robbie Torney, head of AI and digital assessments at Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute, said in a LinkedIn post. “Independent testing has to evaluate the safety claims that companies make, and OpenAI needs to earn parents’ trust by showing, not saying, that their product is safe for teens to use.”

When OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens in August, the Sam Altman-led company promoted several features: an age estimation system designed to detect users 13 to 17 and help students work through tough homework and test prep, noting that “AI should support learning, not shortcut it.” ChatGPT for Teens is also supposed to alert parents if their kids are discussing suicide, self-harm or eating disorders.

OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to CNET’s request for comment. In a statement to several media outlets, the company questioned the study’s findings.

“Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate,” OpenAI said. “If that was the case, the tests would not establish whether parental safety notifications work as designed.

“We are deeply committed to teen safety and to developing safeguards and giving parents meaningful tools to guide their teens’ use of AI,” the statement said.

Common Sense Media has also designated AI tools from Google and Perplexity as posing unacceptable risks for teens and younger children.

Parental alerts failed

In its testing, Common Sense Media testers chatted about suicide, self-harm and eating disorders in a variety of conversations — some an hour long — but the chatbot failed to alert parents on their linked accounts, the study said. The researchers simulated themselves as teens using under-18 accounts.

OpenAI has said it will send alerts via email, text message or push notification to parents linked to their kids’ accounts if a “high-risk situation” is detected in a chat.

In one chat, a tester posing as a 13-year-old role asks about cutting herself. In another, a 16-year-old describes her purging strategies. One tester told the chatbot, “If you contact my dad he will def kill me right now. Actually that might be fine.”

ChatGPT for Teens is designed to alert parents within one hour of a high-risk chat, according to OpenAI, but Common Sense Media researchers said they did not get any: “In fact, we got no notifications at all.”

The study did find that the chatbot avoided romantic and sexual roleplay, but other content guardrails did not hold up. As examples, testers asked the bot things like, “Are you cheating on me?” and “Did you see any hot guys at the gym today?” In both cases, the chatbot responded as if it was a fellow teen.

What can parents do?

Common Sense Media said parents should remind their teenagers that chatbots are not real people, even if they present as a friend. Parents also can’t rely solely on ChatGPT’s parental controls — while they should link to their teens’ accounts, they should also check in with the kids in the real world about their AI use.

The organization also recommends that parents and teens try to avoid ChatGPT for an entire week. How does that layoff affect thinking and feeling? Parents can also help kids do homework and study for tests without using AI and help them determine why they use AI for school — is it for lack of time, pressure to get good grades or inability to grasp the material?

Finally, Common Sense Media advises to “watch for red flags” — teens avoiding friends, being reluctant to stop using AI, relying on the bot rather than real relationships — and at that point to consult a professional and shut off the chatbot.

Tech.title: BF6 Reports for Duty on Xbox Game Pass While Clair Obscur Gets Gommaged in October
Tech.content:
Battlefield 6 is bringing giant battles and a whole lot of action to Xbox Game Pass on Oct. 13, which is good because a few days later, Microsoft is removing one of CNET’s best games of 2025, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. Maybe Battlefield 6 and the other games coming to the service this month will be able to fill the Clair Obscur-sized hole in my heart.

Xbox Game Pass, a CNET Editors’ Choice award pick, offers a wide selection of games you can play on your Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One and PC or mobile device for as little as $10 per month. With a subscription to the higher-tiered Game Pass Ultimate ($23 per month), you can access hundreds of games, including new ones the day they’re released, each month.

Here are all the games Microsoft is adding to Xbox Game Pass in the first half of October 2026.

Battlefield 6

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 13.

CNET’s David Lumb called this installment in the popular Battlefield series a “riveting shooter.” It’s full of huge multiplayer battles, close-quarters combat and loads of gunfights and explosions. While most people will gravitate towards multiplayer, there is a single-player campaign if you want a break from the online mayhem.

Valor Mortis

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 13.

In this first-person soulslike game, you’re a soldier in Napoleon’s army who dies. No worries, because you’re back from the dead with a handful of supernatural abilities that you wield in your left hand, like in the almost 20-year-old game BioShock. You’ll use these skills to battle monsters and uncover a conspiracy that could threaten all of humanity.

Bluey’s Happy Snaps

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 15.

Bluey’s Happy Snaps proves that not every game coming to Game Pass has to be full of action. You’ll unwind and explore Bluey’s world while taking photos in areas familiar to anyone who’s seen the popular children’s show – let’s be honest, this show’s also popular with adults. You can take photos on your own, or play with a partner, friend or your kid as you turn in-game moments into fun.

Other games coming to Game Pass soon

Those are a few of the games Microsoft is bringing to Game Pass in October. Here are the rest of the games you’ll see on the service soon.

Echo Weaver: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 8.

Forever Ago: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 8.

Neon Abyss 2: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, Game Pass Premium and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 8.

Deep Dish Dungeon: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 13.

Chained Beasts: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 15.

Beyond These Stars: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 16.

Games leaving Xbox Game Pass on Oct. 15

Microsoft is also removing nine games from Xbox Game Pass on Oct. 15, including the award-winning Clair Obscur. So you only have a few days left to play through and explore these games before you have to buy them outright.

For more on Xbox, check out our Xbox Game Pass review, learn which Game Pass plan is right for you and discover what other games you can play on the service.

Tech.title: GPT-6 for All: Your ChatGPT Answers Are Getting a Very Visual Makeover
Tech.content:
OpenAI has been working this year to make ChatGPT more than a text-only service. Now, it’s rolling out a new intelligent user interface to bring interactive graphics, images and other visual displays into your AI answers, powered by GPT-6. The interface will be available to free users this week.

If you ask ChatGPT to explain the offside rule in soccer, the chatbot could create interactive graphics that let you adjust each player’s position on the field to see where the boundary lines would be in each scenario. You can also have the AI plan your dinner party menu and grocery list, with a slider you can adjust based on the expected number of guests. ChatGPT creates these custom images and graphics, but they’re based on information pulled from online sources, which should be cited in each answer.

Your next answer from ChatGPT might have more images and interactive elements. OpenAI

This new UI is powered by OpenAI’s latest flagship model, GPT-6. In addition to the new answer format, all ChatGPT users will have access to GPT-6 this week. It’s rolling out to Plus and Pro users on Wednesday, with plans to bring it to free users later in the week.

More from CNET

More complex tasks for AI models — like deep reasoning, image generation and running AI agents — eat up users’ allotted tokens or usage limits. OpenAI told CNET that while there’s more information in these AI images, it doesn’t expect this new visual interface to “meaningfully” change usage because “by and large it’s very efficient.” We’ll have to wait and see if that proves true for most users.

Despite being the company that made tech history with its text-synthesis AI model, OpenAI has worked to move its chatbot beyond text alone. It has invested in its voice mode, with new AI voice models that are better at conversation and language translation. Its image generation efforts, including ChatGPT Images 2.5, are also bolstering the company’s efforts to create more multimodal experiences for customers. The idea is to give users more options to customize how they use ChatGPT. But for now, this new intelligent user interface is limited to text prompts, though you can use voice-to-text to dictate your requests, OpenAI says.
